When the app has the graph open, it answers these commands. With no app holding the graph, a read or write command automatically starts `tine serve GRAPH` in the background. You can also run that command yourself in a terminal; it owns the graph without opening a window, takes a launch snapshot unless the newest backup zip is less than 6 hours old (see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]]), and exits after 30 idle minutes. This keeps scripted edit/restart loops from filling the backup slots. A future-dated zip does not suppress a snapshot.

Settings → **Journals** → **Journal date format** controls the display titles and how new `[[date]]` titles are written (saved to `:journal/page-title-format`, traveling with the graph). The choices match Logseq’s built-in formats, including weekday and `yyyy年MM月dd日` titles. `E`, `EE`, and `EEE` show abbreviated weekdays (such as `Fri`); `EEEE` shows the full name (`Friday`). Graphs using the older `:date-formatter` setting are also supported: `:journal/page-title-format` takes precedence when both are present, and opening a graph keeps the legacy setting untouched. A hand-edited format may use pattern parts Tine does not support, such as quoted text (`'w'`) or week numbers (`ww`): when today's journal shows the `config.edn` queries, a note above them names the setting, the pattern and those parts. Tine does not interpret them as Logseq does, so such journal titles or file names may differ from Logseq's, but it renames and rewrites nothing. It renames no files: journal *file* names are untouched and existing journals keep working. If some journal files are named after their title instead of their date, their days look empty; Settings → **Backups & recovery** lists them under **Journal files named by title** with a **Rename to date names** button, which never runs on its own. For files, duplicate days, and the on-disk layout in general, see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

A query runs only if Tine can read every clause of it. If any clause is outside the supported subset (a `:result-transform` other than Logseq's default priority sort, an unsupported input, a rule Tine does not know), the whole query is refused: a notice names the clauses Tine could not run and shows no results, because an answer to part of a query would be wrong. String page/tag inputs and numeric or relative date windows are supported; [[Reference/Tine query model]] lists the exact shapes.
[[Reference/Tine query model]] — every way a query's answer can differ from Logseq's, and why.

A part Tine does not understand refuses the whole query: it never runs half of it, because a partial answer could both add and hide blocks. A `:result-transform` function (other than Logseq's default priority sort), authored rules or an unsupported input is such a part. Common page/tag string inputs and numeric or relative date windows run; [[Reference/Tine query model]] lists the supported shapes.

**If Tine crashes or quits while a page cannot be saved,** that page's unsaved text is kept in Tine's app data (never in your graph). On the next start Tine puts it back on the page and saves it, and a message names those pages: “Recovered unsaved edits … — Tine is saving them”. If the file changed on disk in the meantime, the page shows the changed-on-disk banner instead (see [[Reference/Troubleshooting and recovery]]), so nothing is written over unseen. Text that saved normally is not kept there. Crash-recovery copies from an older Tine are left untouched as a backup; a message names their file once.

A labelled page link such as [read the welcome]([[Welcome to Tine]]) shows your words while opening the page. External `[label](https://…)` links are ordinary Markdown, bare URLs and emails autolink, and **Mod+L** inserts a link around the selection. `http`, `https` and `mailto` links open in your browser or mail app. A `file:` link — `[Test](file:///home/you/report.odt)`, or `[Test](file://D:\test.txt)` on Windows — opens that file or folder in whatever application your system uses for it, on desktop; a file that is no longer there is reported instead of doing nothing. A file path is read from the graph folder, from any page or journal: `[report](files/report.pdf)` opens `files/report.pdf` inside the graph, while `[report](../files/report.pdf)` opens a file in the sibling `files` folder outside the graph. Parent steps such as `../../` are preserved. Absolute paths such as `/home/you/report.pdf` and `D:\notes\report.pdf` also open through the same desktop file opener as `file:` links. These links look ordinary and show the resolved path on hover. Use `[spaced](<../files/my file.txt>)` for spaces. Links into the graph's assets folder keep Logseq's established graph asset route. Opening local files is available on desktop only, including for `file:` URLs; Android and iOS report the refusal. Tine does not rewrite links when you move files or graphs. A link to another app, such as `zotero://…`, `obsidian://…` or `shortcuts://…` on iOS, first asks whether to open it, showing the whole link, and then opens it in that app. `javascript:` and `data:` links never open.

children.raw: A **formula column** is an extra column whose value Tine works out for you from the other columns in the row. You never type the result — Tine recomputes it live, shows it on screen, and never writes it back onto your bullets. Open the same file in Logseq and you just see ordinary bullets with a harmless `tine.formula.*` property.

blocks.raw: # Formulas

children.raw:
Sketch the outline
hours:: 2
done:: true

Write the first draft
hours:: 5
done:: false
The **plan** column is a formula. Tine reads `hours` from each row and shows *focus block* or *quick task* — you never type it, and it updates the moment `hours` changes.

blocks.raw:
## A formula in action
tine.view:: table
tine.fields:: task=text;hours=number;done=checkbox
tine.formula.plan:: if(hours > 3, "focus block", "quick task")

children.raw: 1. Make a table (see [[Features/Sheets]]) with at least one field to compute from, for example a `hours=number` column.
2. **Right-click a table column header** — or right-click the table body / open its **⋮** menu — and choose **Add formula…**. Give it a short lowercase name like `plan`.
3. The **visual builder** opens. You build the value by clicking *faces* — no syntax to memorize. Press **Save** and a read-only column appears, filling in live.
4. To change it later, right-click the formula column and choose **Edit formula…**.

blocks.raw: ## Add one yourself

children.raw: **Field** — one of your own columns (or type a custom field name).
**Formula** — another formula column on the same table, shown as `formula.<name>`.
**Literal** — a fixed number, a bit of text, or **True** / **False** / **Empty**.
**Function** — `if condition`, `is empty`, `now`, `today`.
**Transform** — tweaks like *lowercase*, *trim*, *round*, *year*, *format date*, *length*.
**Value face** — click it to open a picker with these sections:
**IF / THEN / ELSE** — pick the **if condition** function on any value to branch: *IF* a condition *THEN* one value *ELSE* another value.
**Condition** — compare two values with an operator (`=`, `≠`, `<`, `≤`, `>`, `≥`), and join several with **AND** / **OR**.

blocks.raw: ## The building blocks

children.raw: The **`</> raw`** button at the top-right of the editor switches from clickable faces to a plain text box, where you can type the expression yourself — for example `hours * 2` or `if(hours > 3, "focus block", "quick task")`. The chips below insert your fields, other formulas, and built-in functions at the cursor. Flip **Builder** back on whenever the text is something the faces can show again.

blocks.raw: ## `</> raw` — type it directly

children.raw: The visual builder handles **one level**: a single IF/THEN/ELSE, simple comparisons, and a value that is at most one arithmetic step of two simple values (like `hours * 2`).

Anything more nested — a formula inside a THEN branch, or arithmetic of arithmetic like `(hours + extra) * 2` — shows up as a small raw box instead of pretty faces. Use **`</> raw`** to type those directly; they still evaluate exactly the same, they just do not get a visual face.
Formula values are **read-only** and are never saved onto your rows, so they always reflect the current data and round-trip cleanly back to Logseq.

blocks.raw: ## Honest limits

children.raw: 1. Start from a table with a numeric or enum field.
2. Right-click the column header and choose **Add/Edit formula**.
3. Build the value from the faces — pick a field, add a comparison, wrap it in IF / THEN / ELSE.
4. Use the `</> raw` toggle when you would rather type the expression, such as `hours * 2`.
5. What you should see: a read-only computed column whose values evaluate live and are never written onto the rows.

blocks.raw: ### Create one yourself — formula

children.raw: Open a PDF that lives in your graph's `assets/` (or drop one in). On desktop it opens as a tab in a companion pane, keeping your notes visible. On a phone it opens in the same one-pane history.
Opening and reading a PDF changes no graph files. Its highlight sidecar and notes page are created when you first highlight or annotate; existing highlights and notes stay available.
**Select text** in the PDF to highlight it; click a highlight again to change its color.

Hold **Shift** while dragging a rectangle on Linux or Windows, or **Command** on macOS, then choose a color to clip a figure or equation as an image highlight. Dismissing the color chooser writes nothing.
Use the reader toolbar to choose a persistent **Light**, **Warm**, or **Dark** page theme, and open **Outline** to navigate a PDF's nested table of contents.

Zoom, find text, and jump to a page from the toolbar. **Ctrl/Cmd + wheel** or a touchpad pinch zooms around the pointer. On a touchscreen, pinch with two fingers to zoom around their midpoint; use one finger to scroll. Your page and zoom are restored when you reopen the PDF. At high zoom, only visible page regions are rendered sharply.

On desktop, choose **Open another view** in the reader's **⋯** menu to read two parts of the same PDF side by side. Each view keeps its own page and zoom; a highlight made, recolored or removed in one appears in the other at once.
On a phone, select text or long-press a highlight to open its annotation actions.

Every highlight becomes a **block** on a notes page named after the PDF, so you can write underneath it, link it, and reference it like any other bullet — and each note jumps straight back to its spot in the document.

An area highlight shows its clipped image on that notes page, in a `((block reference))`, and in an embed. Right-click the rectangle and choose **Copy ref**, then paste into another page to cite the image. Click the image to open the PDF at that highlight. A missing image stays as an asset placeholder until it arrives through sync.

If the highlight file changes outside Tine, choose **Keep mine** to merge your edits or **Use disk version** to discard them. If the disk highlight file cannot be read, **Discard my changes** asks for confirmation, clears only your local highlight edits, and leaves the disk file untouched; an unused local area image may remain.
If an area image cannot be cleaned up after a highlight saves, choose **Retry cleanup** in the PDF viewer. Closing or switching graphs waits until that cleanup succeeds.
It's how you turn a paper into linked, searchable notes without ever leaving Tine.
For the end-to-end path from dropping a PDF in to quoting its passages, see [[Workflows/Research a document]].

blocks.raw: # PDF annotation

children.raw: 1. Put a PDF in your graph's `assets/` folder, or drop it into a page.
2. Open the PDF from its asset link. On desktop, its tab can be moved into another pane or split. On a phone, use **Back** to return to the page with the link.
3. Select text to create a highlight, or hold **Shift** (Linux/Windows) or **Command** (macOS) and drag a rectangle for an area highlight, then choose its color.
4. Write notes under the generated highlight blocks.
5. What you should see: each highlight is a normal block that links back to the exact PDF location.

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: Tine plugins are capability-limited WebAssembly guests. They are **not Logseq or Obsidian plugins** and cannot use those apps' plugin APIs.

Plugins cannot directly access the DOM, Tauri, files, processes, the network, or arbitrary graph paths. Tine owns the commands, slash actions, decorations, settings controls, and any narrowly authorized block edit that a plugin can request.
[[Workflows/Extend Tine]] walks the hands-on install → review → enable → disable path; this page remains the detailed reference.

blocks.raw: # Plugins

children.raw: Open **Settings → Plugins → Browse** for the signed community catalogue. Each entry shows its source, supported platforms, declared capabilities, publication review, and a digest-verified safety report.
Choose **Install** on a compatible entry. Local developers can instead choose **Install a local package** and select its `manifest.json` and `.wasm` together.

Tine supports plugin API 0.2 and 0.3. API 0.3 adds the `color` setting type for host-rendered color choices. The catalogue offers only versions your Tine can run, so an older Tine keeps the last compatible version of a plugin.
Every version is installed disabled. Open **Installed**, review its identity and capabilities, then enable it explicitly.

blocks.raw: ## Browse and install

children.raw: Open a plugin's **Details** or **Settings** page to change its host-rendered options. Plugins receive only validated scalar values; they do not draw their own settings UI.
Disable a plugin at any time without removing it. **Uninstall** removes only that app-local package version and never changes your graph or notes.
Signed revocations are checked before saved plugins start. A revoked version stays disabled even when the live catalogue is temporarily unavailable.

**Bullet threading** highlights the focused block's continuous ancestor path even with **All nested outlines** selected. **Active ancestry only** keeps ordinary guides on unrelated branches; **All nested outlines** ends each thread at its last child's elbow. Its **Settings** offer line thickness from 0–10 px (0 hides the lines), a custom color (empty uses the current theme accent), and optional **Color by hierarchy level**, off by default, repeating every four levels. Disabling the plugin restores normal guides without changing your notes.
**Active ancestry only** emphasizes the edited block's connectors in the theme accent color by default, following the path through its ancestors.

blocks.raw: ## Control a plugin

children.raw: Declarative themes live under **Settings → Appearance → Themes**, separately from executable plugins. They contain validated colors and may select bounded Tine-owned presentation styles rather than running code: editorial reading type, a larger journal header, or a compact Today task count. **Style** (typography, journal headings and other presentation) and **Color scheme** (Default, Nord, Solarized, Gruvbox, Soft, or an installed package's colors) are chosen independently, so you can keep one package's style with another palette. They contain no scripts, selectors, imports, downloaded fonts, or remote assets, and no theme ever reads or writes your graph.

A Today summary, when selected, is rendered by Tine from the journal page already on screen: it counts open task markers there and calls the `DOING`, `NOW`, `STARTED`, and `IN-PROGRESS` subset “in progress.” The theme receives neither those tasks nor a query interface.
A selected theme remains subordinate to your graph's `logseq/custom.css`, so your own CSS still wins; [[Workflows/Customize Tine's look]] explains that file and the stable `--tine-*` tokens.

blocks.raw: ## Themes

children.raw: 1. Open **Settings → Plugins → Browse**.
A command or slash action reads only the block you run it on. A decoration sees the text of visible blocks only if the plugin declares `graph.read.visible`.
2. Inspect a plugin's capabilities and safety report, then install it.
3. Switch to **Installed**, open its details, and enable it.
4. What you should see: only the host-owned command, slash action, or decoration that the plugin declared; disabling it removes that behavior while leaving your graph readable.
For authoring, packaging, API versioning, and registry submission, see the [developer guide](https://github.com/martinkoutecky/tine/blob/master/docs/plugins/README.md).

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: A **query block** is a live list of every block (or page) in your graph that matches a filter. Write it once with `{{query …}}`; Tine keeps the results current as you edit, and the file stays an ordinary Logseq query block. Where an answer can differ from Logseq's, [[Reference/Tine query model]] says how and why.

blocks.raw: # Queries

children.raw: Queries refresh when an edit can affect their results. Queries over links, graph-wide tag targets or the property registry wait until you pause typing for 1.5 seconds, then read the latest saved publication. Continuous typing keeps the last answer visible until that pause.
While a query refreshes, its previous results stay visible, including in **Scheduled & Deadline** and other journal sections. A journal section with no results hides once the refresh finishes.
Every open task in this graph:
{{query (task TODO DOING)}}

blocks.raw: ## A query in action

children.raw: 1. Type `/query` and choose **Query**, or write `{{query (task TODO)}}` yourself. The slash command opens the query sheet on its empty condition list; press **+ Add condition** to choose the first field.

2. At rest a query block shows its title, result count and results. Click the title to rename it. Fold the query block's bullet to hide its results, as in Logseq; the small arrow in the query's header is the same fold, so clicking either one shows in both and is saved as the block's ordinary `collapsed::` property. A query written with `{:collapsed? true}` starts folded, and unfolding it is saved as `collapsed:: false`. Hover over or focus the query to reveal the pencil (**Edit query**) and **⋯**; on touch screens both are always visible. The pencil, or **⋯ → Edit**, opens the inline builder; **View** for display choices, or **Edit as text** for TQL. Advanced datalog keeps its original block-text editor.

3. The sheet says what the query finds — **Find blocks ▾ where …** — and shows one row per condition: a handle to drag it (or move it with the arrow keys), a box to select it, the field, operator and value, a switch that turns it off without removing it, a ⋮ for the rest, and an × to remove it. **+ Add condition** adds one.

4. Tick two or more rows in the same list and press **Group selected ▾** to make them one **All of**, **Any of** or **None of** group. A group's ⋮ **Ungroup** puts its rows back. Groups are set off by a heavier rail and a divider, and a query whose top level is **Any of** says so above its rows.

Drag a row's handle onto another group to move that condition into it; a group left with one condition dissolves into the list around it. The **Task** field has an **Any status** choice (every task marker), and **In a journal page** keeps only blocks that sit on a journal day. Scheduled and Deadline ranges read in plain words (*Scheduled: next 7 days*), and nothing the builder wrote is labelled *advanced*.

While the inline builder is open, the real results below it follow every change you make, before you save. The builder stays in the outline, and only the latest answer is shown. A new empty query says **Add a condition to see results.** instead of listing every page. Removing the last condition returns to that same empty state, even if a sort remains.

5. Press **Done** (at the bottom right of the builder) or **Escape** to close the inline editor; the title, count and results remain. The results show as blocks grouped by page, or as pages when the query finds pages; choose **⋯ → View → Search**, **List**, **Table** or **Board** to change how they are shown — the matches stay the same. Matches that share a parent show that parent's breadcrumb once. A block that matches directly under another block that also matches is not a result of its own, as in Logseq: it shows inside its parent (the List draws the parent's children), and the count, Table and Board list the parent only; a match under a block that does not match is its own result. Search and List page results show the page title with the page's properties as text underneath; press the pencil beside a result to edit those properties in the page's property panel (the change is written to the page's file, and the row updates). In **Find blocks ▾** choose **Pages and blocks** to see both answers of the same conditions, Pages above Blocks; the builder then reads *Find pages and blocks*, the Blocks section follows the List, Table or Board you picked, and a section that a **Sample** cut short says *More pages match than are shown* (or *blocks*) (stored as `tine.result-kinds:: pages-and-blocks`; Logseq ignores that property and reads the query as before).

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: Renaming keeps the current results visible. An unsaved text draft leaves the results unchanged until **Save query text**. Saving keeps focus in the editor; **Escape** or **Done** closes it and returns focus to the query's **⋯** menu.

**Open search tab** in Ctrl+K search for a friendly search tab with separate **Pages** and **Blocks** sections. An alias result opens its owner page. Choose **Pages match** to search names and aliases, containing block text, or both; saving that search writes `tine.page-match-scope:: content` or `both` beside the ordinary query block.

Use each section's **Display** control independently. Sort orders all matching Pages or Blocks before that section's limit; Sample keeps the first N of that order, separately for each section. A Pages board groups adjacent results by its chosen field while keeping their sort order. A Pages table can show authored page properties as columns while Blocks use a different view. **Save page** stores the choices as `tine.page-*` and `tine.block-*` query block properties.

The query text is hidden by default: press **Edit as text** in **⋯** to open the **query text** box: the same query the rows show, written in Tine's text query language (`@block` or `@page`, then conditions joined with `and`, `or`, `not`). Type in it and Tine re-reads it as you go; press **Save query text** (bottom right) to make it the block's query; **Cancel** beside it drops unsaved text.
When Tine cannot read the text it names the problem, and a **Show me** button selects the part of the text it points at when it knows where that is.
A `{{tine-query …}}` block holds this language directly and runs like any other query block.

blocks.raw: ## Query text

children.raw: Some queries have no `{{query}}` spelling — scheduled/deadline date windows, grouping, column totals, typed comparisons. When you save one, Tine renames the block's macro from `query` to `tine-query` and moves the view choices into `tine.*` properties on the same block.
For a scheduled window, use `{{tine-query @block scheduled between today and '+7d'}}`; use `deadline` for a deadline window.

To list the blocks that mention a day after today, use `{{tine-query any(direct_refs, day > today)}}`. It finds a block that links or tags a journal day, such as `[[Oct 22nd, 2026]]`, `#[[Oct 22nd, 2026]]` or `[[2026-10-22]]`, whether or not that day has a journal file yet. Only the block's own links count, not those of its parent, and a `SCHEDULED:` or `DEADLINE:` date is not a mention (use `scheduled` or `deadline` for those). Combine it like any condition, for example `task = 'TODO' and any(direct_refs, day between today and '+7d')`. Inside `any(direct_refs, …)` a link has `name`, `journal` (true for a journal day) and `day`. *Today* is your computer's local day when the query runs. Logseq ignores scheduled/deadline date windows in `{{query}}`, so Tine shows a cue and refuses to run those blocks as written. Click **Convert** to keep the same date-window meaning in `{{tine-query …}}`; the change can be undone.
A notice under the query says so: **This query now uses Tine features Logseq can't read.** **Undo that change** puts the block back to exactly the bytes it had; **Keep it** dismisses the notice.

blocks.raw: ## When a query needs Tine features

children.raw: Tine's query text can follow links between pages. These are page conditions (`@page`), and Logseq's `{{query}}` has no spelling for them, so a query that uses one is saved as `{{tine-query …}}`.

`any(links, …)` — pages that link to a page matching the condition; `any(linked_by, …)` — pages linked to by one. A link is exactly what the **Linked References** panel shows: `{{tine-query @page and any(links, name = 'Reading list')}}` lists the same pages as Reading list's panel. `every(…)` and `none(…)` work too: `{{tine-query @page and none(linked_by, true)}}` lists pages nothing links to.

`near(…, k)` — the pages matching the first condition plus every page within `k` link steps of them, both directions: `{{tine-query @page and near(name = 'Project', 1)}}` is Project, the pages it links to and the pages that link to it. Add `'out'` to follow links forward only, or `'in'` to follow them backwards only: `near(name = 'Paper', 3, 'out')`. `k` is a whole number; `0` means the matching pages alone.

The default, `'both'`, is the pages within `k` steps forward together with the pages within `k` steps backward. Each path keeps one direction, so it is **not** every page within `k` steps when you may switch direction along the way (what other graph tools call "both"): a page that merely links to the same page as Project is not near Project. Write two `near(…)` conditions joined with `or` to combine other shapes.

A path goes through every page it reaches, journal days included. To leave pages out of the results, add a condition: `near(name = 'Project', 2) and journal = false`. `near` takes at most three arguments; a fourth is reserved for a later version and is an error today.

A page that is only linked to, with no file of its own, counts as a page here: `near(name = 'idea', 1, 'in')` lists the pages that link to it. Renaming a page also updates the names inside `near(…)` and `any(links, …)` of a share or export definition.

blocks.raw: ## Links between pages

children.raw: `(task TODO DOING)` — blocks with one of these task markers; `(priority A)` — by priority.

`(task)` with no markers and `(priority)` with no levels add no condition, exactly as in OG Logseq: `(and (task) [[x]])` finds what `[[x]]` finds, and a query with no other condition shows nothing. A note on the query says so and offers **Open tasks** (every block that has a task marker except `DONE`, `CANCELED`, or `CANCELLED`, so `WAITING`, `STARTED` and `IN-PROGRESS` count), **Any task** (every task marker), or **A, B or C**; each rewrites the clause to an explicit list and saves the block like any query edit. The visual builder always writes explicit marker lists such as `(task TODO)` or `(task DONE)`, which keep their usual meaning.
`[[Page]]`, `(page-ref Page)`, `#tag` — blocks that reference a page.

`(page "Page")` — blocks on a page; `(namespace Project)` — blocks on the pages directly under a namespace (`Project/Alpha`, but not `Project/Alpha/Beta`; an advanced query's `namespace` clause matches every depth).

`(property status active)`, `(page-property type book)`, `(page-tags public)` — by block or page properties and tags. `(all-page-tags)` lists the pages that some page uses as a tag. A page-level filter returns pages, not blocks.

`(between -7d today)` — journal blocks in a date range. Dates are `today`, `yesterday`, `tomorrow`, `2026-01-31`, a journal title like `[[Jan 31st, 2026]]`, or an offset like `-7d`, `+2w`, `-1m`, `+1y` (lowercase units, at most 10,000 years).

`(between created-at -7d now)` — blocks whose `created-at::` (or `created_at::`) property falls in the range; `last-modified-at` works the same. The first bound is included and the second is not, and the two may be given in either order. Besides the date forms, these bounds also take `now` (the current moment) and offsets in hours `h` and minutes `n` such as `+36h` or `-90n`; day-based offsets and `h`/`n` count from the start of today, not from the current time. A bound that is not one of these makes the whole query invalid.

`(sort-by priority asc)`, `(sample 10)` — order the results (by `priority`, `page`, `scheduled`, `deadline` or any property; like Logseq, the order is descending unless you write `asc`), or keep a random N of the matches (chosen before sorting, so each run can show a different few). A query made only of these directives, with no condition, shows nothing. Without a sort, results are grouped by page: journal days newest first, then the other pages by name.

A bare word or quoted text finds the raw block text, including property lines and drawers. Query text is case-sensitive and accent-sensitive, like Logseq: `Alpha` does not find `alpha`, and `cafe` does not find `café`. TQL `content match` uses search syntax with this same exact matching; `content like` is exact too. Ctrl+K, search tabs and in-page Find still ignore case and remove accents unless `:feature/enable-search-remove-accents? false` is configured.
The simple query language is Logseq's. Combine filters with `(and …)`, `(or …)` and `(not …)`:

Explicit `#tags` and `[[page references]]` are separate values even without commas, in page and block properties: `tags:: #eng #exec #founder` matches `(page-tags eng)` and `(property tags eng)`. `#[[multi word]]` is one tag. In `tags:: #a plain text #b`, the plain text is also a value; in a custom property only the explicit references become values. Quoting the whole value keeps it literal.

Property values ignore case: `(property status Done)` also finds `status:: done`. Commas split values only for `tags`, `alias`/`aliases`, and keys in `:property/separated-by-commas` in `logseq/config.edn`. Each comma item of those properties is also its own page link where the property is shown. Other values stay whole: `(property list "Foo, Bar")` finds `list:: Foo, Bar`, while `(property list Foo)` does not.
A block property on the query block itself can set the view: `tine.sort:: priority desc` and `tine.sample:: 10` win over the same directive in the query text.

blocks.raw: ## Simple queries

children.raw: Open **⋯ → View** to choose Search, List, Table or Board; add ordered sort fields and table columns, choose grouping, add count/sum/average summaries, or set a sample limit. The column picker offers only columns found in the current results, starts with the visible default columns checked and offers **Select all** and **Select none**. A saved column choice stays intact when that column disappears from the results; its checkbox returns when the column appears again. Choosing **Page** shows each block's owning page. The controls save on the query block as existing `tine.*` properties; `tine.fields::` remains the table's schema and is not changed by a column choice.
Scheduled and Deadline conditions offer **>**, **>=**, **=**, **<** and **<=**, with today, yesterday, tomorrow or today±N days (for example `+5d`). The Rust query engine decides which results match.
Task checkboxes in Search, Table and Board edit the original block through its ordinary save path. Click a table title or board card to open its source. Board columns scroll when they cannot fit.

In List view, **⋯ → Collapse all / Expand all** is one toggle that folds the result trees together. This writes the source blocks' ordinary `collapsed::` property and can be undone. **⋯ → Search** opens the same query in a Search tab.

blocks.raw: ## Display and property types

children.raw: Drag a List result's bullet to move that source block into your outline. Hold **Alt** when dropping one block to insert a block reference instead, leaving the source in place. The reference is inserted only after the source's ID has been saved. The same Alt gesture works on an ordinary outline bullet; a selection of several blocks still moves together.

**⋯ → Copy results** opens the same **Copy / export as…** dialog as an outline selection, with Text, OPML and HTML options. Each result tree sits under its page title; journals use their date titles, and descendants keep their hierarchy. A descendant already inside a selected parent is copied once.

In a Search tab, press **Select results**, tick the results you want (or **Select all / Select none**), then **Copy results** for the same dialog and format. Selection actions stay above the result rows, which keep their page or block labels. Press **Select results** again or **Done** to leave selection mode.

External changes and structural edits refresh the query after pending changes settle. Until then, old results stay read-only. A task click, copy or bulk fold refuses the whole action when its selected results are no longer current; a notice asks you to run the query again. A block with a unique authored `id::` can still be resolved by that identity.

A query whose dates count from today (`today`, `yesterday`, `-7d`, `+7d`, a `:today` input) runs again by itself when the date changes, so a window left open overnight shows the new day's results; after the computer slept through midnight this happens when you return to the window. A query with no such date is not run again.

A saved Scheduled or Deadline comparison offers `>`, `<`, `=`, `≥` and `≤` in its operator menu, plus negation of the current comparison. **Is not set** tests an absent date in the date editor; it never means a negated date comparison.
**⋯ → Open in Search** opens the query in a Search tab. The view (List, Table or Board, with its display choices) and **Pages and blocks** travel with it; results still come from the Rust engine.
The full **All pages** view has a sortable **Backlinks** column: the number of referring blocks computed by the backend. All pages, Search and query blocks remain separate views.
Search and List page results show the page title and its properties as text; press the pencil beside a result to edit them. Table columns stay in the Table view.
Table titles are always shown and are listed as such in the column picker. **Select all / Select none** changes the other fields, preserving the meaning of existing column settings.

A grouped summary says **Grouped by** and names the field. Choose **⋯ → View → Group by → None** to remove grouping. When every result lacks that field, Tine shows the overall totals instead of a table containing only `(none)`. Opening View or choosing a summary does not choose a grouping field.

A query table's footer summarizes the query's **complete sample**, even when a table filter hides some rows. Sample limits the query before its totals are computed. Click a property total to choose **Count**, **Sum**, **Average**, or **None**; the choice is saved with the query's Display settings. Built-in columns such as Page and State have no property total. If statistics are unavailable, Tine leaves the total blank or shows why it is unavailable.

A Logseq query written with `{:table-view? true}`, `query-table:: true` on its block, or a trailing `table` (for example `{{query (task TODO) table}}`) keeps its own table: the block's `query-properties:: [:block :page :status]` chooses the columns and their order, and `query-sort-by:: status` with `query-sort-desc:: false` sets the starting sort (descending unless you write `false`). In **⋯ → View → Columns**, toggle Block, Page or a result property to save the choice in `query-properties::`, readable by Logseq. Clearing every column removes that property and restores the default columns, as in Logseq. Clicking a column heading re-sorts for as long as the page is open without changing the file. The List/Table toggle saves only `tine.view` and never adds `query-table`; an explicit `tine.view:: list` overrides an imported table choice.

The condition picker lists properties found in this graph with their observed type and the number of blocks or pages that carry them. A key found on both blocks and pages has separate choices for those scopes. You can type a key that has not appeared yet.

Beside a property condition, **declare type…** writes `tine.type:: number`, `date`, `checkbox`, `ref` or `text` on the page named for that property key. Select **list of** for multiple values, or remove the declaration. The badge distinguishes an observed type from a declared one and shows mismatches against a declaration.

blocks.raw: ## Copy or revisit results

children.raw: `{{query {:query [:find (pull ?b [*]) :where …]}}}` and `#+BEGIN_QUERY` blocks run a supported subset of Logseq's datalog: task markers, priority, page references, properties, page, namespace, page tags, scheduled/deadline and journal date ranges.

A query runs only if Tine can read every clause of it. If any clause is outside the supported subset (a `:result-transform` other than Logseq's default priority sort, an unsupported input, a rule Tine does not know), the whole query is refused: a notice names the clauses Tine could not run and shows no results, because an answer to part of a query would be wrong. String page/tag inputs and numeric or relative date windows are supported; [[Reference/Tine query model]] lists the exact shapes.
`:inputs [:current-page]` binds the page open in the focused pane, like Logseq: if no page is open it uses your configured home page, then today's journal. It is not the page the query block sits on.

blocks.raw: ## Advanced (datalog) queries

children.raw: **Query source could not be parsed** means the macro itself is damaged. Edit the block text to repair it; the visual builder becomes available once the source is readable. A query with a title such as `{{query (page-property tags gptpro) {:title "gptpro"}}}` needs all three final braces: one closes the title options and two close the macro.

If Tine cannot read part of a query, the block says so — **Tine didn't understand part of this query, so it returned no results** — followed by what it could not read. An empty list without that message means the query is valid and nothing matches yet.

An empty result offers **why empty?**: a table of the query's top-level conditions with how many rows each matches alone and how many the query would match without it, so the condition that emptied it stands out.
A query that would return more than 20,000 rows (or 32 MiB) is refused with a message instead of being cut short. Narrow it, or add `(sample N)`.

blocks.raw: ## When a query shows nothing

children.raw: **Share…** in a query's **⋯** menu (or its share icon) opens the share dialog with this query, reviews the pages it selects and exports them; the export is saved as a definition so it can be repeated. See [[Features/Share pages]].

Use **⋯ → Export…** on a query. Review the complete pages selected by the result, then choose an external folder. Tine creates a new named site there, with a read-only browser view and static HTML fallback. A block result publishes its whole owner page, so review those pages before continuing. The built-in Scheduled & Deadline section has no Export button.

In **Settings → Graph → Publish live site**, choose an external folder to publish pages marked `public:: true`. **Include all pages** is an explicit choice for a graph meant to be public; it still leaves out pages marked `public:: false`. The exported site can be served as ordinary static files.

blocks.raw: ## Publish a query

children.raw: A passing thought shouldn't make you switch windows. Bind a desktop shortcut and a small always-on-top capture box pops up over **any** app — with the full Tine editor — and files what you type straight into your graph. Tine doesn't even need to be focused.

blocks.raw: # Global quick-capture

children.raw: ![The quick-capture window — note the optional page-title field at the top](../assets/quick-capture.png)

blocks.raw: ## What it looks like

children.raw: **GNOME** — Settings → Keyboard → View and Customize Shortcuts → Custom Shortcuts → **+**. Command: `tine --capture`. Pick a key like **Super+N**.
**KDE** — System Settings → Shortcuts → Add → Command/URL. Command: `tine --capture`.
**Other desktops** — add a custom keyboard shortcut that runs `tine --capture`. Use the binary's full path if it isn't on your `PATH`.
Tine listens for a launch with the `--capture` flag, so bind a global keyboard shortcut in your desktop environment to run **`tine --capture`**:
Now press your shortcut from anywhere — the box appears, you type, and it's saved.

blocks.raw: ## Set it up (Linux, one time)

children.raw: If saving takes too long, your text stays in the capture box with a plain retry. Retry **File capture** to finish the same capture without adding it twice. Once that snapshot saves, its unchanged text is removed; additions stay for your next capture. If you rewrote earlier text, the message reminds you that the earlier capture is already saved. A changed title with no remaining body stays in the box with an **Add text** reminder; it is not silently cleared.

If the graph window reloads or switches graphs after taking your capture, but saving is unconfirmed, Tine keeps your text and reports that it may be in the previous graph. Check that graph before capturing it again. A delayed capture that never reached a graph is refused without that warning; retry to capture in the current graph. **Esc** hides an unconfirmed capture without clearing its text or retry identity; reopen the capture box to see it again. **Start a new capture** is offered when the graph took the earlier attempt but saving is uncertain: it keeps the text, so remove anything already saved before filing it again. This protects retries during the running app session; the scratch box does not survive quitting the app.
**Leave the title empty** → the text is appended to **today's journal**. This is the fast path: hotkey, type, done.

**Type a page title** (the field at the top of the window) → it's filed to that **page** instead, created if it doesn't exist yet. Perfect for "add this to my Reading notes" without leaving what you're doing.
It's the real editor in there: `[[` page links, `#` tags, `/` slash commands, and nested bullets all work.

Paste an image (a screenshot) or a copied file into the box and it is saved into your graph's `assets` folder, with a link in the captured bullet. Dragging files onto the capture box is not supported yet.

blocks.raw: ## Where your capture goes

children.raw: 1. Open your desktop environment's keyboard-shortcut settings.
2. Add a custom shortcut whose command is `tine --capture`.
3. Press the shortcut while another app is focused, then type a quick note.
4. Leave the title empty for today's journal, or type a page title to file it there.
5. What you should see: the capture box saves real Logseq bullets into your graph without switching windows.

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: By default **Enter** starts a new bullet and **Ctrl+Shift+Enter** files the capture (so you can jot several lines first). Prefer Enter-to-file? Open Settings and flip **Quick-capture: Enter key**.
If you unbind **Quick-capture: file to today's journal** in Keyboard Shortcuts, the capture box shows a **File capture** button so filing remains available without a key.

The box auto-grows as you type, and it keeps your draft if it loses focus. **Esc** clears an unsubmitted draft. After a refused filing, **Esc** keeps the text too; reopen the capture box to file it into the current graph. Filing clears only the text whose save was confirmed.

blocks.raw: ## Tune the Enter key

children.raw: Captures land in today's journal or on a page you name — [[Workflows/Capture and plan your day]] builds the rest of the daily flow on top. This capture window is a desktop feature. On Android and iOS, the share sheet, the **Quick capture** shortcut and iOS Shortcuts file to the same place: [[Reference/Platforms and mobile]] covers them and what each platform ships.

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Share a page, or the pages a query selects, in two ways. **Folder** writes a static site and read-only app into your graph folder. **Link** uploads an encrypted copy to a secret GitHub gist and gives you a link anyone can open in a browser. Both start from the same **Share** dialog and both leave a definition on the **Exports page**, so you can repeat or update them later.

In the read-only app or a quick-share link, use a bullet's fold arrow to expand or collapse its children without changing the graph. Your viewing choices last while browsing between pages; reloading restores the original folds.
The static HTML version starts with the original folds too. Click the arrow beside a folded bullet to open or close it; this also works with JavaScript turned off.

blocks.raw: # Share pages

children.raw: **Share** opens from the share icon in the top bar (in a narrow window it is **Share this page** in the **···** menu), the share icon beside a page title, **Share…** in a page's **⋯** menu and right-click menu, and **Share…** (or the share icon) on a query block. It shares the page you are looking at; from a query block it starts from that query.

Choose **This page** to share just that page, or **A query starting at this page** to pick the pages with the visual query builder (edit the query and the live preview shows which pages it selects). **This page and its neighbours** is listed as coming with graph queries.

The review lists the pages that will be shared and, separately, the selected pages that are left out: a page marked `public:: false` and the Exports page are never shared, and the review says which and why. It also says when the selection includes the page a query is written on. **Include the query text** is off, so readers see the pages and not the query.
Under **Where to share**, choose **Folder** or **Link**.

blocks.raw: ## Start a share

children.raw: **Folder** exports a static site and read-only app into `published-queries/<folder>/` in your graph, the same export as a query's **Export…**. You name the folder on the next step.

After a successful export Tine saves the selection as a definition so you can repeat it. From **This page** or a query you built in the dialog, it adds a query block with `tine.export:: <folder>` to the **Exports** page, which Tine creates on first use (marked `tine.exports:: true` and `public:: false`, with a block listing every definition; if you already have a page called Exports it uses Exports 2). From a query block you did not change, it adds `tine.export:: <folder>` to that block. Open **Share…** on a definition again and it shows the same selection. Nothing is exported again until you choose Export.

**Re-export** on a folder definition opens its review with **Replace** selected, using the same folder under `published-queries/`. Confirming keeps the previous export in recovery. There is no Delete action for folder exports.

blocks.raw: ## Share into a folder

children.raw: On Android and iOS, use **Link** and **Connect GitHub** just as on a computer; sharing a link does not require a desktop.

Choose **Link**, then **Connect GitHub** the first time. Tine asks for permission to create and delete gists; it only touches the shares it made. You enter a code on GitHub's device page; no password is typed into Tine. No GitHub account? On GitHub's sign-up page choose **Continue with Google**.

Review the pages and size, then choose **Create link**. The full source text of every shared page is included, including properties hidden from display, relative page paths, linked page names and attachment file names. Pages marked `public:: false`, hidden folders, the Exports page and other pages outside your selection are left out. Images and other files are not included. Edits after the preview require **Refresh**; creating a link shares the reviewed copy.

The key is in the link, after `#`. Anyone with the whole link can read the shared pages in a browser, without a GitHub account. Keep it private if the pages are private. GitHub receives encrypted text; tine.page's reader receives the key and plaintext. Both services see your network address when contacted, and GitHub sees the share's size and dates. The reader opens remote media only as links. Every shared page opens under a "User content · Shared by a Tine user" banner with a **Report abuse** link.
The graph records `tine.share:: <login>/<gist_id>` on the definition, without the key. The key stays on this device.

blocks.raw: ## Share pages with a link

children.raw: Choose **Re-share** on a share's query on the **Exports page**, or share that query again, to update the same link. Review **+N new / −M gone** and the changed page names before confirming; nothing is uploaded until then. GitHub keeps old revisions: re-sharing does not remove previously shared text. Readers may see the update after about five minutes. Without the key on this device, choose **Re-share as a new link**; the old share stays separate.

**Update all** beside the Exports page title prepares folder exports and quick shares together. Folder previews show the page count and pages left out, plus **+N new / −M gone** when the previous export's snapshot can be read; quick shares show **+N new / −M gone** and collapsible changed page names. Nothing is written or uploaded until you confirm. Updates run one after another, and each result is shown even if another export fails. Folder exports work even when quick share is off or disconnected. Definitions without a key on this device, pending shares and preparation failures are listed as skipped with a reason. Quick-share previews are held in memory up to a fixed total size (24 MB); if a very large batch exceeds it, the remaining shares are skipped with that reason and can be re-shared after this batch.

**Delete** removes the hosted gist; it cannot remove copies readers saved, forks, clones, caches or GitHub backups. Its link stops working within about 5 minutes (GitHub caches the file that long), and a definition the share added to the **Exports page** goes with it; a share made from your own query block only loses its `tine.share::` line. You can Delete from a share's query on the **Exports page**, after a confirmation, even when its key is on another device: connect the GitHub account that owns the share. **Forget** removes this device's key and record; it does not delete the gist. **Disconnect** removes this device's GitHub connection; revoke Tine's permission in GitHub's Applications settings if needed.

**Settings → Sharing** lists the links made on this device with **Copy link**, **Check**, **Delete** and **Forget**. **Check** asks GitHub whether an upload whose result was uncertain went through. **Find shares on GitHub** lists Tine shares in your account that this device has no record of; you can delete them, but cannot recover their keys. **Pending in this graph** lists query blocks marked `tine.share:: pending/…` (an upload that was not confirmed); **Check** finishes the ones this device recorded, and **Remove marker** clears one that no device is still uploading.

blocks.raw: ## Update, delete, and manage shares

children.raw: 1. Open a page and choose the share icon in the top bar.

2. Leave **This page** selected and choose **Folder**, then **Export to folder…** and name the folder. What you should see: a `published-queries/<folder>/` export and an **Exports** page with one definition.
3. Open the share dialog again, choose **Link**, and **Connect GitHub** (once). Review the pages and choose **Create link**.
4. Open the copied link in a private browser window. What you should see: the page, read-only, under the "User content" banner.
5. On the **Exports** page choose **Delete** on that share and confirm. What you should see: the definition disappears, and the link stops working within about five minutes.

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: Folder exports of a single query, including **Export…**, are described in [[Features/Queries]]. Exports of the whole graph, PDF and **Copy / export as…** are in [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Sheets turn ordinary outline branches into 2-D views — tables, boards, and grids. The same file still opens in Logseq as nested bullets with harmless `tine.*` properties.

Wide Markdown, Org and sheet tables stay centered on the text column and use the free space in their pane. They scroll horizontally only when wider than the pane; tables inside a sheet cell stay within that cell. A table in a query box or a sidebar item never leaves its box; the box scrolls it sideways instead. Long text cells wrap, while numbers stay on one line.
This page starts with the easiest path — viewing bullets you already have — and shows fields, formulas, and grids after.

blocks.raw: # Sheets

children.raw: Sheets never move your data: rows are child bullets, columns are their properties, cards are child bullets. Nothing is converted or copied.
Right-click a parent bullet and choose **Show children as → Grid** or **Table** — or type `/Grid`, `/Table`, or `/Board` on that block.
What Tine writes: plain block properties such as `tine.view:: table` on the view-owning block. Editing a sheet cell writes back into the underlying bullet, so the outline and the sheet always agree.
Formula columns derive values live (the *Typed reading list* below computes `effort` from `rating`); derived values are shown, never written onto the rows.

children.raw: 1. On an empty block, type `/Grid` and pick **Grid**. Tine seeds one editable cell — just start typing.

2. Grow it by its **edges**: hover the grid and click the **`+`** on the right edge for a new column, or the **`+`** on the bottom edge for a new row. Drag row or cell bullets to reshape it; the grid follows the tree.
3. Already have an outline? Right-click its parent bullet and choose **Show children as → Grid** (or run `/Grid` on that block) to turn the existing bullets into a grid in place.
4. What you should see: a live grid whose cells are still ordinary Logseq bullets.

children.raw: 1. On a block, type `/Table` and pick **Table** (or right-click an existing outline and choose **Show children as → Table**).
2. Use the ghost **+ Add row** and **+ Add column** buttons to build it out. Each row is a child bullet; each column is a property such as `owner::` or `estimate::`, edited right in the cells.
A field rename preserves query aggregate configuration too: bare count, average, repeated aggregate entries, and unrelated segments stay in their original order.

3. Right-click a children-backed column header or double-click its name to rename the field and its dependent filter, group, aggregate, and formula references together. Ambiguous or colliding names are refused.

Drag the narrow handle at a Table column's right edge to resize it. Double-click the handle to restore its automatic width. Tine stores widths by column identity in `tine.table-widths::`, so reordering columns keeps their sizes.
The **+ Add row** label stays at the visible edge when a wide table scrolls sideways. **Copy / export…** can produce HTML from the same table content.
4. Press **Tab** after editing a cell to commit its value and move to the next cell.
5. What you should see: each child bullet becomes a row, and properties become editable table columns.

6. Under the hood: the block carries `tine.view:: table` (with optional `tine.fields::` to type columns and `tine.col-aggregates:: prop:estimate=sum` to total a numeric column in the footer). The ghost buttons write these for you.
