children.raw: A quick tour of the things that aren't obvious on day one. (Shortcuts are remappable in Settings.)

On desktop, the formatting toolbar follows your selection, even near the bottom of a long block. It appears below the selection when there is no room above; choose an action there to format the selected words.

With a non-Latin keyboard layout, shortcuts and recording use the physical key's Latin letter or digit: **Ctrl+K** still works when that key types **л**. Latin layouts such as AZERTY and Dvorak keep their letter-based shortcuts. Text you type keeps the selected language.

blocks.raw: # Tips & shortcuts

children.raw: To switch graphs, press **g Shift+G**, choose a remembered graph with **Up/Down**, then press **Enter**. **All graphs** is also in the command palette.

While editing a block beside an embedded YouTube video, press **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Y** to insert its current playback time, just like **/Embed Youtube timestamp**. The inserted `{{youtube-timestamp N}}` macro becomes a clickable time: click it to seek the matching or last played video. Without a ready player, the shortcut inserts nothing. What you should see: the video jumps to the inserted time when you click it.
**Ctrl+K** opens the quick switcher: jump to a page, search the text of any block, or run a command — all from one box. **Ctrl+Shift+P** opens the command palette (commands only).

**Search page names** searches only page names and aliases; **Search block content** searches only block text. Both commands start unbound: assign keys in **Settings → Shortcuts**, or run them from the command palette.

Use **Ctrl+Shift+K** to search only the focused page, including children hidden under folded bullets. In the ordinary Ctrl+K switcher, press **Shift+Enter** on a page or block to send it to the right sidebar without leaving your current page.

Use **Search syntax** for phrases, alternatives, exclusions, and regular expressions. Choose **Open search tab** to keep the complete search in a graph-specific tab instead of choosing only one hit. To open a blank search tab directly in the focused pane, assign a key to **Open search tab** (`go/search-tab`) in **Settings → Shortcuts**; it is unbound by default.

The result tab separates **Pages** and **Blocks**. Pages match names and aliases by default; choose **Pages match → Block content** to find pages containing a matching block, or **Names or content** for both. Blocks still show the matching text. The choice stays with the tab and a saved search uses `tine.page-match-scope:: content` or `both` on its query block.

Each section has its own **Display** control: show Pages as a table with columns from authored page properties while Blocks stay a list, for example. Name the search and choose **Save page** to keep both choices on an ordinary query page. The compact filter button handles friendly fields and date ranges; **Query builder** opens the deeper visual editor when needed.

Page-title matching keeps exact, prefix, substring, and fuzzy results in that order. Repeated choices may break ties inside one class using device-local history; disable or reset this under Search settings if you prefer fixed ordering.

**Ctrl+F** searches the main and split panes and expanded right-sidebar items in that order; **Enter** / **Shift+Enter** move forward / backward through matches. The arrow at the left of the find bar adds **Replace** and **Replace all** for the page you opened Find in.

In a Search tab, clicking a result opens a new tab and keeps the search available (**Settings → Editor → Advanced → Search results open in → This tab** opens it in the same tab instead); right-click a page result for the switcher's page actions.
In the quick switcher or a Search tab, **Ctrl/Cmd-click** a result to open it in a background tab, **Shift-click** for the right sidebar, or **Alt-click** for another pane.

The quick switcher, page search, suggestions, and find-in-page ignore accents, case, and compatibility-width differences by default: `cafe` finds `café`, `lodz` finds `Łódź`, and `Tine` finds `Ｔｉｎｅ`. Marks that form another letter stay significant (`か` and `が` differ). To require accents in these searches, set `:feature/enable-search-remove-accents? false` in `logseq/config.edn`. This changes matching only; page names and Markdown keep their original spelling.

blocks.raw: ## Find anything — Ctrl+K

children.raw: With the caret inside a `[[link]]` or a `#tag`, **Ctrl+O** opens that page and **Ctrl+Shift+O** opens it in the right sidebar. This works while you are editing, so you can follow a name you just typed without reaching for the mouse.

blocks.raw: ## Follow a link without the mouse — Ctrl+O

children.raw: While editing, **Shift+click** another block's text to select the whole range as blocks and leave the editor. The first and last blocks are included in full; cutting or moving the range also takes their children. Shift-click again to adjust the range from the same starting block.

While editing, **Ctrl+A** first selects the block's text; press it again to select the block with its children, and keep pressing to widen the selection to each parent and finally the whole page. **Shift+Up** onto a parent always takes all of that parent's children with it.

**Edit selected block** returns one selected block to editing. It starts unbound; assign a key in **Settings → Shortcuts**. You can bind it to **Escape** if you prefer that way back into editing; without that binding, Escape keeps its ordinary selection steps.

blocks.raw: ## Select whole blocks — Ctrl+A

children.raw: With several blocks selected, right-click any selected bullet: **Copy blocks**, **Cut blocks**, and **Delete blocks** act on the selection; **Copy block refs**, **Copy block embeds**, and **Copy link** sit in the same menu and act on the same selection. Cut and delete take one Undo step; cutting keeps the complete subtrees for pasting. Right-clicking an unselected bullet acts on that bullet.

While editing with no text selected, **Ctrl/Cmd+C** copies a reference `((id))` to the block and **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+C** copies an embed `{{embed ((id))}}`. With text selected, both keep their ordinary copy meaning.

blocks.raw: ## Copy a link to a block — Ctrl+C

children.raw: While editing a block, select a few words and press **Ctrl/Cmd+R**. Tine adds a comment under that block that quotes the words and puts the caret in it. Other routes do the same: the selection toolbar's **Comment** button (the speech bubble at the right edge, also on touch screens), **Comment on selection** in the command palette, and **Comment on selection** after right-clicking words you have selected in a block's text. In Settings → Keyboard shortcuts the shortcut is listed as **Comment on selected text**. With nothing selected, the comment is about the whole block.

A comment is an ordinary child bullet carrying a `tine.quote::` property (with `tine.quote-prefix::` and `tine.quote-suffix::`, a few words on either side, so the comment stays on those words if they appear again later). Context grows until the occurrence is unique; an empty context property marks the start or end of the block. The page stays plain Markdown and opens in other apps as nested bullets. New replies are direct children of the thread root. A bullet with a `tine.author::` property, such as one an assistant or script wrote, shows that name in a small chip.

A comment shows as a tinted card with the quoted words above it, and those words are marked in the block. If the block is later edited so the quoted words are gone, the card keeps the quote struck through with **quoted text changed**; the comment is never dropped. If several occurrences match equally, the card says **quoted text ambiguous** rather than marking an arbitrary occurrence. On a touch screen, select words in rendered text and tap **Comment** in the formatting toolbar; entering edit mode first is unnecessary.

**Replying.** Hover or focus a thread and click its **Reply…** box at the bottom. **Enter** or **Reply** submits, **Shift+Enter** adds a line, and **Escape** or **Cancel** discards the draft. An abandoned empty reply creates no block and does not save the page. Selecting words inside a thread and choosing **Comment** or pressing **Ctrl/Cmd+R** adds a reply with a short quote inside that same thread.

**Deleting.** The **×** button at the top right deletes that comment and its replies; **Ctrl/Cmd+Z** restores them together. Comment and reply editors hide every `tine.*` property on all platforms, including iPad and iPhone; the original property bytes stay in the file when you save the edited words.

**Author marks.** `tine.author::` means who wrote this block's words; it does not inherit from a parent. On ordinary blocks it stays hidden while editing, and the author mark and chip stay visible. Click the chip and choose **Remove author** to remove the attribution. Editing keeps the original author property bytes, including on a blockquote. An ordinary `author::` property, for example a book's author, remains editable.

**Your name.** Type a name under **Settings > Editor > Your name** and the comments and replies you write are saved with `tine.author:: <your name>`, so a graph you share with other people shows who wrote what. You still read **you** on your own screen. While the name is empty nothing is written. The name is stored on this device and used in every graph, not stored in the graph. In a graph that is under git, the first comment or reply you write without a name asks **How should your comments be signed?** once: **Use this name** saves it, **Skip** writes the comment without it and Tine does not ask again (the setting stays available). If two people share a graph without setting their names, both see each other's unsigned comments as **you**.

**Where comments appear.** On a wide pane, a page with comments moves its text left and shows threads in a column on the right, ordered by where their quoted words appear. The journal feed uses the same width rule, with each day's page owning its margin column; split panes also use their own available width. Each thread starts beside its passage when space permits; a focused thread stays there while neighboring cards move away without overlapping. The small number at the right of a commented bullet counts threads, never replies. Click a comment to edit it there. **Enter** in a comment's text adds a reply under the thread root. Hovering a comment marks its words, and hovering marked words picks out their comment. On a narrow pane, in the sidebar or in an embed, comments stay in the outline as cards; zooming into a commented bullet also shows them there. Every response reads at one level in file order, even if another editor nested replies more deeply; viewing them never rewrites that nesting. Right-click the name chip (long-press on a phone) for the block menu, where **Zoom into block** lives.

**Editing body text.** Comments and all their replies are annotations in Tine's editor. **Backspace**, **Delete** and the arrow keys skip whole threads when moving between body blocks. **Enter** at the end of a block whose only children are comments creates a sibling; ordinary children still make Enter create a first child. **Tab** and **Shift+Tab** cannot move a comment or nest a body block inside a thread. Comments cannot be dragged, and body blocks cannot be dropped or pasted inside their threads. Moving or deleting the commented body block takes its comments with it. The file still contains ordinary child bullets, readable in Logseq and other editors.

**Hiding the comments.** To read or write without the threads beside the page, press **t** then **m**, run **Show/Hide comments** from the command palette, or switch off **Show/Hide comments** in Settings > Appearance, next to Wide mode and Document mode. While they are hidden a page shows no comment anywhere (no column, no cards, no marked words, no counts) and the arrow keys skip them; the comments stay in your file and nothing is deleted. Writing a new comment, or opening a link or search result that leads to one, shows them again. The choice is kept on this device. In Settings > Keyboard shortcuts you can give **Show/Hide comments** a shortcut of your own.

blocks.raw: ## Comment on a passage — Ctrl+R

children.raw: To put a bullet *above* an existing one, press **Enter** with the caret at its very start. Some bullets keep Enter for themselves — inside a code block it adds a line of code — so for those, right-click the bullet's dot and choose **Insert block above**. That works on any bullet, including the first one on a page.

blocks.raw: ## Insert a block above

children.raw: **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+V** pastes the clipboard as plain text inside the current block: copied web headings, bold runs and lists are not converted, and multiline text stays in one block instead of becoming several. Ordinary **Ctrl/Cmd+V** keeps converting copied web content and outlines.

**Paste as link** turns what you copied into a link without typing the syntax. Copy a URL or a block reference, select some words in a block you are editing, and run it: `see context` becomes `[context](https://…)` or `[context](((id)))`. With nothing selected the link is inserted bare. It ships without a key, so assign one under **Settings → Shortcuts** (the command palette lists it too, but opening the palette leaves the editor, so use the key). Ordinary paste over a selection is unchanged.

blocks.raw: ## Paste plain text, or paste as a link

children.raw: These commands ship without a key, so nothing you already use changes. Assign keys under **Settings → Shortcuts**; each acts on the selected blocks, or on the block you are editing when nothing is selected.

**Duplicate block below (with children)** puts a copy, children included, right under the block, and the caret follows it, so pressing it again stacks copies. The copy gets its own ids; one Undo removes it.

**Duplicate block above (with children)** does the same above the original. The caret follows the new copy, so repeated presses stack copies upwards. It also ships without a key; bind it under **Settings → Shortcuts**.

**Insert child block** adds an empty last child under the block and starts editing it, which works where **Enter** then **Tab** cannot, such as an embedded block with no children yet. A folded block opens so the new child shows.

**Collapse (one level)** folds the immediate children of the block, and folds the block itself once its children are all folded (or have no children of their own). **Expand (one level)** works the other way: a folded block opens by itself first, with its children still folded; each further press opens the next level with folded children, ignoring leaves, until everything is expanded, and each press is one Undo step. With nothing selected they start at the page's top-level blocks.
**Copy block refs of the selected blocks** copies a `((id))` reference for each selected block, one per line in the order you see them, the same text as **Copy block refs** in the block context menu.
**Search for the selected text** opens search with the selection already typed in. The ready-made key for it, **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F**, is Logseq's *toggle favorite*, so it is left for you to choose.

blocks.raw: ## Block commands you can bind

children.raw: 1. Press **Ctrl+K**.
2. Type part of a page name, a block phrase, or a command such as `Open Guide`.
3. Press **Enter** on the highlighted result.
4. What you should see: Tine jumps to the page/block or runs the command without leaving your graph.

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: Type **/** at the start of a bullet for a menu: tasks, headings, a code block, a `/calc` live calculator (hover a result to copy it), dates (Scheduled / Deadline), callouts, queries, a math block, asset upload, and more. `/Code block` opens a language picker; typing a language after an opening backtick or tilde fence offers the same completion.
On a journal page, **/That day** inserts a link to that journal's date, even when it is an older day. **/Today** inserts today's date. Both use your graph's journal title format.

With Simplified Chinese selected, each built-in slash row shows its English keyword followed by a Chinese gloss in parentheses. English typing still finds the same commands; Chinese glosses are searchable too: type `/表` to find **Table (表格)**. The `<` section picker also searches its Chinese labels, such as `<引用` for Quote. Selecting a row inserts the original syntax.

blocks.raw: ## Slash commands — /

children.raw: **g j** opens the Journals feed. **g h** opens the graph's home page, chosen in **Settings → Graph** or set as `:default-home {:page "Page name"}` in `logseq/config.edn`; Tine also opens it when it opens a graph without a saved session. With a saved session, Tine restores every tab's last page, order and pin state, and the same active tab. Renaming the home page (or a namespace it lives in) keeps it the home page; merging it into another page does not. With no home page set, or when that page no longer exists, **g h** opens the Journals feed. With `:feature/enable-journals? false` in `logseq/config.edn` and a home page that exists, the sidebar shows that page in place of **Journals** (as Logseq does); **g j** still opens the feed. **g n** and **g p** move to the next or previous calendar day from the journal you are viewing. From another page, they start at today.

A configured default journal template is inserted once for each new day, including when Tine stays open through local midnight. Choose a journal display date format in Settings; the three dotted day-month-year patterns are available there too. The display format does not rename journal files.

Opening a graph never renames journal files. If some are named by title instead of by date, their days look empty; **Settings → Backups & recovery** lists them under **Journal files named by title** with a **Rename to date names** button, which takes a snapshot first.

Hover a journal title row or focus one of its controls with the keyboard to reveal the carry buttons, in the feed and on a journal page. On touch devices without hover they stay visible. The buttons under today's journal pull unfinished tasks from earlier days. After midnight, yesterday's button changes to **Carry unfinished tasks → today**.

blocks.raw: ## Journal days

children.raw: **Middle-click** any bullet, page, or search result to open it in a background tab. **Double-click** a tab to pin it, **drag** to reorder, **Ctrl+W** to close. Your tabs come back next launch. In a split view, a pane's only tab still has a close button (it closes the pane) unless it shows the journals.

Bind **Activate tab 1** through **Activate tab 8**, or **Activate last tab**, in **Settings → Shortcuts** to jump within the focused pane's tab order. They start unbound because **Ctrl/Cmd+1–9** already focus panes. A numbered slot with no tab does nothing.

Numbered tab/pane commands and sidebar/pane resize commands stay bindable in **Settings → Shortcuts** and are omitted from the command palette. **Carry unfinished tasks: last N days** uses the day count in Settings → Journals.

**Page links, block references, an outline bullet's dot, backlink headers, the sidebar and query results all take the same modified clicks**: **Shift-click** opens the right sidebar, **Ctrl/Cmd-click** or **middle-click** opens a background tab, and **Alt-click** opens the other pane (splitting one off if you have only one).

When a pane has more tabs than fit, use its tab-overview button to see every full title, activate or pin a tab, close it, or reorder it with the drag handle / **Alt+Up/Down** without guessing from truncated labels.
Use the command palette to **Toggle maximize active pane** and use the pane-size commands to grow or shrink the active pane with the keyboard. Run **Reset interface zoom** to return to normal scale.

blocks.raw: ## Tabs

children.raw: Assign keys in **Settings → Shortcuts** to **Grow left sidebar width** (`sidebar/grow-width`), **Shrink left sidebar width** (`sidebar/shrink-width`), **Grow right sidebar width** (`right-sidebar/grow-width`), and **Shrink right sidebar width** (`right-sidebar/shrink-width`). All four start unbound. Each press changes the width by 48 px within the same limits as dragging, and the width is remembered on this device.
Hover over a truncated page title in the left sidebar to see its full title. Titles that fit show no tooltip.

Below a page, **Linked References** and **Unlinked References** show where it is mentioned, including plain mentions in code and math. Use the copy button at the right edge of either header to select visible results and open the shared Copy / export dialog; an Org source stays Org in source export. An expanded section stays open when the page view remounts. A page with many backlinks opens Linked References folded; Logseq's `:ref/linked-references-collapsed-threshold` in `config.edn` sets where that starts (default 100), and `0` starts every page folded. In Linked References, a reference must match every included chip and none of the excluded chips; typed text narrows both results and available chips. The block-reference locations panel can collapse or expand all source groups.

**t l** toggles the left sidebar — journals, favorites, recents, all pages, and a namespace tree. Favorites and Recent can be folded independently. Choose **+ New group** to arrange favorites under plain-text labels, then drag a row up or down to reorder it, right to nest it under the row above (to any depth), or left to lift it out; deleting a group keeps what it held one level up. Tine keeps that arrangement on an ordinary editable page called **Favorites** (marked `tine.favorites:: true`) and still writes `config.edn :favorites` as the flat list Logseq reads.
Right-click a graph in the left sidebar to copy its folder path, show it in your file manager, open another window, or remove it from the recent graph list.

**t r** toggles the right sidebar; **Shift-click** any bullet's dot to open it there and keep it beside your work. Each right-sidebar item can be folded independently, and its menu can collapse, expand, or close them all. Drag an item by its header to reorder the list.

On a phone-width window (below 640 px), either sidebar opens over the page. Tap the shaded outside edge, use the close button, press **Esc**, or press Android **Back** to return to the page. Wider tablet and desktop windows keep the ordinary persistent, resizable sidebars.

Click the vertical outline guide below a bullet to expand its complete descendant subtree when anything inside is folded, or collapse all of those descendants when everything is open. The bullet itself keeps its ordinary one-level action.

Press **t o** outside a text editor to toggle all blocks on the current page: any folded branch expands everything; otherwise everything folds. In **Commands**, choose **Expand all blocks on current page** or **Collapse all blocks on current page** for an explicit direction. Right-click a bullet for **Expand all** or **Collapse all** in that block's subtree. A bulk fold is one Undo step and persists through the normal page save.

Mouse side buttons navigate **Back / Forward** through the current pane's history on desktop, including macOS. Each press steps once, including repeated presses before the page finishes displaying, just like **Alt+Left** and **Alt+Right**. On macOS, **Cmd+[** and **Cmd+]** also work; **Alt+Left** and **Alt+Right** remain available. A side-button drag keeps its selection or drag action instead of navigating.

blocks.raw: ## The sidebars

children.raw: **t f** (focus mode) hides the sidebars and toolbar so the screen is just your text; layered **Esc** steps back out.
**t b** (dim inactive blocks) fades everything except the bullet you're editing — a typewriter-style spotlight. Use it on its own, or let focus mode turn it on for you.

blocks.raw: ## Focus mode & dimming — t f / t b

children.raw: When Syncthing or Dropbox leaves a conflict copy of a page, or a git or Fossil merge leaves `<<<<<<<` merge markers in a file, an **N conflicts** badge appears at the bottom of the left sidebar. It opens the **Conflicts** page, which lists every page that needs a decision; **Discard copy** moves a sync copy to the graph trash (recoverable). The list comes from your files, not from a list Tine keeps in your graph: to avoid re-reading every page at launch, Tine remembers which pages it has already seen without merge markers in its own disposable launch cache, and reads any page it has not seen from the file.

Open a listed page to resolve it there, block by block: keep one side, the other, or both. Where the merge markers carry the common ancestor, Tine pre-selects the side that actually changed; nothing is applied until you choose **Apply resolution**.

Tine refuses to save a page that still contains merge markers, because rewriting it would re-indent the markers and silently lose one side. **Apply resolution** is the one save that may replace such a file; the file as it was first goes to the graph trash. A merged sync copy goes to the trash too.

blocks.raw: ## Sync copies and merge conflicts

children.raw: Use the **…** beside an ordinary page title for its complete actions menu: open the source file, copy/export, inspect properties, rename, carry tasks, or delete. It is the same menu as right-click and works from the keyboard and touch.

In **Copy / Export**, choose **Plain text** for the text as displayed, without markup markers, or **Markdown** (**Org** on an Org page) to keep the original syntax: bold, highlighting, links, and properties.
Right-click a block and choose **Open in new tab** to keep that block in its own tab (on a narrow window the tab is listed under **Open tabs** in the left sidebar).

In **Settings → Shortcuts**, search by command or key and choose **Unbind** to remove a shortcut; the command stays available from places such as the command palette, and **Reset** restores its default instead. **Settings → Appearance** offers Light, Dark, and System themes. The Settings window can be maximized; it remembers that choice on this device.

**Settings → Help & diagnostics** creates a privacy-safe diagnostic report of this run and the previous one to attach to a bug report: operation names, outcomes, timings, counts, platform and build, never page content, titles, file paths or queries. If Tine did not close cleanly last time, it says so when it starts. Review the report and choose **Copy report**, or on desktop **Save report…**; nothing is uploaded, and the recorder keeps at most 1 MiB in Tine's own app data, never in your graph. The same tab also offers **Rescan graph** and **Verify synchronized graph**.

Renaming a page to the name of another existing page offers to **merge** them, as Logseq does: the blocks move to the end of the page that remains, the aliases join, links to the old name point to it, and the merged file goes to the graph trash (recoverable).

Tine saves pending edits before a rename. A page whose edits cannot be saved stops the rename only if the rename would change that page, or its unsaved text mentions the old name; the message names it. Other pages keep their unsaved edits through the rename. A page named by `title::`, or in Org by `#+TITLE:`, gets the new name in that line.
Change capitalization directly with **Rename**, for example `my note` → `My Note`. The filename, title and references follow together; two distinct files claiming that name still block the rename.
**Carry unfinished tasks** forward into today (from the command palette) — the last 7 / 30 / 365 days, optionally with their context.
**Export to PDF…** saves pending page edits before preparing the printout. If a page cannot be saved, Tine stops the export and shows an error so the PDF does not silently omit your changes.

Select several task bullets and press **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** to advance each one through your workflow in a single Undo step. The selection toolbar can also wrap selected text as a page link or inline code.

**Undo is Ctrl/Cmd+Z and redo is Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z.** On Windows and Linux **Ctrl+Y** also redoes, because that is the key most editors there use; the shortcuts list shows it beside the binding. It is a second default rather than a second command, so remapping Redo replaces both.

**Code blocks**: type ``` (or choose **Code block** from the **/** menu) and Tine offers a language list; picking one fills in the opening fence and the closing fence for you. You can skip the language list by tapping inside the code. Typing continues at your caret. Clicking code edits only its body: only the code itself is in the text box, so Enter adds a line of code instead of splitting the bullet. When prose and code share a bullet after **Shift+Enter**, clicking a code region edits only that region. To edit the language or add text before or after the code, enter the bullet from a neighboring bullet with **Backspace** or an arrow key: the whole bullet opens as source, including its fences. From code editing, **Escape**, moving out of the body with an arrow key, or **Backspace** at its start also reveals the source. These paths work on desktop and mobile. In a mixed bullet, you can edit the whole bullet as source; surrounding text stays intact. To delete the whole code block, right-click its bullet and choose **Delete block**; on desktop, right-clicking inside the code with no text selected opens the same menu. Backspace in an empty code block without child bullets removes the wrapper; if it is the last block, it becomes a normal empty bullet. Code blocks show line numbers and a display-only language label. Hover the card to **Copy code** without its fences. **Settings → Appearance → Wrap code lines** controls wrapping for all code blocks, in both reading and editing; it is off by default and remembered on this device.

**Drag a bullet onto another bullet and move a little to the right** (about 50 px into it) to make it that bullet's last child; nearer its left edge, the upper half places it before and the lower half after. A marker shows where it will land.

Typing `::` at the start of a line inside a bullet starts a property: the name goes to the left of the `::`, **Create** is offered first, and after a comma the value list leaves out values already on the line.
**Namespaces**: name a page `Project/Roadmap` and it nests under `Project` in the sidebar. This page lives under `Features`.

**Page names and files**: put `title:: Project/Roadmap` above the first bullet to give an existing page that name, even when its filename differs. Tine keeps the file at its existing path; links and page search use the title. Markdown and Org pages in other graph folders, such as `archive/`, are pages too. New pages get portable filenames, including names with punctuation.

**Hidden graph paths**: add `:hidden ["archive/private"]` to `logseq/config.edn` to exclude matching graph-relative path prefixes from pages and search. The files stay on disk. This also applies to pages outside the usual `pages/` and `journals/` folders.

**Page icons**: add a property like `tine.icon:: 📚` at the very top of a page (the ⌨️ on this page comes from Logseq's `icon::`, which Tine reads too). `tine.icon` stays visible in the page-properties block; Logseq's `icon`, `title` and `filters` stay hidden there. Use **Page properties…** to change them.

**Hidden metadata** follows Logseq: built-in lines such as `heading::`, `background-color::`, PDF highlight metadata and flashcard scheduling stay out of the text editor. Keys listed in `:block-hidden-properties` in `logseq/config.edn` also stay hidden in editors and rendered property lists. Editing or clearing the visible text keeps the original hidden property lines in the file, in Markdown and Org. Use **Properties…** to change or remove hidden values; heading and block colour also have their own block-menu controls. Ordinary `title`, `icon`, `filters`, `logseq.color` and `logseq.table.*` lines remain visible while editing.

**Page and block properties** are editable from a form, not only as raw `key:: value` lines: use **Page properties…** in the page menu (or `/page properties` while editing), or right-click a block for **Properties…**. The form lists every property the page or block really has; a page's form always offers Aliases, Tags, Display title, Icon and Public. Any other property can be changed or removed, and **Add a property** takes any key you like — it does not have to be plain ASCII. `id::`, `collapsed::` and `tine.` keys keep their own surfaces. Markdown writes `key:: value`, an Org page a `#+key: value` directive, and an Org block its `:PROPERTIES:` drawer. A read-only page offers no property editing at all.

**Toggle code block wrap** in the command palette switches the same device-wide preference as **Wrap code lines** and keeps your reading position, including in split panes and the right sidebar. Code cards above the visible reading row can grow or shrink without moving that row. It never changes note source. Assign your own binding in **Settings → Keyboard shortcuts**; there is no default shortcut.

**Interface zoom** with **Ctrl/Cmd + / - / 0** while the notes pane is focused. To return the whole interface to its default **100%**, open the command palette (**Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P**) and choose **Reset interface zoom**. This leaves PDF/image zoom and block zoom unchanged; a focused PDF keeps its own **Ctrl/Cmd + / - / 0** controls.

blocks.raw: ## A few more worth knowing

children.raw: This page lives in the **Project** namespace, and it doubles as the target for the reference and the embed over on [[Welcome to Tine]].

Tine round-trips your files byte-for-byte, so you can always switch back to Logseq — nothing here is one-way.

See the little count badge on the bullet above? That's how many blocks reference it — click the badge to see them.

blocks.raw: ## A few example tasks

children.raw: The installed desktop program also has a small command-line interface. Run `tine --help` for the current command list and `tine --version` (or `tine version`) for the exact build version.

blocks.raw: # Command line

children.raw: `tine open GRAPH` opens a graph. The older shorthand `tine GRAPH` remains supported. If Tine is already running, the graph opens in a new window of that instance.
`tine capture` opens Quick Capture. The older `tine --capture` spelling remains supported, so existing desktop shortcuts keep working.
`tine --debug` turns on the diagnostic log for that run, exactly like `TINE_DEBUG=1`.

blocks.raw: ## Open Tine

children.raw: `tine export static GRAPH --output PARENT` writes the static HTML publication. `tine export live GRAPH --output PARENT` writes the read-only Tine app and keeps the static HTML site as its no-JavaScript and `file://` fallback.

`PARENT` must be an existing folder outside the graph, given as an absolute path. Tine creates one new child folder in it, named after the graph (or after `--name`), and refuses to replace an existing folder of that name.

Publication follows the graph's existing privacy settings: only pages with `public:: true` are included, unless `:publishing/all-pages-public?` is enabled. Add `--all-pages` to override that selection for one export.
Example: `tine export live ~/notes --all-pages --output ~/Sites --name "My notes"`

A live export opens on the configured home page when it is exported, then **Welcome to Tine**, then the first exported page. Use `--home "Page name"` to choose explicitly; a home page that is not exported is refused.

blocks.raw: ## Publish a graph

children.raw: `tine doctor GRAPH` reads and parses the graph, reports how many pages and journals it found and the configured home page, names every unreadable page and every page name claimed by more than one file, and does not change the graph. It exits with status 1 when it finds a problem.

blocks.raw: ## Check a graph

children.raw: On Linux, macOS and Windows, the read commands below do not change notes. They ask the graph's owner, so `tine page show` and `tine journal` include unsaved edits when the app holds that page; other reads use the graph's indexed view.

Choose a graph with `--graph GRAPH` (or `-g GRAPH`) on each command. Otherwise Tine uses `TINE_GRAPH`, then the nearest folder around your working directory that holds `logseq/config.edn`. Example: `tine page show "Project notes" --graph ~/notes`.
`tine status` shows whether the app or `serve` owns the graph and what it is doing.
`tine page show "Page name"` reads a page's outline. `tine journal` reads today; `tine journal 2026-10-13` reads a specific day that already exists.

`tine block show UUID` reads a block and its descendants using its persisted `id::` UUID. `tine refs "Page name"` shows linked references; `tine refs UUID --block` finds references to a persisted block id.
`tine search "meeting"` searches page names and block text as the app does. `--pages N` and `--blocks N` set the result limits; `0` switches that category off.

`tine query '(task TODO)'` runs the text inside a Logseq simple or advanced query macro. `tine query "task = 'TODO'" --tql` runs the text inside a Tine query macro. [[Features/Queries]] explains the query forms and their supported scope; read diagnostics when a query cannot run whole.

`tine pages` lists existing pages, including journals. `tine pages --namespace Projects` limits it to that namespace and its descendants; aliases and names that only appear in references are not listed.

blocks.raw: ## Read your graph from a terminal

children.raw: These commands change notes, through the same guarded save the app uses. They are meant for scripts and AI agents working beside you; every block they create is marked with an `tine.author::` property so you can see what an agent wrote.

A page read prints each block with a **handle** such as `2.1~k7f2ab`: its position and a short fingerprint of its text. Name a block as `"Page name/2.1~k7f2ab"` exactly as printed, or by its `id::` UUID. If the block has changed or moved since the read, the command refuses with `stale` instead of guessing; read the page again.

`tine add "text" --page "Page name"` appends to a page, creating it if needed; `--journal` appends to today's journal and `--journal=2026-10-13` to that day. `--under BLOCK`, `--after BLOCK` and `--before BLOCK` place the new blocks next to an existing one. The text can hold several blocks with `- ` children; `-` reads it from standard input. New blocks get `tine.author:: agent`, or the name in `--author NAME` or `TINE_AUTHOR`.

`tine edit BLOCK "new text"` replaces a block's text; its children and properties stay, and a property you name in the new text replaces the old one. `--author NAME` sets its `tine.author::`. To remove a property, use `tine prop remove`. `tine prop set BLOCK key value` and `tine prop remove BLOCK key` change one property. `tine move BLOCK --under|--after|--before TARGET` moves a block with its children on the same page.

`tine delete BLOCK` refuses if it would leave block references elsewhere broken; nothing changed. Read the count, then pass `--yes` (or `--force`) to confirm the delete. Every successful reply includes the removed text, including children and properties, as a Markdown or Org fragment for recovery. Keep the reply: there is no CLI undo. Removed text is bounded to 65,536 UTF-8 bytes; a truncated reply says how many bytes were omitted and cannot restore the whole subtree.

`tine page create "Page name"` creates an empty page and refuses an existing page or alias. `tine page rename "Old name" "New name"` uses the app's rename, rewriting references and namespace descendants; an existing destination refuses, so confirm merges in the app. A page's `title::` is its identity even when its filename differs. Open windows refresh the renamed page and its references.

`tine page delete "Page name" --yes` (or `--force`) moves the page to graph trash and prints the count of broken page and block references. Without confirmation it refuses. `--rev` guards deletion against the bytes you read.

`tine ref BLOCK` prints `((uuid))`; `tine embed BLOCK` prints `{{embed ((uuid))}}`. Both ensure a durable lazy `id::` first, as Copy block ref does, preserving the block's author. They print syntax to reuse; they do not insert a new block.

Page rename is graph-wide: `--rev` and `--run` (including `TINE_RUN`) refuse before changing anything. Create, delete, ref and embed support runs. A rename error marked `uncertain` means inspect the graph before retrying.

**With the app open:** text you have typed on that page is saved first, so the command works on what you see, and an open window shows the change at once. If you keep typing on that block while the command runs, it refuses with `stale` rather than overwrite you.

**Comments are ordinary blocks:** `tine add "My comment" --under BLOCK` creates a child; use the new handle it prints as COMMENT in `tine prop set COMMENT tine.quote "quoted words"` to quote a passage of the parent with a `tine.quote::` property. Optional `tine.quote-prefix::` and `tine.quote-suffix::` properties hold surrounding words to distinguish repeated passages. `--author NAME` on `add` names the author; a reply is another child without a quote. The same comment cards and margin display apply as for comments made in the app; see [[Features/Tips & shortcuts]].
Add `--rev REV` (as `page show` printed it) to write only if the page has not changed at all since that read.
A write prints `written PAGE rev REV` and the handles of the blocks it created or changed, so a script can chain the next command.

blocks.raw: ## Write from a terminal (scripts and AI agents)

children.raw: If the graph folder is a git repository, an agent can group its writes into a **run**: `tine run begin` checks the repository and prints a run id. Every write made with `--run ID` (or `TINE_RUN=ID`) is committed right after it is saved, for that one file only, under the agent's name (`--author NAME` or `TINE_AUTHOR`, else `agent`). If the file had edits of yours that were not committed yet, they are committed first under your own git name, so your work never ends up inside the agent's commit.

`tine run show ID` lists the run's commits. `tine run end ID -m "summary"` squashes them into one commit, but only when none of them is pushed, on another branch or tag, or mixed with other commits; otherwise the commits are left as they are and the reason is printed.
`tine run revert ID` undoes the run's edits, newest first, as one change per page. A block you changed since the agent did keeps your text and is listed, so nothing of yours is lost.

A run never touches files it did not write. It refuses before writing when the repository is in the middle of a merge or rebase, HEAD is detached, or the page has a Git `filter`, `ident` or `working-tree-encoding` attribute: committing its raw bytes could expose plaintext or bypass conversion. Tine never runs external filters. If a commit fails after a save, the write is kept and a warning says it was not committed. A branch checkout while the commit is preparing also produces that warning; Tine leaves both branches and the new branch's index alone.

blocks.raw: ## Keep an agent's work in git (runs)

children.raw: When the app has the graph open, it answers these commands. With no app holding the graph, a read or write command automatically starts `tine serve GRAPH` in the background. You can also run that command yourself in a terminal; it owns the graph without opening a window, takes a launch snapshot unless the newest backup zip is less than 6 hours old (see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]]), and exits after 30 idle minutes. This keeps scripted edit/restart loops from filling the backup slots. A future-dated zip does not suppress a snapshot.

When you open that graph in the app, `serve` finishes admitted work, stops and hands over ownership. The app shows **Finishing the command line's work on this graph…** while it waits. If the handover has not finished after 60 seconds, opening fails and names `tine serve GRAPH --stop`; the app does not take ownership on a timeout. Read commands retry through a busy handover for up to 30 seconds.
`tine serve GRAPH --stop` asks the command-line owner to finish and exit. It cannot stop an app owner.

Windows supports the same read and write commands, automatic `tine serve` startup, handover to the app and `tine serve GRAPH --stop`, using a private named pipe for your Windows account. Add the folder containing `tine.exe` to PATH, or run it by its full path. Quote graph paths with spaces, for example `tine page show "Project notes" --graph "C:\Users\me\My notes"`. A busy pipe waits for the owner; after a restart, Tine allows up to 3 seconds for the previous owner's pipe handles to close. An unsafe owner directory or persistently occupied pipe refuses with `owner-unsafe` (exit 5); the app can still open without a command endpoint.
Android and iOS have no command-line interface.

blocks.raw: ## Who owns the graph?

children.raw: Read and write commands print text to stdout by default, with outline addresses such as `1.2` for a second child. Add `--json` for a single JSON result on stdout with schema `tine.cli/1`, for example `tine pages --graph ~/notes --json`.

Successful commands exit 0. Failed commands print errors to stderr; `--json` makes owner and connection errors a JSON error envelope there. Invalid usage exits 2, a missing or ambiguous page/block exits 3, a still-busy owner exits 4, endpoint/startup failures exit 5, a `stale` or refused write exits 6 and a write whose draft could not be saved exits 7 (in both cases nothing changed), and a write whose outcome is pending or unknown exits 8: read the page before retrying. Check the exit status and read any diagnostics or truncation notices before treating results as complete.
The [command-line output contract](https://github.com/martinkoutecky/tine/blob/og/docs/contracts/cli-output.md) documents JSON fields, limits, error codes and the full exit-code table.

blocks.raw: ## Output for people and scripts

children.raw: Every command and subcommand has `--help`, for example `tine export live --help`. Linux `.deb` and `.rpm` packages also install the same generated reference for `man tine`.

blocks.raw: ## Full reference

children.raw: **If closing warns about unsaved changes:** Tine tries to save everything before the window closes. If a conflict or a stuck save prevents it, a prompt titled “Quit without saving N pages?” says so and names each unsaved page. Choose **Go back** to stay (or **Discard and quit** to close anyway): a panel lists those pages with **Retry saving**, open, and **Copy draft**. A failed save's message stays up with **Review unsaved**, which opens the same panel. If a page cannot be saved when you switch graphs, Tine stays on the current graph with your edit and says so. For a conflict, look for the conflict banner or the **N conflicts** badge (below) and resolve it before you close. If a page still cannot be saved after you close Tine's last window, Tine does not quit over it: after half a minute it opens that graph again, and a message names each page whose edits are not on disk yet, and why (changed on disk, or saving fails).

**If Tine crashes or quits while a page cannot be saved,** that page's unsaved text is kept in Tine's app data (never in your graph). On the next start Tine puts it back on the page and saves it, and a message names those pages: “Recovered unsaved edits … — Tine is saving them”. If the file changed on disk in the meantime, the page shows the changed-on-disk banner instead (see [[Reference/Troubleshooting and recovery]]), so nothing is written over unseen. Text that saved normally is not kept there. Crash-recovery copies from an older Tine are left untouched as a backup; a message names their file once.

Your graph content stays in ordinary files shared with Logseq. Tine also keeps device settings and launch snapshots outside the graph. This page maps what is written where, and the safety nets around it.

blocks.raw: # Files, external edits, and backups

children.raw: **Pages and journals** — one Markdown or Org file per page. Existing files may live at the graph root or in nested folders; Tine saves each one back to its exact path. New files use the configured `pages/` and `journals/` folders.
**Assets** — pasted and uploaded files in `assets/`. Deleting a block never deletes its media.

**Copy image** on desktop offers the original asset file to your file manager without changing its bytes or imposing a file size limit. If an image is too large to preview, hover over **Preview unavailable** to use **Copy image**. This also works for `{{img ...}}` image macros. An already-open image viewer keeps copying the original file after an outside asset edit. Missing files keep their missing-image placeholder. Smaller images also offer a bitmap for chat apps and image editors; this compatibility copy keeps the 64 MiB encoded-data limit and decoded-memory limit, including PNG images. Paste files copied in Explorer, Finder, or a Linux file manager to import their original bytes unchanged. A screenshot or other pixel-only clipboard image is saved as PNG. Mobile and remote image copying keep their existing image clipboard behavior.
**Graph configuration** — `logseq/config.edn`, shared with Logseq: journal date formats, macros, and UI choices such as `:ui/show-brackets?` live there.
**Tine's view config** — harmless `tine.*` block properties on the view-owning block (see [[Features/Sheets]]). Everything else stays ordinary graph text.

blocks.raw: ## What lands on disk

children.raw: **If the graph folder moves, is replaced, or disconnects while open:** Tine stops graph writes and shows a sticky notice. Unsaved edits stay on this device. Close the window, then reopen the graph from its new location, or reconnect its drive and reopen it; Tine never recreates the old graph folder to save into it.

**A moved or unavailable graph:** a notice offers **Recover into this graph** and **Not now** when device recovery holds unsaved edits whose graph cannot be found. The graph may be moved or unavailable (for example, a disconnected drive); recover only if those edits belong in the current graph. Recovery is your choice: it saves this graph's pending edits first, then recovers through the ordinary save checks. If another window or host still holds those edits, recovery refuses: close that graph, wait for saving to finish, then try again. An outside change becomes a conflict for you to resolve. **Not now** leaves the edits on this device and the notice returns on the next open; it does not discard anything. On iOS, an app update that changes only the app-container location carries the device state over automatically when neither namespace is held by a host.
Keeping a graph open does not prevent ejecting its drive. After ejecting, saves fail and unsaved edits stay on this device; reconnect the drive and reopen the graph before continuing.
You never press Save: edits are written automatically to the same file the page came from, a moment after you pause.

Writes go through a guarded path: Tine checks that the file still matches what it read before it replaces it, and a save that would overwrite an outside change is refused rather than forced (see external edits below).

A page **rename** finishes once it starts; it is not rolled back. Tine writes the page under its new name and every page-link and tag rewrite that points at it, and removes the old file last. If a file cannot be written yet, the message says the rename finishes once it can be, and Tine keeps trying; if Tine stops in the middle, it finishes the rename on the next start. A crash while the new file also cannot be written can leave the page briefly without a file: its text stays in `logseq/.tine-trash/` or in Tine's crash-recovery copies until the write succeeds.

A page that still carries unresolved git or Fossil merge markers is never rewritten by a rename: its links keep the old name, and a message lists those pages so you can update them after resolving the merge.

Tine saves pending edits before a rename. A page whose edits cannot be saved stops the rename only if the rename would change that page, or its unsaved text mentions the old name; the message names it. Other pages keep their unsaved edits through the rename.
An Org file is rewritten only when Tine can reproduce it byte-for-byte; one it cannot round-trip opens **read-only** so the graph cannot be corrupted.

blocks.raw: ## Saving

children.raw: Tine notices changes made outside it — Logseq, Syncthing, or another editor. Settings (**t s**) → **Files** → **Watch for external edits**: **Live (inotify)** (default, no idle wakeups) or **Poll (3s)** for filesystems where the OS watcher misses edits (some network mounts). Saved per device.

A page updates in place automatically, also while one of its blocks is open in the editor: the editor stays on that block, and closes only if the change deleted it (while you are composing text with an input method, the update waits until you finish). A page with unsaved edits is never overwritten: Tine skips that page in future saves and shows a banner with **Review**, which opens the panel at the top of the page. There you compare your draft with the disk version block by block and choose **Apply resolution**. An outside change that holds exactly your unsaved text (often a sync tool delivering Tine's own write back) is not a conflict: Tine accepts it quietly and still saves your edit. The **N conflicts** page lists such pages under **Unsaved drafts**.

Prefer to approve even clean external updates yourself? Turn on Settings → **Backups & recovery** → **Always ask before applying an external change**. Tine then holds the silent case and offers **Keep mine** / **Use disk version**; changes that already conflict keep their existing safer handling.

Returning to Tine asks the watcher for a fresh pass, covering network mounts, suspended apps, and sync tools that delivered no live filesystem event; typing waits until that pass is in. A large `git checkout`, `fossil update`, branch switch, or sync burst is grouped into one external revision instead of interrupting once per page. Changes inside `.git/` or Syncthing's `.stfolder/` are ignored.

If the system refuses live file notifications (for example the per-user watch limit is reached), Tine says so and checks for external changes every 3 seconds instead, retrying live notifications as it goes.

Files in `assets/` are watched too. An image replaced outside Tine — by an editor, Syncthing, Dropbox, or another Tine window — refreshes where it is shown, without reloading the page, and one deleted outside shows its missing-image placeholder. This also covers an `assets` link to a folder outside the graph that you have approved. An open PDF, audio, or video is not swapped while you use it; it shows the new file the next time you open it.

`logseq/config.edn` is live too. A change made in Logseq, a text editor, or delivered by a sync provider updates favorites, shortcuts, the home page, journal formats, and other shared settings during the session; reopening the graph is not required. A settings change made in Tine edits only its own entry, and is refused rather than written if `config.edn` is half-written or not a map, so a file still arriving from a sync provider is never overwritten.
For file sync between devices, run one app at a time on the graph where you can, and let conflict copies (below) catch the rest.

blocks.raw: ## External edits

children.raw: **Backups of a moved or unavailable graph** appear when you open **Backups & recovery**, with the recorded path. That graph may be moved or unavailable (for example, a disconnected drive). Restore asks you to confirm that location and takes a safety snapshot of the current graph first. **Delete backups from this location** asks before removing those snapshots from this device: these may be the only backups of a graph on a disconnected drive. Backup archives are kept unchanged when a graph moves.

The command-line `tine serve` owner skips its launch snapshot when the newest backup zip is less than 6 hours old, so scripted edit/restart loops preserve the backup slots. The date comes from the zip's name; a future-dated zip does not suppress a snapshot. The app still takes its launch snapshot as usual.

A launch snapshot (in the app, or as a command-line `tine serve` with no window) copies every Markdown/Org page in the graph — pages and journals, and pages kept in other folders or at the graph root — plus `logseq/config.edn` and asset `.edn` sidecars, to a local folder **outside** the graph, once opening has gone quiet (a few seconds after startup finishes, at most three minutes) so the copy does not compete with your first page. Syncthing never syncs it. Binary assets, folders listed in `:hidden`, and Tine's own trash and backup folders are not copied.

Settings → **Backups & recovery** → **Snapshots to keep** (default 12) sets how many survive. A launch where nothing changed writes no snapshot, so the count covers changes to your graph rather than launches; the oldest beyond it are pruned. The snapshot taken before a restore is never pruned and does not count, and neither does one marked **Damaged** (it is removed once it is older than the oldest kept zip snapshot). Tine prunes only after it has checked a newer snapshot and confirmed it is safely on disk; on a disk that cannot confirm that, nothing is pruned and old snapshots pile up.

Backups have a size limit: the files a snapshot copies may total at most 512 MiB, with no single file over 128 MiB (binary assets are not copied, so they do not count). A graph over the limit is not snapshotted: Tine says the backup failed, writes nothing, and a restore or journal rename that needs a snapshot first does not run.
1. Pick a snapshot under **Available snapshots** and choose **Restore**, then confirm.

2. What you should see: Tine saves pending edits, snapshots your current state first, restores backed-up graph text to its original paths, restores config and sidecars, and reloads the graph — a mistaken restore is itself reversible. Pages created after the snapshot are moved into the restore's recovery folder under `logseq/.tine-trash/`, not deleted. Some snapshot folders from an older Tine cover only the pages and journals folders; such a one made under a different pages or journals folder setting is refused rather than restored into the wrong place. Zip snapshots, and the newer snapshot folders, cover pages wherever they live.

A launch where nothing changed since the newest snapshot writes no new one. A snapshot marked **Damaged** in the list failed its check and cannot be restored; pick another. One marked **Made by a newer Tine** can be restored only by that newer version.

blocks.raw: ## Snapshots — automatic backups

children.raw: Each snapshot is one ordinary `.zip` file (snapshots from an older Tine are folders; see below). You can open it with your system's archive tool, without Tine: inside, every file sits at its path in your graph (`pages/…`, `journals/…`, `logseq/config.edn`, asset sidecars under `assets/`), next to `tine-backup.json`, the list Tine checks the zip against. Snapshot names start with the date and time they were taken, in UTC. To get back a single page by hand, copy it out of the zip into your graph; Tine picks it up like any external change.
Linux: `~/.local/share/<app id>/backups/` (Flatpak: `~/.var/app/<app id>/data/<app id>/backups/`)
macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/<app id>/backups/`
Windows: `%APPDATA%\<app id>\backups\`
Android and iOS: the folder is in the app's private storage, which a file manager cannot open; restore from Settings.

The zips are in Tine's app data folder, under `backups/<graph folder name>-<code>.zips/`, one folder per graph. Below, `<app id>` is `page.tine.Tine` for stable Tine and `page.tine.TineBeta` for Tine Beta.

Snapshots made by an older Tine are folders rather than zips, in `backups/<graph folder name>-<code>/`. They stay listed and restorable and count toward **Snapshots to keep**, except folders in the newer folder format that another Tine build wrote: those are never counted or pruned.
Tine has no button that opens this folder; use your file manager.

blocks.raw: ## Where your backups are

children.raw: When Tine will not start, or you want a whole earlier state back without Tine, recover from a snapshot zip yourself:
1. Quit Tine completely, every window, so nothing is saved over the files while you work. If a sync tool such as Syncthing or Dropbox serves the graph, pause it too.
2. In the backups folder above, pick the newest zip from before the problem.
3. Extract it into a new, empty folder, never directly over your graph. Delete `tine-backup.json` from the extracted copy: it is Tine's checklist, not part of your graph.

4. Move your current graph folder aside (rename it; keep it until you are sure), then move the extracted folder into its place. Or copy only the pages you need from the extracted folder into your graph.

5. From the old graph folder, copy over what snapshots do not contain: images and other binary assets, folders listed in `:hidden`, and Tine's trash in `logseq/.tine-trash/`. If your `assets` folder is a link to a folder outside the graph, the sidecars from the zip's `assets/` belong in that folder.
6. Start Tine (and the sync tool) again. Tine reads the files like any external change.

blocks.raw: ## Recovering by hand with Tine closed

children.raw: If your graph folder is in a git repository, Settings → **Graph** → **Commit changes to git** → **Commit automatically** makes Tine commit the graph's changes for you (the default is **Off**, and the choice applies to this device only). Tine commits after a minute without edits, at most once per interval (**At most every** 10 minutes by default; you can set any whole number from 1 to 1440 minutes), once more when you quit, and before and after a rename, merge, delete or backup restore, so each of those is its own commit you can undo with git.

Git is optional. If the graph is not in a repository, Settings → **Graph** offers **Make this graph a git repository**. It adds Tine's `.gitignore` rules and makes a first commit, without changing any page file. Automatic commits and sync stay **Off** until you choose them. Optionally paste an **Empty remote HTTPS URL** to set `origin`, publish the first commit and set the upstream. Tine does not create repositories on a host: create an empty one there first. If sign-in or the transfer fails, your local graph and commit stay safe; use the existing **Sign in** below and **Finish repository setup** to retry, including after reopening the graph. A non-empty remote is refused. Clear the optional URL and finish to keep local history without publishing. Automatic commits and sync remain off while publication is pending.

On Welcome or in the graph menu, choose **Clone a graph from a git URL**, paste its HTTPS address and choose the parent folder. Tine creates a folder named after the repository, refuses a non-empty destination, and opens its default branch with the upstream ready for sync. If it needs **Sign in**, use the same username and personal access token as sync below; the token stays in the same private file on this device. On Android choose a local shared-storage folder; on iOS choose inside Tine's app folders. No computer or separate git tool is needed to clone. Automatic commits and sync stay **Off**. If the repository contains names this device cannot distinguish (case or Unicode normalization), Tine stops before checking out files; its downloaded `.git` folder can remain in the destination. If opening a completed clone fails, **Open the cloned graph** retries without cloning again.

Clone refuses remotes without commits or a default branch. To start with an empty remote, create a graph first and use **Make this graph a git repository** with that URL. A refused clone can leave its downloaded `.git` metadata in the destination; choose another empty location for a later clone.

A commit holds every change git sees in the graph folder, including edits made by other programs; files your `.gitignore` excludes are left out. With automatic commits on, Tine adds two lines to the graph folder's `.gitignore`, each once and only if git does not already ignore those files: `.syncthing.*` for Syncthing's temporary files, and `logseq/.tine-*` for Tine's own files for this device, such as its trash in `logseq/.tine-trash/` (committed, the trash would stop two devices syncing one repository at the first deleted page). Tine tells you in a notice and in the git status in Settings. You can remove a line; Tine will not add it again on this device for this graph path, even after restarting or turning automatic commits off and on. A failed attempt is not retried automatically. Tine's commits always exclude Syncthing temporary files and Tine's own files, even if writing `.gitignore` fails. If an earlier Tine committed its own files, Tine removes them from git (not from disk) in a separate commit, "Tine: stop tracking its own device files", just before its next commit (until then `git status` may list them as changed); a sync never writes another device's copies, and conflict copies (`*.sync-conflict-*`) are still committed unless your own ignore rules exclude them. After repository setup, Tine changes repository config only when you choose the line-ending repair below. To keep another file out of the history, add it to `.gitignore`: a file you only untrack with `git rm --cached` is committed again. Tine pushes and pulls only with a sync option (below). When the graph is a subfolder of a bigger repository, only that subfolder is committed, and changes you staged elsewhere stay staged.

Commits use your git `user.name` and `user.email`, with the message “Tine: autosave” or a description such as “Rename page "old" to "new"”. Every 50 commits Tine packs the new ones together, so the repository does not fill with small files; it never rewrites what is already packed.

With autocommit on, Settings shows the branch Tine commits to and the last commit (its short hash and time). It also says when Tine can't commit and why: another git command holds the repository's `index.lock` (Tine waits; if it stays held for over 30 minutes, Settings names the file so you can remove it after a crash; an empty `index.lock` that has not changed for 10 minutes while Tine itself is not using git is almost always left over from a commit that was cut short, and Tine offers **Remove the stale lock**), a detached HEAD, sparse checkout, a `.gitattributes` filter such as git-crypt or LFS, a missing index (run `git reset`), unresolved conflicts, or on macOS and iOS a repository without `core.precomposeunicode`. A failed attempt shows as "Last attempt failed" with the reason.

If git cleanup fails, Settings says "Git cleanup is waiting; commits continue. Tine will retry automatically." Your commits continue to record changes; cleanup waits at least 10 minutes before retrying on a successful commit cycle. This status clears when cleanup succeeds and does not produce repeated toasts.

**Commit and sync on demand** and **Commit and sync automatically** also exchange commits with the branch's upstream (what `git push -u` or `git clone` set up), so another computer that syncs the same repository sees your changes. **On demand** syncs when you press **Sync now** in Settings; **automatically** syncs after each commit and once per interval as well. A sync fetches the remote, brings this device's graph up to its newer commits, and pushes your commits. When nothing changed on either side it costs one short request to the remote. Tine never merges, rebases or force-pushes. The line-ending repair below changes only this repository's `core.autocrlf`, when you choose it.

Sync needs the graph folder to be the repository's top folder (bringing in a bigger repository would change files Tine does not own), a branch with an upstream, and no line-ending conversion (`core.autocrlf`, or `text`/`eol` in `.gitattributes`). Otherwise Settings says why and offers only the commit options. Settings shows the remote's name and address, and the time and result of the last sync.

For an `https://` remote, press **Sign in** and enter your username and a personal access token that can read and write the repository (GitHub: Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens; GitLab: Preferences → Access tokens; Codeberg: Settings → Applications). Tine keeps the token in a private file on this device, never in the graph, the repository or Tine's settings; **Sign out** deletes it. A remote on this computer (`file://`) needs no sign-in. SSH remotes are not supported yet.

When this device and the remote **both have new commits**, each has commits the other lacks, for example after editing on two computers between syncs. Tine then stops syncing and changes nothing. Merge in git: press **Copy the git command**, run it (`git pull`) in a terminal in the graph folder, resolve any conflicts and commit, then press **Sync now** and Tine pushes the merge. Merging inside Tine comes later.

A sync waits rather than overwrite anything: while a page it would update has unsaved edits, while another program changed a file, or while another git command holds the repository, it tries again at the next sync. If a file it would update is a link, a submodule or staged differently, Settings names the file so you can fix it in git. When a problem needs you, or keeps coming back, a notice also appears above the page with a way to fix it ("Copy the git command", "Open the folder", "Sign in again") and a button to Git settings; it goes away once a sync succeeds.

On Android and iOS git works as on a computer, plus two moments a computer does not have. When you switch to another app, Tine saves your pages and commits pending edits immediately, without waiting for the interval, and, with **Commit and sync automatically**, pushes; switching apps without edits adds no commit. It never starts bringing in changes while in the background. When you come back to Tine, **Commit and sync automatically** syncs at once. If the phone ends Tine in the middle of a commit or push, the repository can be left with a lock file such as `.git/index.lock`: nothing is lost, but Tine waits. Once that lock has not changed for 10 minutes, a notice (and Settings) offers **Remove the stale lock**; Tine checks the file again when you press it, removes only that file and then commits, and never removes a lock by itself. A lock on the branch, such as `.git/refs/heads/main.lock`, is never offered: after 30 minutes Settings names it for you to remove. On Android, shared storage cannot change only the capitalization of a file name in one step, so a rename by capitalization alone (`c.md` to `C.md`, yours or a pulled one) goes through a temporary name in Tine's own `logseq/.tine-respell` folder. If Tine is stopped in between, the page is back under its new name the next time Tine opens the graph; nothing is lost.

blocks.raw: ## Git: automatic commits and sync

children.raw: Git for Windows normally converts LF line endings in commits to CRLF on disk (`core.autocrlf=true`). Tine's sync compares exact bytes and refuses that conversion, including `core.autocrlf=input`. If every tracked file's bytes already match the index and no attribute conversion remains, Settings → **Graph** → **Commit changes to git** and the sync notice offer **Turn off line-ending conversion for this repository**. It changes only `core.autocrlf` in this repository's `.git/config`, never global or system settings, and changes no graph file. A running sync retries without a restart; otherwise choose a sync option after the repair.

Run `git status --short` to review what will be committed. Run `git add --all` to stage your changes, then `git commit -m "Save notes before changing line endings"` to keep them in history. If there is nothing to commit, skip the commit. Run `git status --porcelain`; continue only if it prints nothing. If the commit fails, stop and fix that first.

Run `git config --local core.autocrlf false` to turn conversion off for this repository only. Then run `git reset --hard HEAD` to re-check out the current commit's files, now without conversion. This overwrites tracked files, so run it only after the clean-status check and with no new edits. Your committed edit stays in history and the branch stays at the same commit.

Run `git status --short` again: it should print nothing. Your edits are committed and the files now have the same line endings as their committed blobs (normally LF). Reopen Tine and choose a sync option in Settings → **Graph**, or press **Sync now** if already chosen.

If files differ, the notice gives their count and one example. Do not just turn conversion off: the next automatic commit could record Windows line endings throughout your graph. Save your edits, close Tine and other editors, and pause other sync tools before these steps. Open a terminal in the graph's top folder. Keep it closed to new edits until the checkout finishes.

A `.gitattributes` rule such as `text`, `eol`, `crlf`, `filter`, `ident` or `working-tree-encoding` still blocks sync even with autocrlf off. The notice names the rule and path. Resolve that conversion in git first and commit the result; removing autocrlf alone cannot fix it. Missing files, submodules and unreadable paths also need fixing before the button can be offered. Files intentionally committed with CRLF stay CRLF; this repair never rewrites history or changes committed content.

blocks.raw:
## Git line endings on Windows
id:: e7ad234c-701e-4473-a6e3-111264be9655

children.raw: The changes notice stays at the top while you scroll, so **Mark page seen** remains reachable even in the middle of a long page.

On a graph that is in a git repository, Tine marks what other people or tools committed to a page since you last left it. Open a single page: a thin bar in the margin marks each block that changed, a removed block leaves a line “A block was removed here” where it stood (click it to read the removed text), and the page header says “N changes since you last looked” while N is more than 0. Whenever there is a change, even a single one, **Previous change** and **Next change** in that header step through them in page order, from where you are; each scrolls the block (or the “A block was removed here” line) into view below the header and highlights it briefly, opening a folded parent on the way without changing the file, and “3 of 12” shows where you are, with “wrapped around” when a step crossed the end of the list. They never put a block into edit mode. The same two steps are in the command palette as **Next change since you last looked** and **Previous change since you last looked** with no key assigned (Settings → **Keyboard shortcuts**). Leaving the page (opening another page, closing its tab or pane, or quitting) marks it seen, so the bars are gone when you come back. The journals feed, the sidebar, a zoomed block and references show no bars.

It works only on git graphs, and it compares **commits**, not files on disk. An edit that was never committed (for example one made by an external editor while Tine's automatic commits are off) is invisible until it is committed. Your own commits never count: “You” is the identity Tine's own commits are made under (your git `user.name` and `user.email`), so with **Commit automatically** on, Tine's autosave commits don't appear as changes. If the repository has no identity set, only commits Tine made under its placeholder name count as yours, and the header tooltip says so.

The first time a graph is opened here, everything up to that moment counts as seen. Commits from others that arrive later (for example through Syncthing) show on every page they touch, including pages you have not opened yet. A block you edit yourself after it was marked loses its bar; a page with more than 200 touching commits since you last looked counts every change, yours included, and the header tooltip says so.

**Mark page seen** is in the page's actions menu and the command palette; **Mark whole graph seen** is in the command palette and Settings → **Graph**; **Forget seen state** (Settings → **Graph**) clears what this device remembers, after which every page compares against the moment you press it. The record lives on this device only, never in the graph and never synced.

blocks.raw: ## Git: what changed since you last looked

children.raw: Deleting a page or journal moves the file to `logseq/.tine-trash/pages/` or `logseq/.tine-trash/journals/`, not permanent deletion. Its name gains a timestamp followed by `__`.
Duplicate journal files you trash and unused media from an orphan scan land there too, and discarded sync-conflict copies and a file's pre-resolution version go to `logseq/.tine-trash/conflicts/`.

To restore something, open the matching typed folder, remove the timestamp and `__` from its name, then move it into `pages/`, `journals/`, or `assets/` with your file manager. Tine picks it up like any external change.

Settings → **Files** → **Orphaned media** (**Scan for orphans**) can find media no block links to (a deleted block keeps its files, so unused media accumulates) and trash it, and **Empty asset trash** deletes *asset* trash permanently — page, journal, and conflict recovery files are always kept.

blocks.raw: ## Trash

children.raw: Keep Syncthing or Dropbox on your graph — Tine is built to coexist with them. Two files that resolve to the same journal day are kept, not dropped: the day joins the **N conflicts** queue, where you fold them block by block on the day itself, and Settings → **Backups & recovery** → **Duplicate journal days** offers **Open**, **Merge**, **Rename**, or **Trash** per file.
A `*.sync-conflict-*` (or `(conflicted copy)`) file never appears as a page. Files carrying unresolved git or Fossil merge markers are also quarantined from ordinary saves rather than rewritten.

Both kinds appear in one **N conflicts** badge in the sidebar. Open a conflicted page to compare the two versions block by block: choose **Mine**, **Theirs**, or both for each differing block, accept a suggested **Merged** version when both sides edited separate parts of one block, then **Apply resolution**. A pinned notice keeps the review reachable while you scroll: tap it to unroll the review in place. Nothing is auto-merged or auto-deleted.

Choosing the **N conflicts** badge opens the **Conflicts** page: every page that needs a decision, grouped by source, with how many blocks are left ("—" when not counted). Click a page to resolve it, or shift-click to open it in the right sidebar and keep the list in view. **Discard copy** moves a provider conflict copy to the trash, including a copy whose page no longer exists.

blocks.raw: ## Sync tools and conflict copies

children.raw: Tine does not silently rename journal files when a graph opens. If an otherwise valid journal uses its display title as its filename (for example `Jun 18th, 2026.md`), the day may look empty because the filename cannot be matched to its date.
Settings → **Backups & recovery** → **Journal files named by title** lists these files. Review the list and choose **Rename to date names**; Tine takes a snapshot first.

blocks.raw: ## Journal files named by title

children.raw: Settings → **Graph** → **Export HTML and read-only app…** exports your `public:: true` pages as a standalone site.
