Give the export a name and choose a destination folder outside the graph; tick **Include every page not marked public:: false** to export pages that carry no `public::` property as well. A page marked `public:: false` is never exported, not even with that box ticked or with `:publishing/all-pages-public? true` in `config.edn`, and its blocks never appear in another page's embeds, queries or references. A graph with no `public:: true` page exports 0 pages, and the result line says that only `public:: true` pages are exported. Nothing is uploaded, and your graph is not touched.

**Export…** in a query's header exports the pages its results live on as a standalone site. Pages marked `public:: false` and the exports page stay out even when the query matches them; the review lists what was left out and says when the export includes the page the query is written on. Readers see the pages, not the query itself, unless you tick **Include the query text**. Review the page list first; Tine writes the export to `published-queries/<folder>/` inside your graph. If that folder exists, choose **Replace** (the previous export is kept in recovery and its path is reported) or **Create a separate export**. A query about blocks exports **whole pages**, not just the matched blocks, and the dialog asks you to confirm that.
Queries inside a query export show only results on the exported pages; they do not report how many results were left out on other pages.

A query export carries referenced local assets in its own `assets/` folder, so you can move or share the whole export folder. Missing assets are reported as warnings. Settings → **Graph** → **Query export size limit** sets the copied-asset budget for this device (default **1 GiB**). An export that exceeds it stops before replacing any previous export, with **Adjust limit in Settings…** to raise it.
`published-queries/` output never becomes graph pages and is excluded from graph backups. Back up an export folder separately if you want to retain it.

Serve an export folder over HTTP (any static host, or `python3 -m http.server` inside it) to open it as a read-only app; opening `index.html` straight from disk, or adding `?static` to the address, shows the plain static site instead.

Sheets on an exported page (tables, boards and grids) come out as the same tables, boards and grids you see in the app, including formula columns, filters and aggregate footers: Tine computes them with the app's own sheet code before it writes the export, in **Export HTML and read-only app…**, a query's **Export…** and **Export to PDF…** alike. The command-line export (`tine export static` or `tine export live`) has no app to compute them, so it writes a sheet as the plain outline of its rows. A sheet that cannot be computed, or that changed while the export was being prepared, is written the same way with a visible note, and the export still succeeds. A table or board that shows a query's results is written the same way — the query's own columns and its rows on the page they came from — when the block holds just that one query; a result on a page the export does not publish is left out of the table (and of its counts and totals), and if the results changed while the export was being prepared the block is written as the query's usual result list instead. A query table's exported totals summarize only the rows it exports, so they can differ from the live footer's totals over the query's complete sample.

If a query exceeds the **Print query limit**, PDF export names the reason and stops before opening the print dialog. Narrow the query and try again. Starting another PDF export supersedes the pending export; only the latest request may open its printout.

Right-click a page title → **Export to PDF…** prints one page on a light background. It is offered on desktop only: printing is unavailable inside a mobile WebView, so Android and iOS do not show it. **Export HTML and read-only app…** works on every platform.

To find HTML export quickly, open the command palette and run **Export graph as HTML and read-only app…**; it opens the same Graph settings export control. The folder picker starts at your last successful export destination on this device. The result shows the exported site's path; on desktop, **Show in folder** reveals it in the file manager. Mobile keeps its existing folder picker behaviour and does not offer the desktop reveal action.

Export cleanup removes selected links, tags and emphasis from ordinary text. Text inside inline code and fenced code stays literal in Text, OPML and HTML exports, even when it contains `[[links]]`, `#tags` or emphasis markers.

**Copy / export as…** on a block or page offers **Plain text** (without formatting markers) or **Markdown** / **Org** (with formatting preserved), then Text / OPML / HTML destinations with cleanup and depth controls. Markdown, Org, HTML and OPML resolve block references and expand page and block embeds, without adding source captions. Embedded outlines keep their children; expansion stops after five nested embeds. Internal properties such as `id::` are hidden. Text exports keep user properties as `key:: value` unless **Remove properties** is selected; page properties are omitted.

blocks.raw: ## Export

children.raw: Share a page, or the pages a query selects, as a folder export in your graph or as an encrypted link: see [[Features/Share pages]]. Nothing leaves your device until you confirm in the Share dialog.

blocks.raw: ## Share pages

children.raw: Everything dated lives here: one journal page per day, tasks as plain-text markers at the start of a block, `[#A]`–`[#C]` priorities, and `SCHEDULED:`/`DEADLINE:` planning lines with calendar pickers. This page maps the shipped behavior; [[Workflows/Capture and plan your day]] walks through using it, and [[Feature showcase]] shows each construct rendered.

blocks.raw: # Journals, tasks, and scheduling

children.raw: On opening a graph, today's journal and nearby saved days appear while the graph is still loading. Days mentioned only by other blocks join the feed when the graph is ready, keeping your place and any open editor. References, queries, and embeds fill in as their results arrive.

A date mentioned by another block appears even without a journal file, at any distance in the past or future. Past days appear in chronological order; unreferenced days without files stay out of the feed. Viewing a fileless day creates no file: typing into its empty body creates it through the usual save path. Upcoming is off by default. Add a block containing `{{upcoming}}` to the **Journal sections** page to show referenced future days in a collapsed **Upcoming** group at that position, nearest first. Expand a day to see its **Linked References**, or click its title to open the day page. Adding or removing the last mention updates the feed; deleting a journal file keeps its day listed while another block still references it.

The **Journals** entry in the left sidebar (or **g j**) opens a multi-day feed — one continuous, editable list, newest day first. Today's journal is always shown at the top of the feed. With no daily template, its file is created lazily on your first edit: the feed shows the day, but no file exists until you type.

"Today" follows the calendar of the machine's local time zone as Tine's backend reads it, so today's journal rolls over at local midnight — including when Tine stays open overnight or resumes from sleep — and the Agenda, carry-over and the **Go to date** calendar all use that same day.

**g n** and **g p** step to the next or previous calendar day from the journal you are viewing (from another page they start at today, and they open that day even if it has no file yet). The calendar button in the top bar (**Go to date**) opens a month grid — days that already have an entry are marked — to jump to any day's journal.

**Shift-click** a day in **Go to date**, or its **Today** button, to open that journal in the right sidebar while keeping your current page. Shift-clicking the calendar button itself opens today's journal there.
**Shift-click Journals** in the left sidebar or toolbar to open today's journal in the right sidebar without leaving the main page. A plain click or **g j** still opens the multi-day feed.

**Linked References** appears beneath each day in the Journals feed when other blocks link to that journal, with a count and the same filter, expand, and edit controls as an individually opened page. References load as you scroll to the day. Empty sections stay hidden; the graph’s linked-reference collapse threshold controls whether they start folded.

Settings → **Journals** → **Journal date format** controls the display titles and how new `[[date]]` titles are written (saved to `:journal/page-title-format`, traveling with the graph). The choices match Logseq’s built-in formats, including weekday and `yyyy年MM月dd日` titles. `E`, `EE`, and `EEE` show abbreviated weekdays (such as `Fri`); `EEEE` shows the full name (`Friday`). Graphs using the older `:date-formatter` setting are also supported: `:journal/page-title-format` takes precedence when both are present, and opening a graph keeps the legacy setting untouched. A hand-edited format may use pattern parts Tine does not support, such as quoted text (`'w'`) or week numbers (`ww`): when today's journal shows the `config.edn` queries, a note above them names the setting, the pattern and those parts. Tine does not interpret them as Logseq does, so such journal titles or file names may differ from Logseq's, but it renames and rewrites nothing. It renames no files: journal *file* names are untouched and existing journals keep working. If some journal files are named after their title instead of their date, their days look empty; Settings → **Backups & recovery** lists them under **Journal files named by title** with a **Rename to date names** button, which never runs on its own. For files, duplicate days, and the on-disk layout in general, see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

Settings → **Journals** → **New-journal template** inserts a template into each new day (`:default-templates {:journals …}` in `config.edn`); “(none)” means blank days, the default. Make a template from a block's right-click menu (**Make a template…**). A page can be a template too: put `template:: Name` among the page's own property lines at its top (the lines before the first bullet), and `/Name` inserts those property lines (without `template::`) as one block, as in Logseq.

Unsupported journal date pattern notes also appear in Settings → **Journals**, beside **Journal date format**, even when a Today's sections page replaces the configured queries. The notes update when the format changes, including edits to `config.edn`.

blocks.raw: ## Journals

children.raw: For a checklist inside one block, put `* [ ] item` on a continuation line with **Shift+Enter** (use `+ [ ] item` in Org). Click its checkbox to tick just that item without opening the editor. Nested checklist items use the same indent step as child blocks. Collapsing the block hides child blocks; its own inline checklist stays visible, matching Logseq's default.

The marker set is `TODO`, `DOING`, `NOW`, `LATER`, `WAITING`, `WAIT`, `STARTED`, `IN-PROGRESS`, `DONE`, `CANCELED`, `CANCELLED` — stored as the plain first word of the block's first line, like Logseq.
Settings → **Journals** → **Task workflow** chooses between two cycling lanes, TODO / DOING and NOW / LATER (`:preferred-workflow`, traveling with the graph); NOW / LATER is the default.

Click the marker chip for Logseq's two-state toggle: TODO ↔ DOING or LATER ↔ NOW (a chip click never clears `DONE`). **Ctrl+Enter** (Cmd on Mac) uses the full keyboard cycle TODO → DOING → DONE → none, or LATER → NOW → DONE → none, applied to every selected task when several blocks are selected.

Every open task also shows a checkbox in front of it: click to mark DONE, click again to reopen to the workflow's open marker (TODO or LATER). `DONE` shows a checked box; `CANCELED`/`CANCELLED` show none. The same live checkbox edits the source block inside query results, linked references, embeds, and inline `((block references))`: ticking it there completes the referenced task on its own page.
Queries filter on markers with a task clause, e.g. `(task TODO DOING)` in `{{query }}`, or as a **Task** condition in the visual query builder.

blocks.raw: ## Task markers

children.raw: `[#A]`, `[#B]`, `[#C]` sit directly after the task marker; a block without a task marker can carry one too. Type slash, choose **Priority A** (or B, C), and the chip updates in place.
Queries can filter on priority with a `(priority A)` clause; the [[Feature showcase]] shows the constructs rendered.

A header priority is also a reference to its letter's page: a block with `[#A]` appears in page A's **Linked References**. A task marker such as TODO similarly refers to its marker page. Queries on `[[A]]` or `[[TODO]]` find those blocks, as in Logseq; a priority written later in the body does not create this reference.

blocks.raw: ## Priorities

children.raw: A block's plan is a `SCHEDULED:` and/or `DEADLINE:` line with an Org-style timestamp `<2026-07-07 Tue>`, optionally with a clock time `<2026-07-07 Tue 14:30>`. Convention: use SCHEDULED for the day you intend to work on something, DEADLINE for the day it must be done.

While editing, type / and choose **Scheduled** or **Deadline**. Click a day to select it, then optionally use **+ Add time** for `HH:mm` and the repeat menu (No repeat / Daily / Weekly / Monthly / Yearly, with **from completion**). **Done** or clicking outside applies the chosen date, time, and repeat together. **Escape** cancels all pending changes and returns to the editor at the same caret. The calendar takes keyboard focus: **Left/Right** move one day, **Up/Down** move one week, and **Enter** applies the focused day (or the chosen date when entering a time). Its first weekday follows Settings → **Journals** → **First day of week**. Today is marked in the grid; click it to pick today. **Clear** (at the left, away from **Done**) removes an existing date. The block gains a calendar **date chip** — click it to edit the date, time, or repeat with the same Done/outside/Escape rules.

**/Date picker** opens the same calendar to insert a `[[date]]` link at the cursor in your graph's journal title format. Choose a day, then use **Done**, **Enter**, or click outside to insert it; **Escape** cancels. **/Today**, **/Tomorrow**, and **/Yesterday** insert the corresponding journal date directly; **/That day** inserts the containing journal's date.

You may also type a planning line anywhere in the block: on leaving the editor it moves to its canonical spot — right after the first line, before any properties, SCHEDULED before DEADLINE — like Logseq. A `SCHEDULED:` inside inline code or a code fence stays literal content and is never moved.
The same chips and pickers appear wherever the block does — in linked references, query results, and embeds.

blocks.raw: ## Scheduled and deadline dates

children.raw: Today's journal ends with a **Scheduled & Deadline** list of *open* items whose date falls inside the Agenda window — by default 7 days back and 7 ahead. Settings → **Journals** → **Agenda window** adjusts both on this device; `:scheduled/future-days` in `logseq/config.edn`, when set, controls days ahead for the whole graph instead. The list disappears when nothing matches. Set `:feature/disable-scheduled-and-deadline-query? true` to hide it.

`:default-queries {:journals [...]}` adds queries beneath today's blocks, before the agenda, in the order written. Each uses the same query renderer as a query block; a failing or unsupported query shows its own error while its neighbours remain usable, and a query with no results shows nothing, as in Logseq. String titles and static text in hiccup vectors appear as plain text. `:collapsed? true` starts a query folded. Config edits apply live; malformed journal settings show a config diagnostic. Graph code is never executed; supported advanced query shapes match [[Reference/Queries]].

Logseq's stock **NOW** query lists recent journal tasks in priority order, with missing priorities last. **NEXT** also supports older saved configurations that list NOW, LATER and TODO tasks directly referencing a journal day strictly after today and strictly before 14 days ahead. A reference on a parent block does not include its children. The 0.10.9 default instead selects tasks on journal pages strictly between today and 7 days ahead. Unsupported config queries show their title and a plain explanation; expand **Technical details** to inspect the clauses and source.

Query sections keep the **View** chosen on the sections page, including table or board, columns, sort and aggregates, beneath today's journal too. Change the View on the sections page; result blocks can be edited directly in the journal.

To add Upcoming, copy this as a block on the sections page:
```text
{{upcoming}}
```

**Today's sections page.** To choose what shows under today's journal without editing `config.edn`, hover today's journal and click **Customize today's sections…**. Tine creates a page named *Journal sections* (marked `tine.journal-sections:: true`) holding your current sections: each `:default-queries` entry as a `#+BEGIN_QUERY` block, then the Scheduled & Deadline agenda as a query block. The generated page does not include Upcoming. Today's journal shows query blocks and the Upcoming macro in outline order, including nested blocks; reorder, edit, delete or add them like on any page, and the change shows on today's journal at once. Supported sections are `{{query …}}`, `{{tine-query …}}`, `#+BEGIN_QUERY` blocks, the agenda query seeded by Customize, and `{{upcoming}}`. Other text on the page is just notes. The page can be renamed; the marker is what counts. Delete the page, or set the marker to `false`, to go back to `config.edn`, with Upcoming hidden. Logseq ignores the page and keeps using `:default-queries`, and Tine never writes to `config.edn` for this. While the page exists, the Agenda window setting no longer applies: edit the agenda query on the page instead. The small header on this page opens this Guide in the right sidebar. On ordinary pages, `{{upcoming}}` remains an unknown macro.

Add these entries inside the existing config map (use `false` to keep the built-in agenda):
```clojure
:feature/disable-scheduled-and-deadline-query? false
:scheduled/future-days 7
:default-queries
{:journals
 [{:title "Priority A tasks"
   :query (and (task TODO DOING) (priority A))
   :collapsed? false}
  {:title [:span "Open tasks"]
   :query [:find (pull ?b [*])
           :where [?b :block/marker "TODO"]]
   :inputs []
   :collapsed? true}]}
```

Keyed off the scheduled/deadline date itself, not the page's journal day, over the whole graph: an unfinished item on an old page still shows while its date is in range. A saved equivalent uses Tine's query language: `{{tine-query @block (scheduled between '-7d' and '+7d' or deadline between '-7d' and '+7d') and not task in ('DONE', 'CANCELED', 'CANCELLED')}}`. OG Logseq's simple query language has no scheduled/deadline window condition.
Finished tasks (`DONE`, `CANCELED`, `CANCELLED`) never appear, matching Logseq.

blocks.raw: ## Agenda

children.raw: With Settings → **Journals** → **Time tracking** on (the default), moving into DOING / NOW records a clock-in and moving back to TODO / LATER or into DONE records a clock-out, as OG-compatible `:LOGBOOK:` `CLOCK:` rows (seconds on by default via `:logbook/settings`). This also applies when Ctrl/Cmd+Enter cycles several selected blocks, in one Undo step. Saved to `:feature/enable-timetracking?`.
Blocks with clock rows show a small elapsed-time badge with a Type / Start / End / Span tooltip; the `:LOGBOOK:` drawer itself stays hidden by default, like Logseq.

The logbook stays out of the text editor too. Editing the task keeps its clock history; **Enter** at the end of its text leaves the history on that task. Backspace or Delete merging two blocks keeps only the surviving block's clock history. The absorbed block's hidden properties, including heading and flashcard state, are dropped. Its ID is kept when referenced; if both blocks have IDs and the absorbed ID is referenced, the merge leaves both blocks in place to keep the references working. Undo restores a merge.

A `:LOGBOOK:` drawer you type by hand stays visible until you leave the editor, so you can finish it. Copying or cutting whole blocks carries their clock history, including between Markdown and Org pages.

If an edit cannot safely retain hidden history, the editor stays open with your typed text and shows a red error. Correct the text to continue, or use **Copy** on that message to keep the exact typed text, even if the page later closes. The error stays until you dismiss it.
Toggled off, markers change without writing log rows.

blocks.raw: ## Time tracking and the logbook

children.raw: Put a repeater inside the timestamp, e.g. `<2026-07-07 Tue +1w>` (or pick one in the calendar popup); the units are `d`, `w`, `m`, `y` for days, weeks, months, years.

Marking a repeating task done does not close it: the date advances to the next occurrence and the marker resets to the workflow's open state (TODO, or LATER under NOW / LATER). This works from the checkbox, the marker chip, and Ctrl+Enter.
A timed repeater such as `<2026-09-30 Wed 09:00 +1w>` advances to the next date while keeping `09:00`; the date picker keeps that time and repeater when you re-pick its date.
`+1w` advances from the stored date; `.+1w` counts from the day you complete it; `++1w` skips missed occurrences, landing past today. The repeater survives date re-picks in the calendar.

blocks.raw: ## Repeating tasks

children.raw: In the feed and on a journal page, hover the day's title row or focus a title-row control with the keyboard to reveal the carry buttons. On touch devices without hover they stay visible.

On a past day, **Carry unfinished tasks → today** moves its open tasks (every marker except DONE / CANCELED / CANCELLED) to today. On today, **Carry from previous day** pulls from the most recent day that has content and **Carry last N days** goes further back. The same action is on a past journal day's right-click menu, and the command palette (**Ctrl+Shift+P**) has last-7 / 30 / 365-day presets.

Settings → **Journals** tunes it: **Show carry-over buttons**, **Carry-over keeps context** (on: move whole blocks that contain an open task; off: pull out just the task), **Carry-over header** (add a “Carried over” heading), and **Carry “last N days”**.

blocks.raw: ## Carry-over

children.raw: Settings → **Journals** collects every control above: **Journal date format**, **First day of week**, the carry-over controls, **Task workflow**, **Time tracking**, **New-journal template**, and **Agenda window**. For the ones in use, see [[Workflows/Capture and plan your day]].

blocks.raw: ## Settings quick map

children.raw: The precise rules behind the moving parts: pages and aliases, links and tags, block references and embeds, the two reference panels on every page, and every search surface from the switcher to the saved-search page. [[Workflows/Find and revisit]] walks through using them in order; [[Feature showcase]] shows each construct rendered.

blocks.raw: # Pages, links, references, and search

children.raw: Collapsed Linked References, Unlinked References and Pages tagged with keep their last count. A faint dot labelled **Count may be out of date** means related edits have arrived; opening the section reloads its current answer.
**Pages tagged with** remembers your fold choice for each page when you switch tabs or return to the page, until you switch graphs.

With a Chinese IME, type `【【` for `[[]]` or `（（` for `(())`: the caret lands inside the ASCII reference and the usual page or block search becomes active. Conversion waits until composition finishes, so it does not interrupt choosing a character. Closing is the same: typing `】` before the `]` that `【【` left (or `）` before a `)` when auto-pairing is on) steps over it instead of adding a second closer, so `【【name】】` ends as `[[name]]` with the caret after it. Typing `【` or `（` around selected text wraps it with ASCII brackets or parentheses; a second opener makes a reference. At the start of a line, `《〈` becomes `<` and opens the block command menu.

A page is any name you link to. Type `[[` while editing and completion offers existing pages and their aliases; an alias row is labelled **alias of** its page, so you can tell it from an ordinary page with a similar name. Whether **Enter** prefers the strongest existing match or exactly what you typed is Settings → **Editor** → Advanced → **Link autocomplete default** (**OG adaptive**, **Prefer existing**, **Prefer exactly what I typed**), and an exact existing name always selects the existing page.

A page link whose page does not exist yet renders in a dimmed link color with a dotted underline, still readable and still clearly a link. It still works — opening it lets you create the page. Tags are never dimmed, because most tags in a normal graph have no page of their own. Tine marks the difference on purpose; Logseq only dims untitled pages.

A link to the web or to a file is underlined with a solid line, as in Logseq; a link to a page has no underline, and a block reference is underlined in the link color. Each kind has its own CSS class, and the underline and the missing-page color are `--tine-*` tokens, so your `custom.css` can restyle them: see [[Workflows/Customize Tine's look]].

A page with a `tine.icon::` property (an emoji, such as `tine.icon:: 🏁`) shows it on its title, in links to it, and in front of its name in the sidebar's Favorites, Recent and All pages lists and in the right sidebar. A favorite without an icon keeps the star. The `tine.icon::` property stays visible in the page-properties block; click its row to edit it. A page with no `tine.icon::` uses its `icon::` property instead (Logseq's own icon property, so icons you already set there keep working); when a page has both, `tine.icon::` wins.

**Image page icons:** use `tine.icon:: ![](../assets/quick-capture.png)` in Markdown, or `#+tine.icon: [[file:../assets/quick-capture.png]]` in Org (`icon::` accepts the same links when the page has no `tine.icon::`, but Logseq prints an `icon::` value as raw text before every title, so an image link there shows up as markup in Logseq). The link is relative to the page file and must resolve inside the graph's `assets/` folder, the same containment boundary as images in blocks. Static PNG, JPG and JPEG files no larger than 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) are supported (extensions ignore case). Larger files show no icon. Other graph folders, escapes, remote URLs, other formats, animated PNGs, missing, unreadable and undecodable files show no icon or raw link text; no remote image is requested. Ordinary text and emoji icons keep their existing behavior. The property row still shows the value as written. There are no downloads, copied files, persistent caches or resized copies. The image stays in the emoji-sized box everywhere, including the title; width/height attributes are ignored. Property edits and file replacement update it without reloading. Logseq shows `tine.icon::` as an ordinary property.

To set an icon without knowing the property syntax, open **Page actions** (the ⋯ beside the title), then **Set page icon…** below **Page properties…**. Enter an emoji or short text such as `AB`, then press Enter or **Save icon**. On Windows, Win + . opens the native emoji picker; on macOS, use Control + Command + Space. **Remove page icon** clears it. Icons in the sidebar lists follow edits immediately, including external file changes. Markdown stores `tine.icon::`; Org stores `#+tine.icon:` through the same page-property editor. A page that only has `icon::` is edited in place, and **Remove page icon** clears both properties.

Page names ignore letter case: `[[foo]]` and `[[Foo]]` open one page. On a case-insensitive disk that page opens under the spelling its file already has, so a differently cased link never creates a second page.
A link to a page that does not exist yet is not broken — opening it gives you an empty page, and its file is written only when you first type something into it.

A name with slashes, like [[Project/Roadmap]], is a namespace: it nests under `Project` in the sidebar's collapsible namespace tree, and a namespaced page gains an automatic **Hierarchy** section listing its descendant pages.
Journals are pages too — one per day, reachable from **Journals** in the sidebar. Their formats, templates, tasks, and agenda are mapped in [[Reference/Journals, tasks, and scheduling]].
The application chrome — toolbar, sidebars, buttons — is not text-selectable, so a stray drag never starts a selection there; page content and editors stay selectable.

blocks.raw: ## Pages and namespaces

children.raw: `[[Page]]` links and `#tag` tags run on the same machinery: a tag links and collects references like any page, and a tag with no page of its own is perfectly normal. A page's `tags::` property values render as navigable links too.

A labelled page link such as [read the welcome]([[Welcome to Tine]]) shows your words while opening the page. External `[label](https://…)` links are ordinary Markdown, bare URLs and emails autolink, and **Mod+L** inserts a link around the selection. `http`, `https` and `mailto` links open in your browser or mail app. A `file:` link — `[Test](file:///home/you/report.odt)`, or `[Test](file://D:\test.txt)` on Windows — opens that file or folder in whatever application your system uses for it, on desktop; a file that is no longer there is reported instead of doing nothing. A file path is read from the graph folder, from any page or journal: `[report](files/report.pdf)` opens `files/report.pdf` inside the graph, while `[report](../files/report.pdf)` opens a file in the sibling `files` folder outside the graph. Parent steps such as `../../` are preserved. Absolute paths such as `/home/you/report.pdf` and `D:\notes\report.pdf` also open through the same desktop file opener as `file:` links. These links look ordinary and show the resolved path on hover. Use `[spaced](<../files/my file.txt>)` for spaces. Links into the graph's assets folder keep Logseq's established graph asset route. Opening local files is available on desktop only, including for `file:` URLs; Android and iOS report the refusal. Tine does not rewrite links when you move files or graphs. A link to another app, such as `zotero://…`, `obsidian://…` or `shortcuts://…` on iOS, first asks whether to open it, showing the whole link, and then opens it in that app. `javascript:` and `data:` links never open.

Click a link to follow it. **Shift+click** opens it in the right sidebar, **Ctrl/Cmd+click** opens it in the other pane, and **middle-click** opens it in a background tab. While editing, **Ctrl+O** opens the link at the caret and **Ctrl+Shift+O** opens it in the right sidebar — matching Logseq's shortcuts, no mouse needed.

blocks.raw: ## Links and tags

children.raw: Put `alias:: Another name, Third name` among the page properties at the top of a page — as [[Feature showcase]] does with `alias:: Kitchen sink (features)` — and links under those names land on the same page.

Aliases join pages into an **alias group**, one thing under several names: if Alpha has `alias:: Beta` and Beta has `alias:: Gamma`, all three names are one group. Self-aliases, chains and a name claimed by two pages are all allowed.

Under the title, a page in a group shows two rows. **Also called** lists the group's names that have no page file of their own; a link to one opens the page that declares it. **Related pages in this alias group** lists the other names that do have their own page; a link to one opens that page. So you can tell at a glance whether a group is many names for one page or several pages. Their blocks are never merged into one view. The right sidebar shows the same rows. In the main pane, click beside the names to edit the header. The raw `alias::` property stays out of the under-title property list.

A name that is an alias of two or more pages opens the page whose file path comes first in plain character order, for example `pages/Alpha.md` before `pages/beta.md`. Capitals sort before lowercase letters, and `journals/` before `pages/`. The rule is the same on every device and every launch. A name with its own page file always opens that file, even when another page also declares it as an alias.

blocks.raw: ## Aliases

children.raw: Rendered page and block properties use a separate row for each key. Click a property key to open its page; Shift-click opens it in the right sidebar. Keys work the same in Linked References, embeds, previews and query property lists, before and after editing. Click a value or the surrounding row to edit where editing is available. Set `:property-pages/enabled? false` in `logseq/config.edn` to show plain keys instead. The `:property-pages/excludelist` controls which keys create backlinks; it does not remove key links. The earliest property group supplies the display, with the last value for a repeated key. Later groups remain in the file even when they are not displayed.

Properties are the `key:: value` lines at the top of a page and under a block's first line, and every one of them is editable from a form — not only by typing raw lines. Click **Page actions** beside a page's title (or right-click the title) and choose **Page properties…**, or type `/page properties` while editing; right-click a block for **Properties…**. The form lists the properties that page or block really has. Page properties always stay at the top of their page: moving or dragging a block above them, or pressing Tab on the block right under them, does nothing and shows a short notice saying so.

A page's form always offers **Aliases**, **Tags**, **Display title**, **Icon** and **Public**, even when the page has none of them yet. Every other property the page carries follows, each under its own key and each removable outright. **Add a property** takes any key you like.
Machine-managed properties stay out of the form: `id::` and `collapsed::` are never listed, and the `tine.` keys behind Sheets and saved searches are edited from those surfaces instead.

Each property is written in the form its own file uses. A Markdown page gets `key:: value`; an Org page gets a `#+key: value` file directive, and an Org block its `:PROPERTIES:` drawer — the shapes Logseq itself reads back.
A key does not have to be plain ASCII. `klíč:: hodnota` is an ordinary property: it can be added, changed, and removed again like any other.
A read-only page — a bundled Guide page — offers no property editing at all, rather than a form whose writes would be dropped.

blocks.raw: ## Page and block properties

children.raw: Page menus keep reference, embed and link copying under **Copy as ▸**; open that submenu to choose the form you need. A block's menu lists **Copy block ref**, **Copy block embed** and **Copy link** directly, as Logseq does. Page and block menus use the same text size and font, including submenu choices.
Settings → **Editor** → **Click a block reference to zoom in** makes a plain reference click zoom into its source block, including on another page.

Fold a page embed with the host bullet's arrow or the ordinary **Collapse/Expand** keyboard commands. Only its page-name line remains; expanding restores its content. The choice is saved on the host block, never the embedded page. If the host has children, the same fold hides those too. This works in the main pane and right sidebar.

Folds inside a page or block embed belong to the source block: its arrow and the indent guide's **Collapse/Expand all children** save `collapsed::` on the source, keeping every open view in step. Enter after a folded branch creates a visible sibling, just as on the source page. If the source is read-only, its folds stay local to the session.

Hover a page link or block reference for a preview of its blocks. The preview opens after a one-second pause and closes a moment after the pointer leaves, as in Logseq. It stops at 600 pixels or half the window, whichever is taller (never more than the window), and scrolls inside, and shows code blocks, callouts, quotes and folds the way the page does: a block the page keeps folded shows its closed bullet. Its arrow folds or unfolds the source block, saving the same `collapsed::` property as the page; the preview and an open page stay in step, and Undo restores both. If the source cannot be written or has no source block, the fold stays local to the preview. An alias shows its source page's title and page properties. Click the title to open that page in a new tab, a block bullet to open that block in a new tab, or **Open source** to open the preview's source. These actions switch to the new tab. The preview stays open while its **… → Page actions** menu is open. The blocks in a preview are the page's own blocks, as in Logseq: click a block's text to edit it right there, and the change is saved to its page. While you edit, the preview stays open even when the pointer leaves it or the page scrolls; the first **Esc** ends the edit and the next one closes the preview. Inside a preview a query shows as its text and an embed is read-only; open the source to use them. A block reference's preview also offers **Edit link** and **Remove** for that one reference, as described below.

A context menu's **Open in new tab** keeps your current tab active and confirms **Opened in a new tab**. On a narrow window (a phone held upright) the new tab is not in a tab strip; it is listed under **Open tabs** in the left sidebar. Ctrl/Cmd-click and middle-click do the same on any device that has them.

**Settings → Appearance → Advanced → Fine-tuning → Block embed breadcrumbs** optionally shows the source page and parent trail above a block embed. Each parent in the trail opens that block when you click it (Shift-click for the sidebar, Ctrl/Cmd-click for a new tab, Alt-click for the other pane). It starts off and is saved on this device.
A block embed has a subtle shaded background in both light and dark themes, so you can distinguish the embedded occurrence from an ordinary block.
When an embedded block shows its children, pressing Enter at the end of its text adds a first child there, even if the source is folded on its own page. One **Undo** removes the new child.

Type `((` while editing: the popup searches blocks, and choosing one inserts a durable `((reference))`. Tine first writes a stable `id::` on the source block, so the reference survives renames, reloads, and restarts. As in Logseq, a block is listed when it holds all the words you typed as whole words in any order (`draft foo` finds "foo draft"), or every space-separated piece of what you typed as literal text in that order (`fo dr` finds "foo draft"); blocks of the first kind come first. Case and, like Search below, accent marks are ignored (`:feature/enable-search-remove-accents? false` in `config.edn` turns the accent folding off). Letters of one piece are never picked from scattered places, so `fdr` does not find "foo draft".

The reference renders as a link-styled copy of the source text and stays in sync: edit the source and every reference updates. A referenced task keeps its marker and checkbox; tick the checkbox inside the reference to complete or reopen the source task. A per-block reference-count badge reveals the referencing blocks.
Deleting referenced blocks or merging them with Backspace/Delete shows a notice about references that broke or now point to the surviving block, with **Undo** to restore the blocks and their ids.

Click a reference to go to the block; **Shift+click** opens it in the right sidebar and **Ctrl/Cmd+click** in the other pane. Right-click an inline reference (on a touch screen, long-press it) for **Open in sidebar**, **Go to block**, **Copy block ref**, **Copy block embed**, **Replace with text**, **Replace with embed**, **Edit link** and **Remove reference**. **Edit link** opens the block that holds the reference with the reference selected; **Remove reference** deletes only that reference from its block, never the referenced block, and **Undo** brings it back; **Replace with text** swaps that one reference for the referenced block's text (without its `id::`, other hidden properties and logbook) and **Replace with embed** swaps it for an embed of the same block, both changing only the block that holds the reference, and **Undo** brings it back (a labelled reference `[label](((id)))` is replaced whole, label included); with nothing selected, **Mod+C** copies a reference to the block you're editing and **Mod+Shift+C** copies an embed.

`{{embed [[Page]]}}` and `{{embed ((id))}}` inline a whole page or a block with its context. A page embed's bullet row carries the page's name as a link (with a page glyph), and the page's blocks sit one indent step below it, on the same outline grid as ordinary children, under an accent-colored guide. Embeds are live editing surfaces: edit inside an embed and the source changes. A block embed's top block folds per page: until you fold it there, it follows its source's fold state live; folding it in one embed is remembered by that embed alone (as a `collapsed::` property on the block holding the `{{embed}}`), never on the source or on another embed of it. Folding a block further inside the embed folds that source block itself, as in Logseq: it shows folded on its own page and in every embed of it. **Move block up/down** on a page embed's top-level block moves the source block among its own siblings, as in Logseq; a short notice says which page it moved in, with **Show** to open it there. The same notice appears when a move from Linked References or a query result takes the block out of what that panel shows.

**Where a block sits is per page; what it says is shared.** A block embed shows one bullet, the embedded block's own, where the block holding `{{embed ((id))}}` sits. Its position belongs to that block: **Copy**, **Cut**, **Delete** and dragging that bullet, **Tab**/**Shift+Tab**, **Move block up/down** and selecting it act on the block containing `{{embed ...}}`, while its text and children are the source's, so editing them edits the source. A block that has its own text besides the embed keeps its own bullet, with the embed under it. A page embed has its own host bullet, which acts on the block containing `{{embed ...}}` the same way. Every other bullet inside an embed acts on its source block, just like a query result. Cutting and pasting inside an embed really moves the source block, with its properties, ID and children; all its embeds and block references follow it. Deleting inside an embed deletes the source. **Undo** restores these changes. Clicking an embedded bullet zooms into the source block. A block selection stays inside its current outline; extending it across the host/source boundary is refused.

Hover an embed to show **Edit link**, **Open source** and **Remove** just above its top-right corner, clear of the embedded content (in the right sidebar, inside that corner, so a card's close button stays reachable). **Edit link** opens the block that holds the `{{embed}}` with the embed selected, so you can change or copy it. **Open source** goes to the embedded block or page; **Shift**, **Ctrl/Cmd** and **Alt** clicks open it in the sidebar, a new tab or the other pane, as on links. **Remove** deletes only this embed from its block, never the embedded page or block, and **Undo** brings it back. With the keyboard, **Tab** reaches the same buttons and they stay visible while one has focus. On a touch screen, the same buttons appear while you edit a block inside the embed.

blocks.raw: ## Block references and embeds

children.raw: Hover the Linked or Unlinked References count to see **N blocks on M pages**. The number counts referencing blocks, as in Logseq; the count follows the active filter.

Collapsed reference sections keep their last count when relevant edits arrive. A dot beside the count, labelled **Count may be out of date**, marks it as stale. Open the section to refresh its count and results.

**Pages tagged with "X"** appears on page X before Linked References when other pages include X, or any alias of X, in their page-level `tags::` property. It lists the tagged pages as links, each once, and can be folded. Inline block tags still belong to Linked References. A `{{query (page-tags X)}}` matches the name X only, not its aliases, as in Logseq.

**Linked References** sits at the bottom of the page (and of a page opened in the right sidebar): every block that links here, grouped by source page, with a count in its header. It's live — edit in place. A page that links here from its page properties (such as `tags::`) is listed as its properties row; click the row to fix a property name or value right there, as you would on that page. The funnel button opens a filter: a **Search reference text** box, a **Clear** button, an "N of M references" count, and page/tag chips, listed alphabetically with their counts, that cycle include → exclude → off (hover a chip for the reminder).

A page and its aliases share one chip labelled with the page's canonical name. Its count is the number of reference blocks using that page or any alias; a block using two aliases counts once. Include or exclude applies to every alias. As in Logseq, a reference must carry every included chip and none of the excluded ones. Linked References saves these choices in the page's Logseq-compatible `filters::` property; an older filter naming an alias selects the same canonical chip. Unlinked References shares the alias chips but keeps its choices on this device.

One bulk button folds every group at once: it shows **Expand all** if any group is folded, otherwise **Collapse all**. Each group has its own disclosure. The block reference-count panel uses the same toggle.

A page with a lot of backlinks opens its Linked References folded, so the outline stays reachable. Logseq's `:ref/linked-references-collapsed-threshold` in `config.edn` sets where "a lot" starts (Logseq's default is 100); set it to `0` if you would rather every page start folded and open the panel yourself.

**Unlinked References**, folded by default: plain-text mentions of the page title that were never linked — the fastest way to find where a name was written without brackets. Each mention is highlighted inside its excerpt, and the highlight is clickable: it opens the source page with that exact mention selected, ready to link or edit. **Show full block** / **Show excerpt** toggles the whole block and marks every mention; a block whose mentions do not all fit the excerpt also gets a numbered jump row. The block's bullet opens the source block (Shift+click: right sidebar, Ctrl/Cmd+click: new tab, Alt+click: other pane).

Both panels have their own **Copy / export** action. The currently visible entries start selected; uncheck any you do not need, then export the selected blocks grouped by source page as Text, OPML, or HTML. Linked References exports its filtered set, and ordinary page export remains separate.

Hover previews show surrounding context without leaving the page. A preview uses the space above or below the link without covering it, and stays in place as its content changes. Its title and **Open source** stay visible while you scroll inside it.

blocks.raw: ## The reference panels on every page

children.raw: **Ctrl+K**, the quick switcher, searches page titles plus the visible text of blocks. Sections are Pages, Create, Commands, Blocks and — inside a page — Current page; with an empty query it lists recent pages. **Enter** opens the highlighted result; **Shift+Enter** opens it in the right sidebar; **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** opens it in a background tab and keeps the switcher open; **Alt+Enter** opens it in another pane; middle-click opens a background tab. **Load more results…** appears when more are available.

**Ctrl+Shift+K** searches only the open page's blocks. **Mod+F** searches all open main and split panes and expanded right-sidebar items, in pane order then sidebar stack order. The in-page find bar offers next (**Enter**) / previous (**Shift+Enter**) and a "1 / N" count; folded branches are expanded before the match is highlighted, and the match itself is scrolled into view even inside a block taller than the window.

**Find and replace.** The arrow at the left of the find bar opens a **Replace with** row. **Replace** (or **Enter** in that field) changes the highlighted match and moves to the next; **Replace all** (or **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter**) changes every match on the page you opened Find in — not the right sidebar, query results or other pages — as one **Undo** step. Matching ignores case and accents exactly as Find does. It edits the text you see, as typing would: a link's address and hidden properties such as `id::` are never changed, and a match Tine cannot tie to editable text (inside a link's markup, say) is left alone and counted in the message. On a phone, open Find from the page's **⋯** menu → **Find in page**.

The five **Search syntax** forms, listed in the switcher footer: `foo bar` (both terms), `foo OR bar` (either), `foo -draft` (exclude), `"exact phrase"`, and `/[A-Z]{3}/` (case-sensitive regular expression).

Title matches rank exact, then prefix, then substring, then fuzzy, with block text after them. After you deliberately open the same result more than once for a query, it may break ties among equally strong matches; that history stays on this device, and Settings → **Editor** → Advanced → **Learn Ctrl+K choices** disables it, with **Reset ranking** to clear it.

Search ignores accent marks and compatibility-width differences as well as case, so `cafe` finds `café`, `lodz` finds `Łódź` and `Tine` finds `Ｔｉｎｅ`. Set `:feature/enable-search-remove-accents? false` in `config.edn` to turn that off. Marks that make a different letter still count: `か` does not find `が`, `и` does not find `й`, and `क` does not find `कु`; `елка` finds `ёлка`. Page identity stays narrower: those spellings may still be separate pages.

Search scans your loaded graph text directly, so results are always current with your own edits; while it works the switcher says **Searching…**, an empty answer says **No matched results**, and **More matches exist — narrow your query to see them.** means the list was cut short.

To find Chinese page titles or aliases without changing your input method, enable Settings → **Editor** → Advanced → **Match Chinese page names by Pinyin**. In Ctrl+K or `[[` completion, `beijing`, `bei jing` or `bj` finds `北京`. Native name matches always come first; block text is not transliterated. This device preference defaults on for a Chinese UI or system language, otherwise off; **Reset Pinyin matching to language default** restores that default. Turning it off refreshes open Ctrl+K results immediately.

Mandarin matching uses one default dictionary reading per character, so polyphonic names may need that reading (`重慶` uses `zhongqing`). Traditional characters also work. Japanese kanji receive Mandarin readings (`東京` matches `dongjing`, not `tokyo`). Names sharing Pinyin remain separate results in a stable order.

blocks.raw: ## Finding things

children.raw: From the search box, press **ArrowDown** to highlight the first result. **ArrowUp / ArrowDown** move through page and block results and scroll the highlighted row into view. **Enter** opens it in a new tab (or in this tab, when **Search results open in** is set to **This tab**, below); **Shift+Enter** opens the right sidebar, **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** opens a background tab, and **Alt+Enter** opens another pane. **ArrowUp** on the first result returns to the search box, so you can keep typing; the list does not wrap around at either end.

**Open search tab** in the switcher footer turns the current search into a graph-scoped search tab titled "Search: …" with its own search box. The tab survives restarts and writes nothing to your graph until you name it. Clicking a result opens a new tab and keeps Search unchanged; if you would rather a plain click or **Enter** open the result in the Search tab itself, with **Back** returning to the results, choose **This tab** in **Settings → Editor → Advanced → Search results open in** (**New tab** is the default, saved on this device). Middle-click or Ctrl/Cmd-click opens a background tab; Shift-click opens the right sidebar and Alt-click opens another pane. Page results offer the same right-click menu as the switcher.

**Search / List / Table / Board** are presentations of one result membership: switching the view never changes which blocks matched. **Filters / Advanced** narrows by friendly fields — all words, any words, an exact phrase, excluded words, a regular expression — and **Edit as visual query** opens the row-by-row builder; **Explain query** shows what Tine understood. Choosing blocks and choosing a presentation are separate steps — see [[Workflows/Structure repeated information]] for that split in action.

A text search returns **pages** and **blocks**, shown as two sections in that order, each with its own count and its own display control (**Display pages** for the pages, **Display** for the blocks). An empty section says **No matching pages.** or **No matching blocks.** rather than hiding.

**Pages match** takes three values: **Names and aliases** (the default — exact, prefix, substring, fuzzy and regular-expression matching, not exact equality only), **Block content** (a page counts when one of its own blocks matches the same search), and **Names or content** (the union). It changes page membership only; the Blocks section evaluates the same block search either way. The choice is saved as `tine.page-match-scope`.
The **Display** panel offers View, Group by, Sort, Columns, Summarize (count, sum, average) and Sample, then **Done**.

Naming a search tab — typing into "Name this search to save it as a page" and pressing **Save page** — creates one ordinary page whose only block is a `{{query}}` plus the `tine.view::`, `tine.page-match-scope::` and `tine.page-*` / `tine.block-*` display lines the two sections were using. From then on it behaves like any page: linkable, searchable, always fresh. A page that already exists with the chosen name or alias is never overwritten — you pick another name ("Choose another title"). The saved block is a single result list with one **Display** control; the two-section Pages / Blocks layout belongs to the search tab.

A `{{query [[Page]]}}` block uses Logseq's path-refs rule: a block matches when it mentions the page, when a bullet it lives under does, or when it sits on that page — so the page's own outline always appears. The backlinks-only answer to the same question is the page's **Linked References** panel.
A query that asks about pages rather than blocks — `(page-property …)`, `(page-tags …)`, `(namespace …)` — lists the pages themselves.
`{{query (all-page-tags)}}` lists every page that some page uses as a tag.

A query's text is edited at the foot of its sheet, in TQL — SQLite expression syntax over a fixed vocabulary of block and page fields, `prop('key')`, page references and the `any`/`every`/`off` forms. The compact reference is [[Workflows/Find and revisit]] → **Query text (TQL)**. A word Tine cannot read is named, and the query returns no results rather than a shorter answer.

When a query finds nothing, **why empty?** under the result asks which condition emptied it: for each condition, how many blocks it matches on its own and how many the query would match without it. That is usually enough to see which one to loosen.
