blocks.raw: ## Related

children.raw: "Does this work on my phone?" hides two different questions: what changes because a **window is narrow**, and what changes because Tine is **running as the Android app** instead of a desktop one. This page keeps them apart and maps what current releases ship on each side.

blocks.raw: # Platforms and mobile

children.raw: Below a 640 px window width — on any device, including a desktop window you shrank yourself — the left and right sidebars stop squeezing the page and become **drawers over it**. Dismiss one by tapping the shaded outside edge, using its close control, pressing **Esc**, or pressing Android **Back**.
At 640 px and wider — including tablets — both sidebars are persistent panes that can stay open together and keep their resize controls.
The boundary is width, nothing else: it follows the window, not the device, so the same desktop shows both faces as you resize it.

blocks.raw: ## Question 1 — is the window narrow?

children.raw: A few things key off the **native app** rather than the window: window controls, file pickers and the system file manager, the updater, and memory limits for large PDFs. Layout and touch behavior never do: they follow room and input. The **tab strip** appears whenever the window is 640 px or wider, on every platform; below that, the **Open tabs** list in the left sidebar shows and switches your open tabs. **Split panes** are off on a touch-first screen whose shorter edge is under 700 px (a phone), so one page keeps the screen; tablets have room for two documents and keep them, and a mouse or trackpad keeps them in a window of any size. Touch swipes, long-press menus and the editing toolbar above the keyboard are there whenever a finger is the input.
The desktop apps (Linux, macOS, Windows) keep the full window model — tabs, pinned tabs, split panes, saved workspaces, and multiple windows — toured in [[Workflows/Keep context visible]].
In both cases your graph is the same ordinary Markdown/Org files, so these are interface and surface differences, never different content formats.

blocks.raw: ## Question 2 — which app is running?

children.raw: **Sidebar, Search, Back and Forward are in the top bar**, in the same place whether or not you are editing, as on the desktop apps. On a very narrow phone (about 320 px wide) Back and Forward fold into the **⋯** menu. To have them within thumb reach, turn on Settings → **Appearance** → **Navigation buttons at the bottom** (off by default, this device only): the four buttons then sit in a row at the bottom of the screen. While the keyboard is up, that row gives way to the editing toolbar, which then carries the same four buttons at its left end, outside the part that scrolls, so they stay reachable while you type; tapping one saves the block and leaves the edit before it acts. When you close the keyboard with Back or the keyboard's hide key, the row comes back at once, although the block stays in editing; tap the block to bring the keyboard and the editing toolbar back. The same setting exists on iOS. The editing actions stay in their separate horizontal toolbar above the keyboard; there are no vertical toolbar pages.

**Your graph is a real folder on the device's own storage.** On first run you grant "All files access" and pick the graph folder (a Syncthing folder works), and Tine reads and writes that folder directly — coexisting with the Logseq mobile app on one graph. Cloud document providers such as Nextcloud can't be opened directly: use your provider's sync-to-local-folder feature, then pick that local folder in **Open graph**. The file watcher polls there by default (Settings → **Files** → **Watch for external edits**), so external edits appear shortly after they land.

**An editing toolbar docks above the on-screen keyboard** with the actions a keyboard lacks: Outdent / Indent, Move block up / down, Soft newline, TODO, **Camera**, **Voice memo**, Undo / Redo, Date picker, `[[ ]]` and `(( ))`, the Slash menu, and a hide-keyboard button. Undo uses an arrow bending left; Redo uses an arrow bending right.

**Format text without opening the block.** Long-press text in a block you are not editing to select it as usual; the system keeps its selection handles and its Copy/Paste menu, and a formatting row (Bold, Italic, `[[ ]]`, inline code, Strikethrough, Highlight) docks at the bottom of the screen, above the navigation buttons when they are at the bottom. Tapping an action changes the selected text in place, keeps it selected and can be undone like any edit; the block does not open and the keyboard does not appear. If you were editing another block, that edit is saved and ends. To add a link, edit the block. A selection across two blocks, or inside an embed, a block reference, a macro's output or a code block, shows no formatting row; selecting it still ends an edit in another block.

**Camera and Voice memo** capture a photo or an `.m4a` recording straight into the graph's `assets/` folder and insert the link at the caret — permission-prompted on first use. One that finishes after you switch graphs is saved into the graph it was started in and not inserted; Tine names the graph and the file.

**Share to Tine from any app.** Pick **Tine** in Android's share sheet to send text, a link, or one or more images. The item becomes a new block at the bottom of today's journal, the same place quick capture files to, and Tine shows **Captured to today's journal**. Shared images are copied into the graph's `assets/` folder. If Tine can't add the item yet, for example because no graph is open or saving fails, it keeps the item and tries again the next time you open or return to Tine. Retrying never loses the item. It can add it twice in one rare case: Tine closed or crashed just after the journal was saved and before it noted the item as done. Reopening an old share from the recent-apps list after Tine was closed or the phone restarted can also add it again. Sharing the same thing twice adds it twice. Tine saves a share whole or not at all: if it can't take every part, for example more than 32 images, a file over 64 MiB, a file that isn't an image, or a file from Tine itself, it says so and saves nothing.

**Launcher shortcuts and a Quick Settings tile.** Long-press Tine's launcher icon for **Today**, **Quick capture** and **Search**. Add the **Quick capture** tile from the Quick Settings editor. **Quick capture** opens today's journal with an empty block at the bottom, ready for typing.
**Hardware Back navigates within Tine** — dismissing a dialog or drawer first and stepping back through page history, exiting to the system only at the root.

**PDFs use that same one-pane history.** Open a PDF link in place, press **Notes** to visit its highlights page, and use Hardware Back to return first to the PDF and then to the source page. Desktop-style PDF tabs and companion splits stay off on a phone.

**Plugins and themes follow the same lifecycle as desktop** — install (always disabled at first), review capabilities, enable, settings, disable, uninstall — and a package that did not declare Android shows **Unavailable** on it. The hands-on path is [[Workflows/Extend Tine]].
The whole interface scales through **Interface size** (saved per device) and the native status/navigation icons follow your selected theme.

blocks.raw: ## On Android

children.raw: **Swipe a block to restructure it.** Swipe a block **right** to indent it, **left a short way** to outdent it, and **left a longer way** to select it and open its action menu. A revealed arrow shows indent or outdent before you let go; it switches to a circled **more** icon when the swipe will open actions. An unavailable indent or outdent has no arrow. The left-swipe outdent band is 40–139 px; actions start at 140 px, giving you more room to outdent. Short or mostly-vertical movements are ordinary scrolling and do nothing. Swiping is off while you are typing in the block, inside tables, code blocks, queries, drawings and media, and with more than one finger, so it never fights text selection or panning.
**Swipe in from the left edge** to open the left drawer; a swipe that starts elsewhere, or that is mostly vertical, does not.

**Back is one ladder everywhere.** It dismisses an open dialog, menu or image first, then closes an open drawer, then steps back through page history. On Android the hardware or system Back gesture climbs that ladder and exits only at the root. Where Tine takes Back from the screen edge instead (iOS), the same left-edge swipe goes Back when there is something to go back to, following your finger and snapping back if you let go early; otherwise it opens the drawer.

**The image viewer takes touch.** Pinch to zoom, double-tap to zoom in and out, drag a zoomed image to pan it (keep dragging past its edge to reach the next image), swipe sideways to move between the page's images, and drag up or down to close. A single tap shows or hides the buttons instead of closing; use the **×** button, drag the image up or down, or press Back to close.

**Turn the block swipe off for chosen pages.** To stop swipes from acting inside blocks that reference particular pages (a kanban board, say), list their names in `config.edn`: `:mobile {:gestures/disabled-in-block-with-tags ["kanban" "board"]}`. A block that references a listed page, and everything nested under it, ignores the swipe. This is the same setting Logseq uses.

blocks.raw: ## Touch gestures on a phone

children.raw: **The always-on-top capture window is desktop-only.** The `tine --capture` desktop shortcut and its window over other apps have no phone counterpart. On a phone, capture with the share sheet, the **Quick capture** shortcut or tile, or iOS Shortcuts and Siri, described above and under iOS below. The desktop setup lives on [[Features/Quick capture]].

**One route at a time on a phone** — pages and PDF readers share one history, with no split panes or second windows; the desktop multi-window model does not exist here. Open tabs live in the **Open tabs** list of the left sidebar (and in the tab strip once the window is 640 px wide, for example a phone held sideways).

**Long-press a page reference or tag to preview its page** without navigating away. Choose the **…** button in the preview header for **Page actions**, the same menu offered by a desktop right-click. Tap outside the preview to dismiss it; a quick tap still follows the link. Other links keep their long-press context menu, and holding ordinary text keeps the system's text selection and selection toolbar.
**Export to PDF is desktop-only** — printing is unavailable inside a mobile WebView, so the page menu does not offer it here.

**Updates come through your install channel.** The in-app update checker and installer are off on mobile: a sideloaded release-signed APK is replaced by taking each new APK from the GitHub releases page, an F-Droid install updates through F-Droid, and a Google Play install updates through Google Play. The F-Droid build omits the network plugin/theme catalogue and keeps local sideloading.

blocks.raw: ## What stays different on Android

children.raw: Everything the phone skips is here: tabs with pin, reorder, and reopen, split panes, saved workspaces, multiple windows, the modifier-click gestures, and global quick capture. Releases cover Linux and Windows on x64 and ARM64, and macOS as one universal app.

**Installed from the Microsoft Store (MSIX)?** Then the Store keeps Tine up to date: Settings → **About** says "Updates come from the Microsoft Store.", and Tine's own update checker and installer stay off on that install.

**Running the portable ZIP (Windows)?** Tine keeps its settings, sessions, backups, plugins and WebView2 data in the `tine-data` folder beside `Tine.exe`, never in AppData, and it updates by download: quit Tine and extract the new ZIP into the same folder, keeping `tine-data`. A first portable launch starts with fresh settings; to bring the settings of an installed Tine along, quit Tine and copy `%APPDATA%\<app id>` to `tine-data\<app id>\roaming` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<app id>` to `tine-data\<app id>\local` (`<app id>` is `page.tine.Tine`, or `page.tine.TineBeta` for Tine Beta). Your notes stay in your graph folder.

**Installed from a distribution's package manager (for example Nixpkgs)?** A package built with the packager's `TINE_PACKAGED_BY` setting never checks for updates, shows no update notification and offers no installer: Settings → **About** says "This copy of Tine is packaged by <name>. Update it there.", and the package manager delivers new versions.

Automatic checks are ON by default. In Settings → **About**, turn off **Check for updates automatically** to stop startup checks and update notifications on this device. You can still use **Check for updates** manually; turning automatic checks off does not change how package-manager or manual-download installs receive updates.

**In-app updates** run on Windows, Linux and macOS — the app checks once per launch and Settings → **About** → **Check for updates** offers **Install update**, which downloads, verifies and installs in place after saving your changes. Windows and Linux relaunch immediately; **macOS offers Restart** after installation, saving any further changes before restarting. Releases ship signed macOS updater archives for Intel and Apple Silicon from the signed and notarized universal application. If the updater cannot fetch, verify or install an update, Tine opens the releases page so you can download and replace the app manually. If a failed macOS installation cannot restore the previous app, look beside the original app or in your home folder for **Tine (previous version).app** (or **Tine Beta (previous version).app**). If neither folder is writable, the updater keeps its temporary backup. The updater shows the saved location when it reports one; open that bundle to recover or download and replace the app manually.

**Install as a Flatpak (Linux, Beta).** Each Beta release also carries a Flatpak bundle for 64-bit Intel/AMD, named like `Tine-Beta_<version>_x86_64.flatpak`, among the other downloads on the Beta release page. Install the downloaded file with `flatpak install --user Tine-Beta_<version>_x86_64.flatpak`, then start it from your app menu (`flatpak list` shows its application id for `flatpak run`). It installs next to a stable Tine Flatpak and keeps its own settings, and it can read and write graph folders **inside your home folder only**: a graph on another disk or under `/mnt` or `/media` is out of its reach, unlike the other Linux builds. **Updates are manual**: the in-app updater does not apply to it (it offers a download link instead of installing), so download the new bundle from the release page and run the same command again.

**System tray (optional).** In Settings → **Appearance**, turn on **Show Tine in the system tray** to get a tray, notification-area or menu-bar icon. Its menu has **Open Tine**, **Quick Capture** and **Quit**; clicking the icon shows and focuses the main window, or hides it when it is already in front. Two more switches appear once the icon is on: **Minimize to tray** makes minimizing the main window hide it (instead of leaving it in the taskbar) until you open it from the tray, and **Start minimized to tray** launches Tine with the main window hidden (your graph still loads, so it is ready the moment you open it). All three are off by default and apply to this device only. Closing the main window still quits Tine, and other windows are never hidden by the tray. If your desktop has no tray (some Linux desktops need an AppIndicator or StatusNotifier extension), Tine says so under the switch, shows its window as usual, and ignores the two minimize options until a tray exists. If the tray disappears while Tine is running (the panel that hosted it quits), Tine shows its window again and turns the two minimize options off until you re-apply the setting. A start-minimized launch at login waits a few seconds for a late tray before it gives up and shows the window. The tray needs the system's `libayatana-appindicator3` library; the `.deb` and `.rpm` recommend it, the Flatpak bundle carries its own, and the AppImage uses the one on your system. Starting Tine again shows the main window if the tray had hidden it, and opening a graph or link always shows it.
Any folder on your disk can be a graph — choose it with the ordinary folder picker; there is no sandboxed document picker.

**On macOS, Tine draws its window with the system's web engine** — the same one Safari uses — and needs the engine of **Safari 15.4 or later**, which means **macOS 12.3 (Monterey) or later**. Apps get the engine that came with macOS: updating the Safari app on an older Mac leaves the one Tine uses unchanged, so the app bundle declares 12.3 as its minimum system version. If the web engine is too old, Tine explains this at startup instead of opening half-working. Opening PDFs needs Safari 17.4 or later; the rest of Tine does not.

blocks.raw: ## On desktop (Linux, macOS, Windows)

children.raw: Tine is on the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/tineoutline/id6804403687) as **TineOutline**. An App Store install updates through the App Store.

iOS Betas use the separate **Tine Beta** app with an **amber icon**, installed through Apple's TestFlight app from [the Tine Beta link](https://testflight.apple.com/join/f2HQgJGn). It installs alongside the stable **TineOutline** App Store app. Each app updates through its own channel: TestFlight for Beta, the App Store for stable. An older TineOutline TestFlight invitation belongs to the stable app, so use the Tine Beta link instead.

**Tine Beta starts on Welcome with fresh settings and no remembered graph.** It cannot see the stable app's settings or iCloud folder. Its own folders are **On My iPhone → Tine Beta** and **iCloud Drive → Tine Beta**. To try your existing notes, copy the graph into a Beta folder using Files; that copy and the original are independent. Earlier TestFlight data under the stable app stays with TineOutline and is not imported automatically.

**Graphs live in the app's own folders.** Open or create a graph inside **On My iPhone → TineOutline** or **iCloud Drive → TineOutline**; Tine refuses folders from other Files providers for now and says so. Creating a graph asks for its name after you choose the parent folder, and creates a child folder with that name. An iCloud graph is downloaded to the device before it opens, and a remembered graph reopens after an app update.
The iPhone and iPad app uses the same mobile interface as Android, so the notes above about one route at a time, bullet context menus and desktop-only features apply there too.

**Share to Tine.** Pick **Tine** in the share sheet to send text, a web page, a link, or up to five images. The sheet confirms **Saved to Tine**. The next time you open Tine, the item becomes a block at the bottom of today's journal, exactly as on Android.

**Spotlight finds your pages.** Pages of the graph open in Tine show up in iPhone search by title, with a short excerpt, and tapping one opens it in Tine. Hidden pages are never added. Only the current graph is indexed, and switching graphs replaces the index.

**Shortcuts, Siri and the Home Screen.** The Shortcuts app and Siri offer **Add to Tine journal** (it saves without opening Tine, and the block appears the next time you open it), **Search Tine** and **Open page**. Long-press the app icon for **Today's journal**, **Quick capture** and **Search**.
**Plugins do not run on iOS yet.** Themes work; downloadable WebAssembly plugins stay off until Tine has the extra review surface Apple requires for them.

blocks.raw: ## iOS today

children.raw: When an Android share brings Tine forward, Tine opens the journal where it saved the item and reveals the shared block, like following a block reference. With several shares, it reveals the last item in the batch. The **Captured to today's journal** notice stays. Retries leave your current page open, as do iOS shares and App Intents saved without opening Tine. In-app quick capture keeps the page you are editing open.

Shared items follow Logseq's mobile rules for each platform. On Android a link becomes a titled link, YouTube and similar video links become `{{video …}}`, posts on X or Twitter become `{{twitter …}}`, and text highlighted in a browser goes before its link. On iOS the shared text is kept as it is and the link follows it unchanged, as Logseq's iOS share does. Images follow as asset links, one per line.

The block uses Logseq's `:quick-capture-templates` from `config.edn`. The default text template is `**{time}** [[quick capture]]: {text} {url}`, and on Android `:media` sets the template for a single shared image. `{time}` is when you shared the item, and `{date}` is the date of the journal it is added to.

The same destinations open from `tine://today`, `tine://capture`, `tine://search?q=…` and `tine://page/<name>` (a page of the open graph). Each one only opens something in Tine and never writes to your graph.

blocks.raw: ## Shaping a shared item

children.raw: [[Workflows/Keep context visible]] for tabs, panes, sidebars and workspaces (desktop), [[Features/Quick capture]] for the desktop capture window, [[Workflows/Extend Tine]] for the plugin and theme lifecycle, and [[Features/PDF annotation]] for the full reader tour.

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Tine reads Logseq's query syntax — `{{query …}}` blocks and the common advanced (datalog) queries — but runs them on its own engine, not on a datalog database. This page lists every place where the answer can differ from Logseq's, and why. How to write and display queries is on [[Features/Queries]].
This page describes Tine Beta. Tine 0.6 (stable) gets several of these wrong in ways Beta has fixed; see the last section.

blocks.raw: # Tine query model

children.raw: **A query in Tine finds everything the same query finds in Logseq, and may find more — never less.** Someone moving a graph over from Logseq should never lose a result.

**Looking at results never changes your files.** Sorting by a column heading, collapsing a query or opening a result changes only what you see; only settings you save on purpose (Display, the query text) are written to the block.

blocks.raw: ## The rule

children.raw: **Text is exact.** A bare word or quoted text in a query matches the raw block text, property lines included, with case and accents significant: `Alpha` does not find `alpha`, and `cafe` does not find `café`. A query is a deliberate filter, so it matches what you wrote. Ctrl+K, search tabs and in-page Find are for finding things quickly, and ignore case and accents.

**References include the outline above a block.** `[[x]]`, `#x` and `(page-ref x)` match a block that references `x`, and also its child blocks, because a child sits under that reference. `#x` and `[[x]]` mean the same.

**Page properties count as properties.** `(property type book)` also matches the first block of a page whose header says `type:: book`, as in Logseq. Use `(page-property type book)` to ask about pages.

**Commas split only list properties.** `tags`, `alias` and keys listed in `:property/separated-by-commas` are lists; every other value is one piece of text, so `(property list "Foo, Bar")` finds `list:: Foo, Bar`.
**Results sort newest first** unless you write `asc`, `(sample N)` picks before it sorts, and a query of only `sort-by`/`sample` shows nothing.
**Table settings from Logseq are read**: `query-table::`, a query ending in `table`, `query-properties::` and `query-sort-by::` / `query-sort-desc::`.

**`(task)` with no markers and `(priority)` with no levels add no condition.** Logseq drops such a filter, so `(and (task) [[x]])` finds what `[[x]]` finds, and a query left with no condition shows nothing; Tine does the same. A note on the query says so and offers to rewrite the clause to open tasks, any task, or priorities A, B or C.

blocks.raw: ## Where Tine behaves exactly like Logseq

children.raw: **Property values ignore case.** `(property status Done)` also finds `status:: done`. Logseq requires the exact spelling.
**Property names ignore case.** `(property Status x)` works; Logseq's parser lowercases names anyway, so this rarely shows.
**Numbers and dates compare as numbers and dates** when a property holds them (or its page declares `tine.type::`), so `count:: 01` equals `1`. Logseq compares the stored value.
**A single word finds every block containing it.** Logseq's desktop app runs a search instead and shows its top 30 hits.
**`(sort-by …)` knows built-in fields**: priority, page, scheduled and deadline as well as any property. Logseq sorts only by a property of that name.

blocks.raw: ## Where Tine finds more

children.raw: **There is no datalog engine.** An advanced query runs only if Tine understands every clause: task markers, priorities, page references, properties, pages, namespaces, page tags, scheduled and deadline, and journal dates. If any clause is outside that, the whole query is refused and the notice names the clauses — half an answer would look complete and be wrong.

**Advanced-query shapes that run:** marker and priority triples (literal, variable, `_` or omitted value), `contains?` marker sets and their negation, attribute comparisons, missing scheduled/deadline checks, block-to-journal-page joins, and the built-in `task`, `priority`, `between`, `page-ref`, property, page and namespace rules. A named page joined through `:block/page`, `:block/refs` or `:block/path-refs` accepts a literal name or a string input. `:block/refs` means direct references only; `:block/path-refs` and the `page-ref` rule also include ancestors and the owning page. TQL's `direct_ref('project')` preserves the direct form. A simple query in an EDN `:query` map, such as `(and (todo DOING) (priority A))`, uses the existing simple-query engine.

**Tagged-page name results** run for `[?t :block/name ?tag] [?p :block/tags ?t] [?p :block/name ?name]` with `:find ?name` and a string `:inputs` binding. They show pages once each, using Tine's own display. Ordinary strings retain case: `"programming"` matches a stored page name, `"Programming"` does not; `"[[Programming]]"` and `:current-page` are lowercased like Logseq.

**Entity bindings are not guessed.** A property-map pair such as `[?p :block/properties ?props] [(get ?props :class)]` asks about that entity's own properties in Logseq, not the properties of each returned block's page. Tine does not translate these pairs, even with a page join: the whole query is refused with a notice. A self-page constraint such as `[?b :block/page ?b]` is also refused. Supported page conditions must bind the returned block to a distinct page variable explicitly.

**Quoted operands use EDN string escapes**, as in Logseq: `"\u0041"` means `"A"`, and `\n`, `\t`, escaped quotes and backslashes are decoded. Invalid escapes refuse the query. Your stored query text keeps its authored spelling.

**Print and static exports keep query refusal notices**, including the explanation to convert a legacy scheduled/deadline window to a Tine query. An unavailable answer shows a notice too. Only a successfully answered query with no results says there are no matches; a sheet that cannot run falls back to the query's notice.

**Date windows** accept numeric `yyyymmdd` inputs, `:today`, `:yesterday`, `:tomorrow`, signed day/week/month/year offsets, and Logseq's older `:7d`, `:7d-before`, `:7d-after` spellings. Comparisons preserve strict `>` / `<` and inclusive `>=` / `<=`. The common `(or [?b :block/scheduled ?d] [?b :block/deadline ?d])` shape applies both bounds to each alternative's date. The advanced `between` rule includes both bounds in authored order; reversed bounds return nothing.

**Children of matching blocks.** As in Logseq, a match directly under another match is shown inside its parent and is not a result of its own. An advanced query that sets `:remove-block-children? false` keeps every match as its own result, children included, exactly as in Logseq.

**The rest refuses whole:** arbitrary joins, authored rules, multiple find columns, aggregates, custom pull projections, timestamp inputs, and `:current-block`, `:parent-block` or `:query-page`. An unfiltered page-name query also includes Logseq's reference-only page entities and is not translated. One `:result-transform` runs: Logseq's default NOW query sort, `(fn [result] (sort-by (fn [h] (get h :block/priority "Z")) result))`, which orders rows by priority with a missing one last. Any other refused `:result-transform` with translatable underlying rows suggests their TQL filter; choose Tine's Display settings for sorting or totals. The suggestion does not execute automatically.

**`:view` and `:result-transform` never run as code**, because they are ClojureScript functions. Tine will not run them; it only recognises the exact priority sort above and performs it itself. Its own Display choices (List, Table, Board, grouping, totals) cover the common uses.
**A query that would return more than 20,000 rows or 32 MiB is refused**, with a message to narrow it or add `(sample N)`. Logseq has no such limit; Tine stops instead of freezing.

blocks.raw: ## What Tine does not run

children.raw: **Clicking a table heading sorts** for as long as the page is open. Logseq writes `query-sort-by::` into the file.

**Collapsing a query's results** is the block's own fold, written as `collapsed:: true` like Logseq. Only a query that is not on a block of an editable page (a default journal query, a read-only page) remembers its fold on this device instead.

blocks.raw: ## Where Tine keeps things on your device instead of in the file

children.raw: **Queries are always live.** Logseq stops refreshing a query that takes longer than 50 ms and shows a refresh button; Tine keeps every query current.
**`:current-page` in a split view** is the page in the pane you used last.
**Pages and blocks are separate answers.** A query finds blocks or pages. To see both from the same conditions, choose **Pages and blocks** in the query sheet.

**Tine-only features** (scheduled and deadline ranges, grouping, totals, typed comparisons, inline-tag and parent, child or descendant conditions, a bare has-a-scheduled-date or has-a-deadline check, `search`, `content-regex`) have no equivalent `{{query}}` spelling. Saving one turns the block into `{{tine-query …}}`, says so, and offers **Undo that change**. For example, `{{tine-query @block scheduled between today and '+7d'}}` checks a scheduled date; OG Logseq drops the condition in `(between scheduled …)` or `(between deadline …)`.

blocks.raw: ## Other differences

children.raw: Tine 0.6 differs from this page where it has known bugs, fixed in Beta: it sorts ascending by default; `(sample N)` sorts first; a query of only directives returns everything; `(namespace x)` matches every depth; `(all-page-tags)` returns the tagged pages; `not` with several operands, `(priority [A])`, `(between created-at …)` and page-header properties misbehave; journal groups run oldest first; an advanced query with an unknown clause runs the clauses it understands; query text ignores case and accents; every property value is split on commas; Logseq's table settings are ignored.

blocks.raw: ## Tine 0.6 (stable)

children.raw: Only recovery paths Tine actually ships, each as numbered actions with the outcome to expect. For where everything lives, see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

blocks.raw: # Troubleshooting and recovery

children.raw: Meaning: the file changed elsewhere (a sync tool or another editor) while you had unsaved edits. The banner reads “*Page* changed on disk. Your unsaved changes weren't written.” Nothing was written over — your unsaved text is still on screen.
If the banner reads “*Page* changed on disk while you were editing it” and offers only **Review**, choose it and continue at step 3: Tine never overwrites the file with a draft you have not compared.
1. If your version is right, choose **Keep mine** — Tine writes yours over the file.
2. If the disk version is the one you want, choose **Use disk version** — Tine re-reads the file. Copy your unsaved text somewhere first if you still need parts of it.

3. To keep parts of both, open the page: a panel at its top compares **Your unsaved edits** with **The file on disk now** block by block. Choose per block, then **Apply resolution**. When Tine still has the version you started editing from, it pre-selects each side's own change. If the file changes again before you apply, nothing is written and the comparison refreshes.

4. What you should see: the banner clears and the page saves normally again. Until you choose, that page is skipped by saving rather than silently clobbered. If Tine closes first, your unsaved text is kept, and the same comparison appears on that page after the next start, with the same banner until you choose. If the file was deleted on disk, the banner reads “*Page* was deleted on disk”: **Use disk version** accepts the deletion, and **Keep mine (overwrite)** writes your text back as the file.

blocks.raw: ## “Changed on disk” banner

children.raw: A failed delete keeps your unsaved text, including conflicted edits. Deleting a conflicted page discards local input only after deletion succeeds; the deleted disk file goes to the pages or journals trash below. Live conflict resolutions keep the external version in `logseq/.tine-trash/conflicts/` before replacing it.
1. Open `logseq/.tine-trash/pages/` or `logseq/.tine-trash/journals/` inside your graph. Deleted files have a timestamp followed by `__` before their original name.
2. Remove the timestamp and `__`, then move the file into the configured pages or journals folder. For a page that originally lived elsewhere, you may return it to that location instead.
3. What you should see: Tine notices the restored file like any external change, and the page reappears.

blocks.raw: ## Restore a deleted page or journal

children.raw: 1. Open Settings (**t s**) → **Backups & recovery** and find the snapshot from before the damage under **Available snapshots**. (Tine snapshots your Markdown/Org files on every launch; **Snapshots to keep** controls how many survive.)
2. Choose **Restore** beside it and confirm.

3. What you should see: your current state is snapshotted first, backed-up graph text returns to its original paths, config and sidecars are restored, and the graph reloads — so even a mistaken restore can be undone by restoring the snapshot it just made.

blocks.raw: ## Restore an earlier state of the graph

children.raw: 1. Choose the **N conflicts** badge in the sidebar to open the **Conflicts** page, then choose the page to resolve. Tine uses the same queue for sync-provider conflict copies and files carrying unresolved git or Fossil merge markers.

2. On the page, compare the two versions block by block. For each differing block choose **Mine**, **Theirs**, or **Both**; when both sides edited separate parts of one block, Tine may offer a combined **Merged** version. **Apply all suggested** re-applies Tine's own suggestions and leaves your choices on the other rows, and the page's own properties have a separate choice. Then choose **Apply resolution**.

3. What you should see: the chosen page is saved through the normal guarded path. A provider conflict copy moves to the trash; before a version-control page is written without conflict markers, its exact pre-resolution file is kept in recoverable trash. If a conflict copy's original page no longer exists, use **Discard copy** on the **Conflicts** page.

blocks.raw: ## Resolve a sync or version-control conflict

children.raw: 1. Choose the **N conflicts** badge and open the day from the **Duplicate journal days** group, or open the day itself. Tine compares its two files block by block, the same review as a sync conflict, and lists each file with **Open**, **Rename**, and **Trash** actions. The same list stays in Settings → **Backups & recovery** → **Duplicate journal days**, which also offers **Merge**.

2. Choose which version of each differing block to keep (or keep both), then **Apply resolution**. Where the two files hold different blocks, the pre-selected choice keeps everything, as **Merge** does. A Markdown file and an Org file for one day cannot be folded together; use the file actions instead.

3. What you should see: the kept content saved as the day and the other file moved to `logseq/.tine-trash/`, where you can still recover it. Tine kept both source files until you decided rather than dropping one.

blocks.raw: ## Reconcile a duplicate journal day

children.raw: Meaning: the journal file may be named after its title (for example `Jun 18th, 2026.md`) instead of its date, so Tine cannot place it in the feed.
1. Open Settings → **Backups & recovery** → **Journal files named by title**.
2. Review the listed renames and choose **Rename to date names**.
3. What you should see: a snapshot is taken first, the files take their date names, and the days appear in the journal feed.

blocks.raw: ## Journal days look empty

children.raw: 1. Set `TINE_DEBUG=1` in the environment when you launch Tine, reproduce the problem, then quit.
2. By default the log is `tine-debug.log` in your platform's temporary folder (portable Windows Tine: in `tine-data\<app id>\local\logs` beside `Tine.exe`); `TINE_DEBUG_LOG=/path` overrides it.
3. What you should see: a timestamped trace covering the environment, startup milestones, and any panic with a backtrace. It records no note content — send that file with your report.

4. On Linux, Tine automatically disables WebKitGTK's DMABUF renderer when an NVIDIA driver older than version 610 (or of unknown version) is loaded, to avoid a blank window. Newer NVIDIA drivers and other drivers keep the default rendering path. If the window still stays blank or never appears, launch once with `TINE_GPU=0` to request the software rendering fallback. An explicit `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER` value takes precedence; `TINE_GPU=1` opts out of the automatic NVIDIA workaround.

blocks.raw: ## Tine will not start

children.raw: Meaning: at launch Tine tried to reopen the graph you last used and failed. The Welcome screen shows **Tine could not open your last graph** with the graph's path and the reason.
1. **Try again** — attempt the same open again. This is safe to repeat.
2. **Copy details** — copies the path and reason for an issue report. Use this before anything else if you plan to report it.
3. Or open a different graph from the same screen and leave this one untouched.
4. What you should see: the card says nothing was changed on disk, and that is the case — retrying, opening another graph, or relaunching Tine are all safe before any manual recovery.

blocks.raw: ## Tine could not open your last graph

children.raw: Meaning: one region — a page or PDF pane, a sidebar item, query results, a dialog, plugin settings, or the conflict panel — hit an error it could not render through. Tine reports it in place with a **Retry** button instead of blanking the app, and the rest of the window keeps working.
**Copy details** — copies the region and error details for a report. Review the copied text before sharing: an error may include a file path or your own content.
1. **Retry** — re-renders just that region. A failure caused by something transient, such as a command that lost a race with a slow startup, usually clears on the first retry.

2. If the card says Tine is still waiting on operations that have been running for a while, give it a moment and retry again: the region is failing because the backend has not answered yet, not because anything is wrong with your notes.
3. If it comes back every time, use **Create a privacy-safe diagnostic report** below and include the message shown in the region.
4. What you should see: your notes on disk are untouched either way — a region that cannot be displayed is a display failure, not a data failure.

blocks.raw: ## Part of the window says it could not be displayed

children.raw: Meaning: a panel could not fetch what it needed, and says so instead of drawing itself empty, because an empty panel would tell you there is nothing there, which is a different thing from not being able to find out. Linked and Unlinked References say “Couldn’t load references”; the references under a block say “Couldn’t load references to this block” with a **Retry** button; Search says “Couldn’t load search results” instead of “No matched results”; a page in the right sidebar says “Could not load this sidebar page. Collapse and expand to retry.”

1. Where the panel has a **Retry** button, press it: it re-fetches just that panel. For a sidebar page, collapse and expand its entry to try again. For Linked and Unlinked References, reopen the page or navigate away and back.

2. Smaller pieces degrade quietly rather than saying anything: a code block that could not be highlighted shows as plain text, a formula that could not be typeset shows its LaTeX, a preview that could not load shows nothing in its place. These are display-only, and reopening the page tries them again.
3. If it keeps failing, create a diagnostic report as described below.
4. What you should see: the rest of the window is unaffected, and nothing on disk changes.

blocks.raw: ## A panel says it could not load something

children.raw: Meaning: something actually went wrong — a save, a read, or a check Tine could not finish. A red message stays on screen until you close it, so there is time to read it; the brief states Tine passes through while it starts or opens a graph never show one.
1. Choose **Copy** on the message to copy its full text for a report.

2. Close it with **×** once you have what you need. If you closed it too soon, Settings → **Help & diagnostics** → **Recent error messages** lists the last 20 of this session, newest first, each with **Copy**; they are kept in memory only and are gone when Tine closes.

3. What you should see: the message stays until you close it; if the same error happens again it shows a count (×2, ×3) instead of a second message. The privacy-safe diagnostic report below notes that it appeared (not its text), and with `TINE_DEBUG=1` its full text is also in the detailed debug log.

blocks.raw: ## A red error message appears

children.raw: To compare live refresh behavior while investigating a problem, enable **Refresh everything on every save (debug)** in Settings → **Help & diagnostics**. Every save then refreshes all subscribed views. Turn it off to restore target-specific refreshes; the switch stays in memory for this run only and changes no graph files.

If typing freezes, reproduce it before creating the report. It includes the worst renderer stalls while typing (up to 32, at least 100 ms), with bundled script attribution where supported. These samples stay in memory until you close the window or clear recorded events; no typed text or key values are recorded.

1. Open Settings → **Help & diagnostics** and choose **Create diagnostic report**. Tine previews its bounded flight recorder for the current and previous run: fixed operation names, outcomes, timings, counts, platform, version, and build information.

2. Review the report, then choose **Copy report** (or **Save report…** on desktop). Nothing is uploaded automatically. The recorder excludes graph content, paths, page titles, queries, URLs, credentials, and the opt-in detailed debug log.

3. What you should see: a report you can attach to an issue without first setting up `adb`, SSH, or a terminal. **Clear recorded events** removes the retained flight-recorder history after you are done.

4. For a graph that opens or saves slowly, the report's `graphs` section is the part to attach. It holds, for the last time the graph was opened, how long each step took (listing the folder, checking file dates, reading files, parsing, building the index, becoming ready) with how many files and bytes each step handled, so a slow disk or antivirus scan shows up as read time rather than parse time. It also lists how often opening restarted and why, the most recent full rescans and saves with their durations, and the shape of the graph: how many pages, journals, Windows line-ending files, non-normalized file names and sync-conflict files it has, and the spread (median, 90th and 99th percentile, largest) of file sizes, blocks per page, nesting depth, links, tags, embeds, block references, queries, properties, backlinks per page and namespace depth. These are numbers only: never a page name, any text, or a hash of either.

blocks.raw: ## Create a privacy-safe diagnostic report

children.raw: Meaning: Windows Defender real-time protection scans each file the first time Tine reads it. On a graph of tens of thousands of files the first open after install, or after Defender updates, can take several times longer than later opens; the time shows up as read time in the diagnostic report, not parse time. Nothing is wrong with the graph.

1. When a graph's first open is slow and real-time protection is on, Tine shows a one-time notice for that graph: “Opening this graph took a while, and Windows Defender is scanning each file as Tine reads it.” Close it with **×** to dismiss it for that graph.

2. To act on it, choose **Add an exclusion for this graph folder**. Windows asks for administrator approval; only then does Tine run `Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath` for the graph's folder. Tine never changes Defender without that choice. You can also do the same yourself in Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Manage settings → Exclusions.

3. What you should see: “Windows Defender now skips this graph's folder” on success. If you decline the prompt, nothing changes and the notice returns the next time this graph opens slowly. If Defender is managed by your organization or another antivirus, Tine says it did not accept the exclusion and changes nothing.

4. The exclusion tells Defender not to scan that folder, which is a security tradeoff: only exclude folders you trust. The diagnostic report records only whether real-time protection is on (`windowsDefenderRealtime`: on, off, unknown, or not-applicable), never any path.

blocks.raw: ## Opening a large graph is slow on Windows

children.raw: Meaning: Tine notices files changed outside it (another app, Syncthing, Dropbox) by itself. If you suspect it missed a change, or want to time a full check for a diagnostic report, you can ask for one.

1. Open Settings → **Help & diagnostics** and choose **Rescan graph**. Tine ignores everything it has remembered about your files: it reads and parses every file of the open graph again from disk, rebuilds its pages, links and search index from them, and shows whatever changed outside Tine. It does not freeze the app and it does not overwrite what you are typing; a page you have open keeps its place, and saving over a file that changed on disk is refused as usual. It takes longer than the quick check Tine does whenever you return to the window, which is why it is a button.
2. What you should see: the button reads **Rescanning…** while it works, then **Last rescan finished at** followed by the time. Create a diagnostic report afterwards to see how long that rescan took.

blocks.raw: ## Rescan the graph on demand

children.raw: Meaning: after syncing a graph with Syncthing, Dropbox or a similar service, you can confirm that both devices hold the same Markdown and Org files, byte for byte, and see exactly which files differ if they do not.

1. On each device, open Settings → **Help & diagnostics** and choose **Create graph verification report**. Tine reads every Markdown and Org file of the open graph, shows its progress, and lets you **Cancel**.
2. On one device choose **Copy graph report** (or **Save graph report…** on desktop) and paste it into the box **Report from the other device** on the other, then choose **Compare reports**.

3. What you should see: either “The source file sets and bytes match”, or lists named **Only on this device**, **Only on the other device** and **Different bytes** with the file paths. The report holds paths and checksums, never file contents; nothing is uploaded and nothing in your graph changes.
4. If a file changed while Tine was reading it, the report says **Incomplete** and no match is confirmed: let the sync settle and create the report again.

blocks.raw: ## Check that two devices hold the same graph

children.raw: If **config.edn could not be read** appears, the graph opens read-only so a missing setting cannot send new files to the wrong folder. Read your available pages, repair the file or its permissions in `logseq/config.edn`, then reopen the graph. Settings shows the same problem until that reopen.

If **custom.css could not be read** appears, Tine applies no custom CSS for that open if the failure happens while the graph opens; if it happens on an edit while the graph is open, the previous version stays applied (Tine retries once before it tells you). Repair `logseq/custom.css` or its permissions and save it again; Tine re-applies the file when it changes, and reopening the graph tries again too. **Settings → Appearance → Custom CSS → Disable custom CSS** ignores the file for the rest of the session if a stylesheet makes the window hard to use.
If **Some page files couldn't be read** appears, the notice names those files (the first five, then how many more), and **Copy** on the notice copies the full list.

Files still arriving from an editor or sync service retry quietly while the write settles. If a file stays unreadable, the notice includes its reason and Tine keeps its last readable page. For a file over the 64 MiB limit or invalid UTF-8 text, repair the file; Tine checks it again when it changes. An unchanged invalid file does not keep being read in the background. For denied read permission, repair its permissions; Tine checks access again on the next file event, regular check, or return to the window, even if the file's contents have not changed. A persistent access or disk error does not start a repeating full-graph check.

A failed journal scan or page discovery does not mean those files are absent. The graph remains open; repair the unreadable file or folder and retry. A failed conflict refresh keeps the last successful conflict list, which may be out of date.

An asset that gained a reference after an orphan scan is kept when you choose Trash. Refresh the orphan scan before trying again. With external editors or sync, wait for their changes to appear in Tine first: a change it has not observed can still race deletion.

Cancelling graph verification makes no report and raises no error message. If a source file is replaced during verification, its report is incomplete; finish syncing or editing and create another report.

blocks.raw: ## A graph file could not be read

children.raw: Each Beta has its own release page, tagged `vX.Y.Z-beta.N`. Beta's in-app updater checks `https://tine.page/updates/beta/latest.json` for the newest Beta; older Betas still find the new release. For a manual download, choose that version's Beta release page.
Master ships stable **Tine**; **Tine Beta** is a separate app for testing upcoming changes, with its own settings and Beta updates. Stable gets only stable updates, and Beta gets only Beta updates.

Close Tine before switching builds. On its first configured desktop launch, Tine Beta copies compatible settings from stable Tine and leaves stable app data intact. If it opens Welcome, choose your existing graph folder; do not delete application data to recover it. Android's separate Beta app needs its graph folder selected again.

To return to stable Tine, close Tine Beta and launch stable Tine; your graph files stay where they were. Save your edits before switching. In Settings → About, **Copy version** copies the app name and full version, including the Beta sequence, for a bug report.

blocks.raw: ## Switch between stable Tine and Tine Beta

children.raw: Tine works directly on the same Markdown/Org files as Logseq — no import, no export, no lock-in.

blocks.raw: # Bring an existing graph

children.raw: 1. On the Welcome screen, choose **Open an existing graph** and pick the graph's top-level folder — usually the one containing `pages/`, `journals/`, and `logseq/`. On Android, grant "All files access" when asked; Tine then continues to the folder picker.

2. Later, use the graph-name menu at the top of the left sidebar → **Open graph…**, or Settings (**t s**) → **Graph** → **Open another graph…**. Graphs you have opened appear in the same sidebar menu for one-click switching.
3. On desktop, from the command line, `tine /path/to/graph` (or `tine open /path/to/graph`, or `TINE_GRAPH=/path/to/graph`) opens a graph directly.
4. What you should see: the same pages and journals Logseq finds. Existing Markdown and Org pages may be at the graph root or in nested folders, not only under `pages/` and `journals/`.

If the graph you used last time cannot be opened at launch — the folder moved, a drive is unplugged, a file is unreadable — the Welcome screen says so in a card that names the graph and the reason, with **Try again** and **Copy details** buttons. Nothing was changed on disk; you can also open another graph from the same screen.

blocks.raw: ## Open your graph

children.raw: Press **g Shift+G** (g, then Shift+G), or run **All graphs** from the command palette. This page lists the same remembered graphs as the sidebar graph menu.

Use **Up/Down** to choose a graph, **Home/End** to reach the first or last, and **Enter** to open it in this window. On desktop, **Shift+Enter** opens it in a new window. **Tab** reaches each graph's actions, including **Remove from this list**, which leaves its files untouched, plus **Open graph…** and **New graph…**.
What you should see: after Enter, the sidebar shows the chosen graph's name and its pages replace the previous graph's pages.

blocks.raw: ## Switch graphs from the keyboard

children.raw: Choose **Create a new graph** on Welcome, or **New graph…** in the sidebar graph menu. Choose its parent folder on desktop or iOS; Android uses its default graph location.

Enter a **Graph name**. Tine suggests the first unused name: `notes`, `notes-2`, `notes-3`, and so on. The graph is always a child folder of that name, even when the parent is empty. Cancel creates nothing.

An existing empty child folder can be used. A nonempty folder is refused without replacing its files; the name prompt stays open so you can choose another name. Names must be one portable folder name, without path separators, Windows device names, invalid characters, or a trailing dot or space.

On Windows, use `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\…` for a graph in WSL: Windows access through a distro package's `LocalState\rootfs` can corrupt Linux files, so Tine refuses new graphs there and warns when opening an existing one.

blocks.raw: ## Create a new graph

children.raw: The usual layout is `pages/`, `journals/`, `assets/`, and `logseq/config.edn`, but Tine also finds eligible `.md`, `.markdown`, and `.org` pages elsewhere inside the graph.

Root-level and nested pages are named from their file names (or their `title::`) and save back to their exact existing paths. Tine skips hidden/internal trees, assets, publish output, and sync-provider conflict copies; `:hidden` prefixes in `config.edn` are honored too.
Your journal settings are honored: Tine reads the journal date formats from `config.edn`, so old files are recognized and new journals are created in your format.
An Org file Tine cannot reproduce byte-for-byte opens **read-only** rather than being rewritten imperfectly.

blocks.raw: ## What Tine reads

children.raw: Edits save automatically into the same file each page came from, preserving that file's exact formatting; files with no changes are not rewritten.
New pages and journals are ordinary `.md` or `.org` files in the configured pages and journals folders (Settings → **Editor** → **File format** chooses what new files use).
A Tine view (grid, table, board) attaches harmless `tine.*` properties to its own block; Logseq shows them as ordinary property lines — see [[Features/Sheets]].

blocks.raw: ## What Tine writes

children.raw: While Tine is open, it watches the files, so changes made by Logseq, another editor, or a sync tool appear automatically (Settings → **Files** → **Watch for external edits** switches to polling on filesystems where the live watcher is unreliable).
Avoid editing the same graph in two apps at once. A second Tine window on the same graph is refused; concurrent edits across other apps or devices are handled as conflicts, not assumed safe.

If a page changes on disk while you have unsaved edits, Tine overwrites nothing — a banner offers **Review**, which compares your draft with the disk version on the page. The mechanics are in [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

Syncthing and Dropbox keep working on the folder as before; Tine detects their conflict copies, shows an **N conflicts** badge in the left sidebar, and helps you merge them — also in [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

blocks.raw: ## Coexisting with other tools

children.raw: 1. Confirm you opened the graph root: Settings (**t s**) → **Graph** → **Graph folder** shows the current graph path; on desktop, **Show in folder** beside it opens that folder in Finder, File Explorer or your file manager. In a standard Logseq graph, this is the folder containing `pages/`, `journals/`, and `logseq/config.edn`.
2. Skim [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]] now — know where snapshots, conflict copies, and the trash live before you need them.
3. What you should see: no conflict banner, your existing pages in their original locations, and edits from Tine landing in the same files Logseq reads.

blocks.raw: ## First safety checks

children.raw: [[Start/Where things are]] maps the page, sidebars, tabs, and Settings and Help you will meet on the way; [[Workflows/Capture and plan your day]] starts the journal-first daily flow.

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: A short map of Tine's main places, so the recipes in this Guide make sense on first read: the page in the middle, the left sidebar, the tab strip, the right sidebar, and Settings and Help. Each place links to the workflow that teaches it — nothing here is a rulebook.

blocks.raw: # Where things are

children.raw: Each pane shows the **page or PDF** its active tab points to. Tine opens on the **journal feed** — one continuous, editable list of days — and the **Journals** item in the left sidebar takes you back to it. With `:feature/enable-journals? false` in `logseq/config.edn`, the sidebar shows your configured home page instead of Journals.
Everything you write is a **block** (one bullet). Blocks nest under other blocks to form the outline, and any block can carry a task, a date, a link, or its own id for references from elsewhere.
Press **Ctrl+K** at any time to jump to a page by name or to text inside any block.
Mouse back and forward buttons navigate page history on desktop. On macOS, **Cmd+[** and **Cmd+]** also go back and forward; dragging with a side button does not navigate.

A page in a namespace has a **Hierarchy** section below its outline. Click its title, or focus it and press **Enter** or **Space**, to fold or expand the paths. It starts expanded and remembers your choice for that page until you switch graphs.

The reading column has a width cap. Press **t w** to toggle wide mode, which drops the cap; Settings → **Appearance** → **Advanced** holds **Standard page width** and **Wide page width** if you want your own numbers.
On desktop, resize any graph window down to 390 pt wide to use it beside another app.

If one region of the screen — the page, the sidebar, a references section, or the conflict panel — fails to draw, that region shows a small card saying so, with a **Retry** button, instead of leaving the whole window blank. Your files on disk are not touched by it.

blocks.raw: ## The middle: one route per pane

children.raw: At the very top sits the workspace switcher — saved window layouts, covered in [[Workflows/Keep context visible]]. Just under it, the graph-name menu switches between the graphs Tine knows, with **Open graph…** and **New graph…** beside them — on desktop, Shift-click a graph row to open it in a second window instead of switching this one. Right-click a row for the same thing as a menu item — **Open in a new window** — along with **Open here**, **Show in folder**, **Copy path**, and **Remove from this list**. The row for the graph you already have open shows the two open actions greyed out, so the menu keeps its shape wherever you click.

Below the menu: **Journals**, then fold-up **Favorites** and **Recent** (each appears once it has something in it), **All pages**, and the **Namespaces** tree, where `Project/Roadmap` nests under `Project`. Namespaces appears only when the graph has namespaced page names. Favorites and Recent remember whether you left them open or folded.

The **All pages** entry opens the full **All pages** view in the main pane: every page in your graph, however many, as one scrolling table. On a phone, choosing it closes the navigation drawer. It opens with the most recently changed pages first: the **Updated** column shows when each page's file last changed (a dash when Tine has no time for it). Click **Updated**, **Page** (name) or **Backlinks** to sort by it, and click again to reverse; type in the filter box to narrow by name, and tick **Show journals** to include the daily pages, which also adds the **Journal date** column (click it to sort by date). Rows open exactly like sidebar rows — click for this pane, Shift-click for the right sidebar, Ctrl/Cmd- or middle-click for a background tab, Alt-click for the other pane, right-click for the page menu.

Every row is a whole-row click target: clicking the blank space to the right of a short page name opens that page, just like clicking the name itself. Shift-click a row for the right sidebar, middle-click for a background tab, right-click for the page menu.

Favorites can be arranged without changing what Logseq sees: choose **+ New group**, rename the plain-text label, then drag favorites or groups left/right to lift or nest them to any depth. On a touch screen, hold a favorite still for a moment to open its menu (the one a right-click opens), or hold it and then drag to pick it up and move it; a finger that moves first scrolls the list, and a tap still opens the favorite. Deleting a group keeps everything it held one level up. Tine stores that richer arrangement on an ordinary editable page while keeping `config.edn :favorites` as Logseq's flat list; [[Workflows/Find and revisit]] walks the safe path.

The **+ New page** button at the bottom opens the same Ctrl+K box; a name that matches nothing becomes a page you can create. When Syncthing, Dropbox or a merge leaves pages that need a decision, an **N conflicts** badge appears beside it — see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]]. Press **t l** to fold the whole sidebar away, and **t l** again to bring it back.

blocks.raw: ## The left sidebar: your graph's contents

children.raw: Every open page or PDF keeps a tab along the top, browser-style: click to switch, **Ctrl+W** to close. Middle-click anything that opens a page — a link, a search result, a bullet's dot — to park it in a background tab without leaving this one. PDF links open in a companion pane by default, and their tabs can be dragged between panes like page tabs. Tabs come back after a restart.

The strip needs room: in a window narrower than 640 px (a phone held upright, a small desktop window) it gives way to the **Open tabs** list in the left sidebar, which shows your open tabs, switches to one with a tap, and closes one with its ✕; drag its rows to reorder them or nest one tab under another ([[Workflows/Keep context visible]]). It appears once a second tab is open, on every platform.

blocks.raw: ## The tab strip: what's open

children.raw: Anything you want **beside** the current page rather than instead of it — another page, or zoomed into one bullet — goes to the right sidebar: **Shift-click** a link or a bullet's dot. Items there are live editors, not previews. Press **t r** to show or hide the whole sidebar.

blocks.raw: ## The right sidebar: parked context

children.raw: The gear at the top right (or press **t s**, **Cmd+,** on macOS or **Ctrl+,** elsewhere) opens **Settings**: appearance (Light, System or Dark, interface size, wide mode), editor behavior, journals, files, backups & recovery, the graph, plugins, help & diagnostics, and the remappable **Keyboard shortcuts** list. The search box at the top shows only matching settings, with matching words highlighted. Choose a result to leave search and reveal its control, including Advanced settings; the setting is highlighted for about two seconds so it is easy to spot. Names that match come before descriptions that match, and a result found through text outside its visible name shows the matching description, keyword, alias or English name with the match highlighted. A single character matches only the text shown in your interface language, not the English names behind a translated interface. Clear the search to restore the normal tab. In **Keyboard shortcuts**, search filters commands and keys within that tab.

**Themes** is the first section under Settings → **Appearance**, followed by Language and Mode. **Advanced** holds Fine-tuning, Custom CSS and content widths; Settings search reveals these controls too. Tine's menus, settings and messages can be shown in English or Simplified Chinese (简体中文); **System default** follows your system's language. The choice applies at once, in every open window, and is remembered on this device. Your notes, page names, properties and queries are never translated. Simplified Chinese covers the complete interface catalog, including settings, queries, context menus and recovery dialogs.
Settings opens as a small dialog. The button beside its search box makes it fill the window, which is easier to read through; Tine remembers which size you left it at and opens it that way next time.
The **?** button at the bottom right (or press **Shift+?**) opens Help: this Guide, the shortcut reference, the features documentation, the bug-report and release-notes links, and the Welcome screen.

blocks.raw: ## Settings and Help

children.raw: Below a 640 px window width, either sidebar opens as an overlay on top of the current route instead of shrinking it — tap the shaded outside edge, press Esc, or use Android Back to dismiss. Split panes are off on a phone-sized touch screen; open tabs are listed under **Open tabs** in the left sidebar.
[[Reference/Platforms and mobile]] separates narrow-window behavior from native-app behavior and maps each platform's shipping surface.

blocks.raw: ## Feature showcase

children.raw: 1. Open one of the Guide pages above and follow its numbered steps.
2. Use **Copy the guide into your graph** when you want an editable sandbox.
3. Tine creates the real `tine-guide/` namespace, rewrites guide links to that copy, and leaves existing copied pages untouched.
4. What you should see: normal Logseq pages you can edit, delete, or keep as a reference.

blocks.raw: ## Create one yourself

children.raw: Tine is a fast, local outliner that reads and writes the **same Markdown files as Logseq** — the very folder you point it at. Edit here or in Logseq; it's one graph, no import, no export. We have a lot of respect for Logseq — Tine just tries to improve a few things.
**Everything you see here is a real Markdown file** in this graph's `pages/` folder. Open that folder in your file manager and look — nothing is locked away.

blocks.raw: # Welcome to Tine 👋

children.raw: Click any bullet to edit it. **Enter** makes a new bullet, **Tab** indents, **Shift+Tab** outdents. Drag a bullet's dot to move it (and everything under it).
TODO Click this checkbox to complete me
DONE This one is already done

Tasks — type `TODO` / `DOING` / `DONE` at the start of a bullet, or press **Ctrl+Enter** to cycle one; clicking a `TODO`/`DOING` (or `LATER`/`NOW`) label flips between the pair and never clears `DONE`:
Rich text: **bold**, *italic*, ==highlight==, `inline code`, and even math like $e^{i\pi} + 1 = 0$.
Links: type `[[` to link a page or `#` for a #tag; a suggestion that is an alias is labelled **alias of** its page. Here's a link to [[Project/Roadmap]] — click it.

And here is that same bullet **embedded** inline — it stays in sync with the original:
