When you're ready, point Tine at your **own** Logseq graph: open Settings (**t s**) and pick a different folder — [[Start/Bring an existing graph]] walks you through it. Your notes stay exactly where they are.

blocks.raw: ## Keep exploring

children.raw: The shortest path: open **Journals** in the sidebar and start typing. Everything below adds one tool at a time — a task marker, a priority, a date — and ends with the two things that keep a plan current: the Agenda and carry-over.

blocks.raw: # Capture and plan your day

children.raw: 1. Click **Journals** in the sidebar — the feed opens with today first (today is the current day on this machine's local calendar, and it rolls over at local midnight). Click into today's first bullet and type what happened or what you mean to do.
2. Press **Enter** for the next bullet, **Tab** / **Shift+Tab** to nest or flatten it.

3. To put a bullet *above* an existing one, press **Enter** with the caret at its very start. Some bullets keep Enter for themselves — inside a code block it adds a line of code — so for those, right-click the bullet's dot and choose **Insert block above**.

4. What you should see: the text saves to today's journal file on its own — there is no Save button. For where writes go and what happens if a file changes on disk, see [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

blocks.raw: ## Describe your day in bullets

children.raw: When a thought arrives while you are in another app, press your desktop quick-capture shortcut, type, and the note is appended to today's journal without switching windows. One-time setup, the optional page-title field, and the Enter-key tuning are all in [[Features/Quick capture]].

blocks.raw: ## Not at your desk? Quick capture

children.raw: 1. With the caret anywhere in a bullet, press **Ctrl+Enter** (Cmd on Mac). The bullet becomes `TODO …`; press again for `DOING`, again for `DONE`, once more to drop the marker. (Under the NOW / LATER workflow — the default — the cycle is LATER → NOW → DONE.)
2. Prefer the mouse? Click the marker chip to toggle between the workflow's two open states (TODO ↔ DOING or LATER ↔ NOW), or click the checkbox in front of the task to finish it in one step.
3. Select several blocks first and the same keypress cycles every selected task at once.
4. What you should see: a colored marker chip at the start of the block, plus an empty checkbox until the task is done.

blocks.raw: ## Turn a bullet into a task

children.raw: Type **/** and choose **Priority A** (or B, C) — the marker line becomes `TODO [#A] Call the bank`.
What you should see: a colored `[#A]` chip right after the marker; swap it by running the command again.

blocks.raw: ## Rank it

children.raw: 1. Type **/** and choose **Scheduled**, then pick the day in the calendar popup — use **+ Add time** if the hour matters.
2. Add **Deadline** the same way when the task has a hard due date.
3. What you should see: a small calendar chip next to the block for each date. Click a chip any time to change or remove it.

blocks.raw: ## Give it a date

children.raw: Copy this Guide into your graph and look at these example tasks:

TODO [#A] Collect the audit receipts
SCHEDULED: <2026-08-12 Wed>

TODO Book the flights
DEADLINE: <2026-08-15 Sat>
LATER Read the harvest notes

Water the office plants
SCHEDULED: <2026-08-12 Wed +1w>
Then this query lists them:
{{query (task TODO DOING NOW LATER)}}

What you should see: the marked tasks above, plus tasks elsewhere in the graph that use `TODO`, `DOING`, `NOW`, or `LATER` (the [[Feature showcase]] has a few; a copied Guide adds your own). The query covers the whole graph — a task written on any page turns up here, not just the ones on this page; DONE tasks and tasks using other markers do not appear.

blocks.raw: ## Try it: from bullets to an open-task query

children.raw: 1. Look at the bottom of today's block in the Journals feed (the first day): the **Scheduled & Deadline** list shows open items whose date is near today, wherever in the graph they were written.

2. What you should see: your dated tasks, each with its date chip; click one to jump to it. Widen or narrow the range in Settings → **Journals** → **Agenda window** (default: a week back and a week ahead). The Agenda sits under today in the feed, not on a journal page you opened by itself, and the list vanishes when nothing is dated in range.

blocks.raw: ## See the plan: the Agenda

children.raw: 1. Scroll to a past day in the feed, hover its title row (or focus a title-row control with the keyboard), and click **Carry unfinished tasks → today** under its title. Blocks with open markers move to today; DONE and CANCELED stay put.
On touch devices without hover, the carry buttons stay visible. The same controls appear on a journal page opened by itself.
2. What you should see: a "Carried N items to today" toast — or "No unfinished tasks to carry" if none were open.

3. Variants: on today, **Carry from previous day** pulls the latest earlier day in; **Carry last N days** goes further back (N is set in Settings, default 7). The past-day action is also on that day's right-click menu, and the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) has 7 / 30 / 365-day presets.
Settings → **Journals** also tunes it: hide the buttons (the right-click menu keeps working), move the whole block with its context or just the task line, add a “Carried over” heading.

blocks.raw: ## Carry-over: let unfinished tasks follow you

children.raw: All of this remains plain text. Journal entries use the graph's configured journal directory; tasks on ordinary pages stay in their own Markdown or Org files. Within a task, the marker comes first, then `[#A]`, then the `SCHEDULED:`/`DEADLINE:` lines — readable by Logseq and by any editor. The companion reference page [[Reference/Journals, tasks, and scheduling]] maps the marker set, repeaters, time tracking, and the stored query behind the Agenda. If something looks wrong — a banner, a conflict copy, a duplicate day — [[Reference/Troubleshooting and recovery]] has the recovery steps.

blocks.raw: ## Where everything lives

children.raw: Change colors, fonts, widths, bullets, and embed shading without a plugin: write a few lines of CSS in your graph's `logseq/custom.css`. This page shows where the file is, which names Tine promises to keep stable (the `--tine-*` tokens), ten copy-paste recipes, and how to find out what styles any element.

blocks.raw: # Customize Tine's look

children.raw: 1. Open Settings (**t s**) → **Appearance** and look at **Color scheme**. Default, Nord, Solarized, Gruvbox, and **Soft** are built in. Soft is a medium-brightness palette: warm gray in light mode and lifted slate gray in dark mode, with warm highlights and quiet active tabs. Its page, sidebars, menus, and code surfaces move together while text stays readable.
2. Pick one. It applies at once and is remembered on this device.

3. Precedence, lowest to highest: Tine's stock palette, then the color scheme you picked, then the **Fine-tuning** choices below, then device-wide `global.css`, then your graph's `logseq/custom.css`. Your CSS always has the last word, and an installed theme package never edits it. A **Style** preset such as editorial reading type keeps its own look, but the font and size tokens below still override its fonts and text size. A theme package's **Use typography** choice (fonts and line height) sets the same font tokens at the theme layer, so your own tokens below still win over it, and it wins over a **Style** preset's fonts.

4. Open **Advanced** in Appearance for **Fine-tuning**, a few visual details that are not worth a theme of their own. **Embedded blocks** shows embeds as a shaded box (the default) or with only the accent line and dot. **Links to the web or a file** is a solid underline (the default), a dotted one, or none; links to pages never have one, so the two kinds read differently. **Links to pages that do not exist yet** is the dimmed link color (the default), a stronger one, or the same color as other links. Every choice starts at Tine's default look, takes effect at once, and has its own **Reset**. Settings search also finds these controls and opens Advanced.

**Arrows and dashes** (`->`, `<-`, `=>`, `--`, `---`) show exactly as you typed them, as in Logseq. To see them as glyphs (→, ⇒, –, —), set Settings → **Appearance** → **Typographic replacements** to **On (while reading)**, which changes only what you see and leaves your Markdown as typed, or **On (while typing)**, which rewrites the text itself as you type. It is **Off** by default; a device that used the earlier default, where arrows were drawn as glyphs, needs to pick **On (while reading)** once.

Fine-tuning choices are saved on this device (under `style.knobs.v1` in Tine's device settings), never in your graph, so they do not follow the graph to another computer. **Disable custom CSS** switches them off for the session along with your stylesheet, and your `custom.css` outranks them.
**Block embed breadcrumbs** is off by default. Turn it on to show a muted source page and parent trail above block embeds.

What you should see: the whole window recolors together. Anything you then set in `custom.css` overrides only what you set. A Fine-tuning choice changes its one detail at once and **Reset** puts it back.

blocks.raw: ## 1. Start from a color scheme

children.raw: Style one tag with `a.tag[data-ref="ai-note"] { color: #b45ee8; }`. Tags and page links carry `data-ref` with the lowercased page name, as in Logseq. Keep the full namespace (`parent/elias`); an alias label uses the link's target name, not the displayed label. For a page link, use `.page-ref[data-ref="parent/elias"]` (or `.ref[data-ref="parent/elias"]` in a static export).

1. Settings → **Appearance** → **Advanced** → **Custom CSS** → **Edit custom.css** opens `logseq/custom.css` in Tine's text editor, including on mobile. Or press **Ctrl+K** (**Cmd+K** on macOS), type `css` or `custom.css`, and choose **Edit custom.css**. A missing file starts empty and is created only when you save.

Switching apps or backgrounding Tine starts saving CSS alongside your pages. If a conflict refuses the save, reopening the same CSS file restores the recoverable draft with its original revision; copy it before reloading from disk.

2. Press **Save** to apply changes immediately, or **Save & close** to return to your notes. **Cancel** closes without saving (it asks first if you have unsaved edits), and clicking outside the editor closes it only when nothing is unsaved. If another editor or a sync tool changed the file, Tine refuses to overwrite it and keeps your text open. Copy your edits before choosing **Reload**, then combine them with the latest file and save again.

3. **Edit global CSS** opens `global.css` in Tine's per-user config directory, outside every graph. It applies to every graph on this device and loads before each graph's `custom.css`, so the graph can override it. The quick switcher also finds **Edit global CSS (global.css)**. Saving applies it across open graph windows. This device file does not travel with a synced graph.

On desktop, **Open in default app** beside either Edit button opens that CSS file in the app your operating system associates with `.css`, creating it if missing. The command palette also offers **Open custom.css in default app** and **Open global CSS (global.css) in default app**. Saves from your external editor apply live to Tine, including global CSS across open graph windows. The in-app Edit buttons remain available on every platform.
What you should see: a rule such as `:root { --tine-bullet-color: orange; }` recolors every bullet as soon as you save.

Something went wrong? **Settings → Appearance → Advanced → Custom CSS → Disable custom CSS** ignores both CSS files and Fine-tuning for this session only. It is never saved, so restarting Tine always brings custom CSS back; fix the file, then switch it back on. If the stylesheet hides Settings itself, open the command palette (**Mod+Shift+P**) and run **Toggle custom CSS (safe mode, this session)**.

blocks.raw: ## 2. Open your custom.css

children.raw: A token is a named setting. Each starts unset, which means "use the theme's default", so nothing changes until you set one. Set tokens on `:root` or `html`, like the recipes below; any selector you write wins over Tine's own, because Tine declares them with no specificity. These sixteen names are the ones Tine promises to keep: if one is ever removed or renamed, the changelog says so.

| Token | Controls | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--tine-danger-color` | Error and destructive-action text and error borders (also the asset trash button's hover fill) | A contrast-checked red for the theme's light or dark mode |
| `--tine-embed-bg` | Background of an embedded block or page | The theme's secondary background |
| `--tine-embed-accent` | The accent line and bullet of an embedded block | 35% accent mixed into the bullet color |
| `--tine-bullet-color` | Color of the block bullet dot | The theme's bullet color |
| `--tine-bullet-size` | Diameter of the block bullet dot | 6px |
| `--tine-tag-color` | Color of `#tags` and tag chips | The theme's tag color |
| `--tine-highlight-bg` | Background of `^^highlighted^^` text | The theme's highlight color |
| `--tine-missing-page-color` | Color of a link to a page that does not exist yet | A dimmed tint of the link color |
| `--tine-external-link-underline` | The line under a link to a web address or file | `1px solid` (use `none` to remove it) |
| `--tine-content-width` | Maximum width of the page column | 810px |
| `--tine-content-width-wide` | Maximum width of the column in Wide mode | 100% |
| `--tine-page-title-size` | Font size of a page title | 28px |
| `--tine-font-size` | Base font size of page text | 16px |
| `--tine-content-font` | Font family of the interface and page text | Inter, then your system fonts |
| `--tine-mono-font` | Font family of code and other monospace text | MonoLisa, then your system mono fonts |
| `--tine-editable-font` | Font family of text while you edit it | Inter, then the emoji font, then your system fonts |
The code and formula editors always edit in the monospace face, so `--tine-editable-font` does not reach them; `--tine-mono-font` does.
Colors beyond these still use Logseq's `--ls-*` variables (for example `--ls-primary-background-color`), exactly as in Logseq, so a Logseq snippet you already have keeps working.

The page widths you set in Settings → Appearance → Advanced (**Standard page width**, **Wide page width**) outrank `--tine-content-width` and `--tine-content-width-wide`. Reset those two fields if a token seems to have no effect.

blocks.raw: ## 3. The supported names: `--tine-*` tokens

children.raw: Paste any of these into `logseq/custom.css` and save. Combine as many as you like.
Remove the shade behind embedded blocks:
Give embedded blocks a warm accent instead of the theme's:
Change the bullet color, and make bullets a little bigger:
A wider page column, in normal and in Wide mode:

A different reading font, for display and for editing (it also overrides the editorial reading style). Keep `var(--tine-editable-emoji-font)` in the editing list; it protects emoji from crashing some Linux systems:
Larger text everywhere the base size applies:
A different code font:
A different tag color and highlight color:
Smaller page titles:
A different value only in dark mode (Tine marks the window `light` or `dark`):
Recolor the page itself with a Logseq variable, light mode only:

blocks.raw: ## 4. Ten copy-paste recipes

children.raw: 1. Settings → **Appearance** → **Advanced** → **Custom CSS** → **Developer tools** (desktop), or press **Ctrl+Shift+J** (**Cmd+Shift+J** on macOS), opens the inspector. It is part of every desktop build, release builds included. Use its element picker, then read the **Styles** pane.
2. Look for a `var(--tine-…)` or `var(--ls-…)` in the rule that draws what you want to change. Setting that variable in `custom.css` is the stable way to change it.

3. When no variable exists, a class selector such as `.embed-block` works today, but class names and the structure of the page can change between releases, so a rule written that way may need a touch-up after an update. Prefer a token.

4. One class is a promise to theme authors, because a stylesheet cannot work it out from the page: `just-toggled`. When you press a task's checkbox or its marker word (also the checkbox of a task shown inside a block reference), Tine adds `just-toggled` to that task's `.block-task-checkbox` and `.block-marker` for about 0.7 seconds, then removes it. It is never there when a page loads, when a row scrolls back into view, or when a sync or another editor changes the task. So `.block-task-checkbox.just-toggled { animation: pop 300ms; }` (with your own `@keyframes pop`) plays on your own toggle and nowhere else, which a bare `animation` on `.block-task-checkbox` cannot do. Put motion inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`.
What you should see: the inspector opens and highlights the element you point at, with its rules listed in the **Styles** pane.

blocks.raw: ## 5. Find out what styles an element

children.raw: A token seems to do nothing: check that you set it on `:root` or `html` (or `html[data-theme="dark"]`) and that the page-width Settings fields are reset for the two width tokens.
The whole window became unreadable: **Disable custom CSS** in Settings, or restart Tine with the file edited.
If a **custom.css could not be read** message appears, fix the file's permissions or size with an external text editor, then try **Edit custom.css** again.

blocks.raw: ## 6. If it does not look right

children.raw: [[Workflows/Extend Tine]] covers theme packages and plugins.
[[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]] explains what else lives in your graph's `logseq/` folder.

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Add a plugin or a theme in a few minutes, know exactly what authority you granted, and take it back cleanly. This page is the hands-on path; the detailed rulebook stays on [[Features/Plugins]].

blocks.raw: # Extend Tine

children.raw: Tine plugins are capability-limited WebAssembly guests. They are **not** Logseq or Obsidian plugins, and plugins written for those apps do not run here.
The plugin API is experimental. An app update may leave an incompatible plugin installed but disabled; it must not make your graph unreadable or discard the plugin's local settings.

A plugin declares capabilities from a short, closed list, and Tine performs each one on its behalf: command-palette actions, slash commands, small block decorations (thread lines, badges), declarative settings, and narrowly preconditioned edits to a focused block.

A plugin cannot access the DOM, Tauri, the network, files, processes, or your graph directly, and it cannot inject HTML or CSS — everything it shows is drawn by Tine. The one capability that can change your text is `graph.write.block`, and even it may edit only the block Tine handed the plugin, and only if that block's text is unchanged since Tine handed it over.

blocks.raw: ## Know what a plugin can touch before you install one

children.raw: 1. Open Settings (**t s**) → **Plugins** → **Browse**. Each community-catalogue entry lists its source, license, supported platforms, and declared capabilities, plus a safety verdict — "Automated review passed", "Low-risk automated pass", or "Human-reviewed before publication". Open its **Safety report** for the digest-verified detail, and keep the reminder under it in mind: *automated review is evidence, not a guarantee.*
2. Choose **Install**. Nothing runs yet — every plugin version is **installed disabled**, and Tine takes you to the **Installed** tab with its details open.
3. Review what it claims: name, version, author, license, platforms, capabilities. If they match what you expected, flip the toggle to enable it.

4. Developing or sideloading instead? **Install a local package** (under **Browse**, button **Choose package…**) takes a `manifest.json` and its `.wasm` file together — with the same installed-disabled rule.

What you should see: exactly the contribution the plugin declared — a command-palette entry, a slash command, or a decoration — and nothing else. If the package does not support your device, its button reads **Unavailable on …** instead of Install.

blocks.raw: ## Install one — it starts disabled

children.raw: A plugin that declares settings gets a **Settings** section on its details page (**Settings…** beside it in the **Installed** list), but Tine draws the controls — toggles, dropdowns, numbers, text — from the plugin's declared schema. Values are validated scalars, **stored on this device only** and never written into your graph. A changed key offers **Reset**; **Reset all settings** restores the schema defaults.

blocks.raw: ## Change its settings — Tine's controls, your device

children.raw: Flip the same toggle (on the details page or in the **Installed** list) to disable: the behavior stops, the package stays installed, and your pages remain exactly as readable as before — a plugin may not invent a format your graph would depend on.
**Uninstall…** removes only that package version from this device. Tine asks first and states the boundary: it removes the plugin from this device and does not change your graph or notes.
Behind the scenes, signed revocations are checked before a saved plugin starts, so a version revoked as unsafe stays disabled even when the live catalogue is temporarily unavailable.

blocks.raw: ## Disable it, or take it out

children.raw: Themes live separately under Settings → **Appearance**. **Style** controls typography, journal headings, and other Tine-owned presentation styles; **Color scheme** selects Default, Nord, Solarized, Gruvbox, Soft, or the colors from an installed package. Style and colors are independent, so you can keep one package's style while using another palette. Declarative packages install from the **Theme packages** list or a local `theme.json` file (**Choose theme.json…**) and contain no scripts, selectors, imports, font files, or remote assets. The choices stay on this device, and no theme ever reads or writes your graph.

A package written for theme API 0.3 can also name the fonts it was designed with (body, monospace, titles) and a block line height. Installed rows then offer a separate **Use typography** button, next to **Use colors** and **Use style**, and Settings → Appearance gets a **Typography** selector (choose **Default** to return to Tine's own fonts). A package can only name fonts already installed on your device, never ship or download one: if its first font is missing, the row says so, Tine uses the package's fallback fonts, and nothing fails. Your own `logseq/custom.css` still overrides them. Theme authors: see `docs/themes/README.md`.

A Today summary, when selected, is rendered by Tine from the journal page already on screen: it counts open task markers there and calls the `DOING`, `NOW`, `STARTED`, and `IN-PROGRESS` subset “in progress.” The theme receives neither those tasks nor a query interface.

Your own `logseq/custom.css` outranks every theme: themes recolor Tine through Logseq's `--ls-*` variables, and your CSS loads last. Uninstalling a theme package leaves it untouched, too. [[Workflows/Customize Tine's look]] shows how to open that file, the `--tine-*` tokens Tine keeps stable, and ten copy-paste recipes.

blocks.raw: ## Themes change presentation; they never run

children.raw: Desktop and Android share the same plugin and theme lifecycle; a package that did not declare your platform shows as unavailable rather than failing later.

The F-Droid build omits the network community catalogue to comply with the store's runtime-code-download policy. The plugin host, your already-installed plugins and themes, local `manifest.json` + `.wasm` and theme packages, and the built-in gallery all keep working there.
The iOS beta runs themes but not plugins: the iOS plugin host is not enabled yet. [[Reference/Platforms and mobile]] carries the full platform map.

blocks.raw: ## Platform and distribution lines

children.raw: [[Features/Plugins]] keeps the detailed reference, including the safety-report fields and the cascade order — and links the authoring, packaging, and registry guide used by plugin developers.

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Three moves cover most of finding things: jump to what you remember, follow the trail of links, and keep a search that's worth keeping. No syntax is needed up front. The exact rules live in [[Reference/Pages, links, references, and search]].

blocks.raw: # Find and revisit

children.raw: 1. Press **Ctrl+K** (Cmd on Mac) and type any words from the title or the text you remember. The switcher matches page titles and the visible text of blocks.

2. Too many hits? Narrow with the **Search syntax** forms listed in the switcher footer: `-draft` excludes a word, `OR` offers alternatives, quotes pin an exact phrase, `/…/` is a case-sensitive regular expression.

3. **Enter** opens the highlighted result; **Shift+Enter** opens it in the right sidebar beside your current page; **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** or a middle-click opens it in a background tab without closing the search; **Alt+Enter** opens it in another pane.

Click or tap a result to open it in the pane you were using. **Commands** (**Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P**) works the same way: click or tap a command, or highlight it and press **Enter**. Search and Commands keep your focused split pane.
Picking a slash command or a `[[` page suggestion while editing also keeps that editor's split pane focused.

4. Sure it's on the open page? **Ctrl+Shift+K** searches only that page's blocks, and **Ctrl+F** searches the open main and split panes plus the right sidebar, in pane order then sidebar order. Its slim find bar shows match counts and expands folded branches to show a match. The arrow at its left opens **Replace with**: **Replace** changes the highlighted match, **Replace all** every match on that page, as one Undo step. On a phone, open it from the page's **⋯** menu → **Find in page**.

Select a single line of text in a block editor or rendered content, then press **Ctrl/Cmd+F**: Find opens with the selected text and highlights the first match. With no selection or a selection spanning lines, it keeps your previous query.
In Journals, Find and Replace search loaded days only; “N older days not searched — search all journals” counts retired days and opens graph-wide search with the same query.
If the switcher cannot read results, choose **Retry** to run the same search again without clearing what you typed.

What you should see: Tine jumps to the page or block. Exact title matches lead the list; over time Tine may prefer a result you deliberately picked before, but only among equally strong matches — Settings → **Editor** → Advanced → **Learn Ctrl+K choices** disables that, and **Reset ranking** clears it.

blocks.raw: ## "I saw it somewhere" — jump with Ctrl+K

children.raw: 1. Click any `[[link]]` or `#tag` to open its page. A link to a page that does not exist yet isn't broken — opening it gives you an empty page that is saved once you type in it. Linking `[[foo]]` and `[[Foo]]` always reaches one page. While editing, **Ctrl+O** follows the link at the caret and **Ctrl+Shift+O** opens it in the right sidebar.

2. On the page you reach, scroll to **Linked References**: every block that points here, grouped by source page, with a filter (the funnel button) to narrow to blocks that also mention something else. Open **Unlinked References** to catch plain-text mentions you never linked.

Click an ancestor in a **Linked References** or **Unlinked References** breadcrumb to show that ancestor and its subtree inline, without leaving the page. The ancestor opens while collapsed descendants stay folded. **Shift+click** opens the ancestor in the right sidebar instead. This context is temporary: leaving and returning resets it. Breadcrumbs become clickable once the source page has loaded.

3. Need several references outside Tine? Use the copy/export button on **Linked References** or **Unlinked References**. Every visible entry starts selected; uncheck a subset, then use the ordinary Text / OPML / HTML export choices. Linked References honors the text and chip filters already applied.
4. Found a line worth quoting in your own note? Edit the note, type `((`, and search the line's text to insert a block reference — a live copy that updates whenever the original changes.

The `((` picker says **Searching blocks…** while reading, offers **Retry** if the read fails, and says **No matched blocks** only after a successful empty search. Retry keeps your text; **Escape** closes the picker.
What you should see: the reference renders as link-styled text with the source's current words, and the source block gains a small reference-count badge that lists its referrers.

blocks.raw: ## Follow the trail: links, tags, and references

children.raw: Choose **Copy link** in a graph's menu or a block's context menu, or **Copy as ▸ → Copy link** in **Page actions**, then paste the `tine://` address into a task manager, calendar, chat, bookmark, or another note. **Copy as ▸** also offers page references; a block's context menu lists **Copy block ref** and **Copy block embed** beside **Copy link**. A block link uses its saved ID alone and survives moving the block to another page.

The first copy stores a small graph ID in `logseq/tine-graph-id`; copying a block also saves its ordinary `id::` property. Browsing and opening links never create IDs, pages, blocks, or captured content.

Links work with Tine closed or already running. A page or block opens in a new tab of the focused pane in its graph's window. A missing graph or target shows an error. After moving or renaming a graph folder, open that folder once so Tine knows its new location. If two known folders are copies of one graph, choose which to open; Tine remembers that choice on this device.

blocks.raw: ## Open a note from another app

children.raw: 1. Favorite a page from its title: the star beside the title (or **Page actions** → **Add to favorites**). It appears under **Favorites** in the left sidebar and remains in Logseq's ordinary flat `config.edn :favorites` list.

2. Choose **+ New group**, type a plain-text name, and drag a favorite onto it. Drag right to nest under the preceding row, left to lift out, or vertically to reorder without changing depth. Groups and favorites can both contain children. In the left sidebar the whole row is the link, so a short name is still an easy target — a row is reordered by dragging it, and a drag only has to move a few pixels to stop counting as a click. In the right sidebar, where items are parked pages rather than a navigation list, only the title itself opens the page and the rest of the row is there to grab.
3. Collapse any row that has children. Delete a group when you no longer need the label: what it held moves up one level and stays favorited.

4. Prefer the keyboard? Open the arrangement page Tine created, named **Favorites**. A bullet that is exactly one `[[page link]]` is a page favorite; a `((uuid))` row is a block favorite; other bullets are labels. Editing, nesting, adding, or removing those bullets updates the sidebar after saving.

Right-click a block and choose **Favourite block** to add a `((uuid))` row to **Favorites**. Tine saves an `id::` on the source first if it needs one. The sidebar shows the block's content; clicking zooms into that block, and Shift-click opens it in the right sidebar. Block favorites stay in the ordinary Favorites page, with a derived star on references from that page; they never add `favorite::` properties or block entries to `config.edn :favorites`. Remove its row from Favorites to stop favoriting it.

What you should see: the richer tree follows page renames and lives in an ordinary graph page, while Logseq continues to read the same flat favorites membership. Tine does not create the arrangement page until you make a group or nest a row.

blocks.raw: ## Keep what matters close: Favorites

children.raw: 1. From any Ctrl+K search, press **Open search tab** in the footer. The whole search becomes its own tab with its own search box — nothing is written to your graph yet, and the tab comes back after a restart.

2. Refine it there: switch **Search / List / Table / Board** freely — that changes only how results are shown, never which blocks matched. Open **Filters / Advanced** for all words, any words, an exact phrase, excluded words or a regular expression, or **Edit as visual query** to edit the conditions one row at a time; **Explain query** describes what Tine understood.

3. A text search answers two questions at once, so the results arrive in two sections: **Pages** and **Blocks**, in that order, each with its own count and its own control — **Display pages** and **Display**. Set the pages as a table of their own properties and leave the blocks as a list if that is what you want. A section with nothing in it says so ("No matching pages." / "No matching blocks.") and keeps its control.

4. **Pages match** beside the Pages section decides which pages count as matches at all: **Names and aliases** (the default), **Block content** — a page counts when one of its own blocks matches — or **Names or content**. It changes page membership only; the Blocks section still lists the blocks that matched, whichever you pick.
5. Worth keeping? Type a name into **Name this search to save it as a page** and press **Save page**.

6. What you should see: the tab becomes an ordinary page in your graph holding one query block (with `tine.*` lines for the view and display choices). You can link to it, favorite it, and its results refresh themselves; an existing page with the same name or alias is never overwritten. The saved block shows one results list with a single **Display** control, so the two-section split stays in the search tab.

blocks.raw: ## Keep the search: make a search tab

children.raw: 1. Text search finds visible words. A page query asks a different question: "which blocks connect to [[Project/Roadmap]]?" — written as the page's name inside a query, like this live example:
{{query [[Project/Roadmap]]}}

2. What you should see in a copied Guide or the public demo: the Roadmap outline itself (a block always counts its own page, and a nested bullet counts whatever its parents mention), the bullets elsewhere in the Guide that link there — [[Welcome to Tine]] has one — and this numbered bullet, which links too. In this read-only Guide the same block runs against your own graph instead, so it lists your pages' mentions — often nothing yet; it comes alive after you copy the Guide into your graph.

blocks.raw: ## Try it: find every mention of one page

children.raw: To insert a query, type **/query** and choose **Query**. It opens the query sheet on its empty condition list; press **+ Add condition** to choose the first field.
1. At rest a query shows its title, result count and results. Click the title to rename it. Hover or focus reveals **⋯**; touch screens show the menu without hover.

2. Open **⋯ → Edit** for the inline builder: **Find blocks ▾ where …** and one row per condition. **+ Add condition** adds one. The real results remain below the editor as your live preview. An empty new query asks you to add a condition.

3. Both **+ Add condition** and a row's `field ▾` open the same list, and that list is your graph: the built-in fields first, then every property key you actually use, each with the type Tine has observed. Type to narrow it. A key the list does not already show is offered by name at the bottom — **Use "…" as a block property** and, on a block query, **Use "…" as a page property** — so a key the graph does not have yet, and a key it has only on pages, both stay writable.

4. Change **blocks** to **pages** and Tine re-reads the whole query before changing anything. If conditions stop applying — `task` means nothing for a page — it says how many, names them, and offers **Remove them**, **Keep anyway**, or **Cancel**. Kept conditions stay as red rows with their reason, so nothing disappears behind your back.

If **Ungroup** is absent, the group has a wrapper that cannot be removed without changing its meaning. For a **none of** group, choose **Remove none of** first; for a disabled group, switch the group on first. These are changes to which results match, so make them only when that is what you intend.

5. Group rows when a query needs a branch. Tick the boxes of two or more rows in the same list, press **Group selected ▾**, and choose **All of**, **Any of** or **None of**: they become one group where the topmost ticked row was, and the rows you did not tick stay exactly where they were. A single row's ⋮ offers **Group with row above** with the same three choices. Ticking only ever selects rows of ONE list, so grouping never quietly carries a condition out of the group it was written in; a condition changes group only when you drag it there (see 7). A group's ⋮ **Ungroup** puts its rows back exactly as they were. Very deeply nested queries fold into one `⟨advanced⟩` row: still saved, still run, and still something you can tick, move, disable and remove. Press that row and Tine opens the **query text** (**Edit as text** at the foot of the sheet) with your cursor in it, which is where the part the rows cannot draw is edited.

6. Turn a condition off instead of deleting it. The enabled switch at the end of a row — and the one on a group's header — keeps the condition in the query and stops it running, so a query can be narrowed and widened without losing the words you wrote. When the group above it is off, a row says **disabled by group**, because switching that one row on by itself would not bring it back.

7. Reorder with the ⋮⋮ handle by dragging; the row's ⋮ has **Move up** and **Move down** as well. Drop the handle onto another group to move the condition into it; a group left with one condition dissolves into the list around it.

8. That list of your graph's own keys is one read Tine makes when the sheet opens. While it is still reading, the list says **Reading this graph's properties…** and the built-in fields below it stay usable. If that read fails instead, the list says what failed and offers **Try again**.

Press **Done** (bottom right) or **Escape** to close the inline editor and leave the title, count and results. The block on disk is still an ordinary `{{query}}` bullet. **⋯ → View** chooses the presentation; **Copy results** keeps page/date titles and hierarchy in the shared export dialog; **Collapse all / Expand all** is one toggle that folds List result trees through their ordinary source properties. **Open in Search** opens the query in a Search tab, with its view and result kinds. **Edit as text** is Tine's reading of the query, written in the language below, rather than a copy of the block's Logseq bytes.

blocks.raw: ## Read a query, then edit it

children.raw: 1. Open **⋯ → Edit as text** for the **query text**. It is the same query the builder shows, written out and always editable. Type in it and Tine re-reads it as you go; press **Save query text** to make it the block's query.

2. The language is SQLite's expression syntax over a small fixed vocabulary. A query is `@block` or `@page` — which kind of row you are asking about — and then conditions joined with `and`, `or`, `not` and brackets:

3. The vocabulary, in full. On a block row: `content`, `task`, `priority`, `scheduled`, `deadline`. On a page row: `name`, `journal`, `namespace`. `[[Page name]]` and `#tag` are page references; `prop('key')` is a property; `page.name` reaches the block's own page. The comparisons are `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `like` (with `%` wildcards), `match` (full-text), `between … and …`, `in (…)`, and `is null` / `is not null`.

4. Three forms are Tine's own. `any(children, …)` and `every(prop('tags'), …)` ask about the things a row contains — a block's children, a page's blocks, a key's values. `off(…)`, or a line beginning `-- `, keeps a condition in the query without running it. And `tag('x')` and `page_tag('x')` spell out what `#x` means on each kind of row.

5. Outline conditions use `any`, `none`, or `every` over `parent` (direct parent), `ancestors` (all parents above), `children` (direct children), or `descendants` (all blocks below, at any depth). The condition inside binds to each related block; the result is the anchor block. The anchor itself and the owning page are excluded. With no related blocks, `any` is false and `none` and `every` are true.
For example, find an action mentioning a budget under a project whose branch contains an approved item:

`content match` accepts the same words, `OR`, exclusions, quoted phrases and `/regex/` as search. Combine conditions on ancestors and descendants to search both directions. These relations belong to TQL; ordinary quick-search syntax and the result layout stay as before.

What you should see: an unknown word is named, not swallowed. When the message comes with a place in the text, a **Show me** button beside it selects exactly that much of what you typed. A query with a word Tine could not read returns **no results** — its result area says "Tine didn't understand part of this query, so it returned no results" — rather than quietly running a shorter query.

blocks.raw: ## Query text (TQL)

children.raw: 1. A property key means more when Tine knows what its values ARE. Open a property in **Edit as visual query** and Tine names the type it has observed across your graph — `text`, `number`, `date`, `checkbox`, or `ref` (a page link) — and says `list of …` when the key normally holds several values at once.

2. Observation can be wrong, and an empty key has nothing to observe. Choose **declare type…** on the property and pick the type yourself; tick **list of** when the key is meant to hold several values. The declared type is then the one Tine uses.

3. A declaration is an ordinary page property, written as `tine.type:: number` on the page named after the key — and the name is the key's normalized form, so a property written `due date::` declares on the page `due-date`. Tine writes that line for you; if you type it yourself, use that spelling or nothing binds. Choose **remove declaration** to delete the line and go back to what Tine observes.

4. The type decides which comparisons you are offered: `is` and `is not` for a checkbox or a page link, `before`, `after` and `between` for a date, `<`, `≤`, `>`, `≥` for a number, `contains` and `starts with` for text. On a `list of …` key the equality operator reads `contains this value`, because the test is against the list.

What you should see: the property shows one type marked observed or declared and, once you declare one, a count of the blocks or pages that do not match it. That count is a to-do list, not an error: the query still runs.

blocks.raw: ## Property types

children.raw: 1. Some queries you can build have no `{{query}}` spelling at all: grouping, column totals, and typed comparisons like "cost > 100" are Tine's, not Logseq's. When you save one, Tine changes the block's macro name from `query` to `tine-query` and moves the view choices — view, sort, group, columns, column totals, sample — into `tine.*` properties on the same block.

2. Tine says so when it happens, in a notice under the query: **This query now uses Tine features Logseq can't read.** Take **Undo that change** to put the block back exactly the bytes it had, or **Keep it** to go on. Nothing else on the page is touched either way.

3. Nothing is lost in Logseq. The block stays ordinary Markdown and the `tine.*` lines stay ordinary properties; Logseq simply shows the bullet as the plain text it is instead of running it. Everything else on the page keeps working there.
4. **Don't show this again** stops the notice. That choice is kept on this device, never in the graph, so it does not follow you to another machine.

What you should see: the block still renders and refreshes in Tine as it did a moment ago; only its first line and its properties changed. Undo is the ordinary undo, so **Ctrl+Z** does the same thing as the button for as long as it is the newest change.

blocks.raw: ## When a query needs Tine features

children.raw: A hand-written advanced query stays editable as text. A `{{query {:query …}}}` or `#+BEGIN_QUERY` block runs only when Tine can read every clause of it; otherwise it is refused whole ("Advanced (datalog) query not run") and the notice names the clauses Tine could not run, rather than show a wider answer than you asked for.

Tine runs Logseq's query rules (`task`, `priority`, `property`, `page-ref`, `between` and the others) and the attribute patterns written on the block the query returns: its marker, priority, scheduled and deadline dates, and whether its page is a journal and which day, alone or narrowed by `contains?`, `=`, `not=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=`, and inside `not`. For example `[:find (pull ?b [*]) :where [?b :block/marker ?m] [(contains? #{"NOW" "DOING"} ?m)]]` lists what you are working on now.

A part Tine does not understand refuses the whole query: it never runs half of it, because a partial answer could both add and hide blocks. A `:result-transform` function (other than Logseq's default priority sort), authored rules or an unsupported input is such a part. Common page/tag string inputs and numeric or relative date windows run; [[Reference/Tine query model]] lists the supported shapes.

blocks.raw: ## Advanced queries

children.raw: The exact rules — ranking, search scope, saved-page behavior — are mapped in [[Reference/Pages, links, references, and search]]. For turning found or structured blocks into tables and boards, see [[Workflows/Structure repeated information]]; the wider shortcut map is [[Features/Tips & shortcuts]].

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Source beside draft, note beside plan: this tour builds a working layout step by step — park a page in the right sidebar, collect places in tabs, split the window for true side-by-side, give a page its own window, and save the arrangement as a workspace. Each part ends with what you should see. The shortcut map is [[Features/Tips & shortcuts]].

blocks.raw: # Keep context visible

children.raw: Scroll down a nested outline: ancestors that leave the screen stay pinned at the top, through the root. Click a pinned ancestor to scroll back to its block. This works in pages, journals, panes, and right-sidebar outlines.
Settings → **Appearance** → **Sticky parent bullets** turns this on or off on desktop and mobile. It starts on and is remembered on this device.

blocks.raw: ## Keep your place in a long outline

children.raw: While editing an embedded source block, run **Select embedding block** from the command palette (**Ctrl+Shift+P**). It leaves the editor and selects the block containing the `{{embed ...}}` macro. Use the ordinary move, indent, outdent, or edit shortcuts on that selection.

The command starts without a key: assign one in Settings → **Keyboard shortcuts** to leave an embed directly from the keyboard. It works for block and page embeds. **Move Block Up/Down** while still editing the embedded source keeps moving that source; the **Moved in <page>** notice still tells you where an unseen move went.

blocks.raw: ## Select the block containing an embed

children.raw: 1. On the page you're writing, **Shift-click** a link (or a bullet's dot) to open it in the right sidebar. It's a full editor, not a preview — you can write in either place.
2. Two more ways to park things: in **Ctrl+K**, press **Shift+Enter** on any page or block result; while editing, **Ctrl+Shift+O** sends the link at the caret across.

3. Crowded? Fold an item with its arrow and keep just its title in reach; its ✕ closes it. The item's ⋯ menu offers **Close others**, **Collapse others**, and, for a page, **Open as page** to move it into the main pane. The sidebar header's ⋯ menu offers **Collapse all**, **Expand all**, and **Close all**. Drag the sidebar's left edge to resize it — up to 70% of the window, always leaving the page beside it room to work. Folding or closing never strands half-typed text — Tine commits the active edit first.
4. Press **t r** to hide the whole sidebar and **t r** again to bring it back just as it was; its items are restored with your session.
What you should see: the source parked beside your page, both editable — and it stays parked while the main page navigates elsewhere.

blocks.raw: ## Park a source in the right sidebar

children.raw: 1. **Middle-click** a link, a search hit, or a bullet's dot to open it in a background tab — you never leave the page you're on. In **Ctrl+K**, **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** (or Ctrl/Cmd-click) does the same for the highlighted result and leaves the search open, so you can fan several out in a row.

2. Navigating to a page that's already open just focuses its tab instead of making a duplicate (Settings → **Editor** → **Advanced** → **Switch to an already-open tab when navigating** turns that off).

3. **Double-click** a tab to pin it. Pinned tabs gather at the left and hold their content: ordinary navigation from one opens a fresh tab instead, and closing a pinned tab asks first — an accidental **Ctrl+W** can't eat it.

4. Closed one too soon? **Ctrl+Shift+T** reopens the last closed tab with its history. **Ctrl+PageDown** and **Ctrl+PageUp** step to the next and previous tab. Tabs stretch to fill the strip and share it evenly as more open; a tab zoomed into a block is named for that block, so two tabs of one page stay apart. When titles stop fitting, the **Show all tabs** button at the strip's edge lists them in full — activate, pin, close, or reorder there.

5. The **Open tabs** list in the left sidebar appears once a second tab is open and shows the same tabs as a column you can organize. Drag a row up or down to reorder (the strip follows), drag it right, under another tab, to nest it there, and drag it left to move it back out; on a touch screen, hold a row still for a moment, then drag. A tab with nested tabs gets a triangle that collapses them in the sidebar list only. Right-click a nested row (on a touch screen, hold it still; or use the context-menu key) for **Move out of group**. Closing a tab never closes the tabs nested under it: they move up one level. Pinned tabs stay at the top and never nest. The groups are only for organizing what is open; they never change a page.
What you should see: the same tabs, pins and groups included, come back after a restart — and as session state kept in Tine's own app data, none of this ever adds a file to your graph.

blocks.raw: ## Gather places in tabs, and pin the ones you live in

children.raw: 1. Desktop only: **Ctrl/Cmd-click** any `[[link]]`, tag, or block reference to open it in another pane — with a single pane, Tine splits right for it. In **Ctrl+K**, **Alt+click** or **Alt+Enter** does the same for the highlighted result. The direct bindings: `Ctrl+Alt+\` splits right with a copy of the current tab, `Ctrl+Alt+Shift+\` splits down.
2. Each pane keeps its own tab strip and its own back/forward history — **Alt+Left** and **Alt+Right** step through it, even mid-edit.

3. Drag the seam between panes to resize them. Drag a tab anywhere onto another pane's tab bar to put it last there (or next to a tab to put it in that spot), onto a pane's body to append it, or onto a seam or pane edge to split that spot and drop the tab into the new pane — **Esc** cancels a drag mid-way. The command palette (**Ctrl+Shift+P**) also has **Toggle maximize active pane** (**Ctrl+Alt+M**) and commands to grow or shrink the active pane.

To split above a pane, drag just below its tab strip. All four edge drop zones grow with the pane; at a corner the nearest edge wins. The preview shows where the new pane will open. The centre appends the tab to the pane, and the tab strip keeps its reorder behavior.

4. PDF readers use the same tabs and panes. Opening a PDF link makes a companion pane while preserving the source page; you can then drag the PDF tab into any pane or quadrant. **Notes** opens the PDF's notes page in its structural companion pane, and that notes tab can be moved in exactly the same way.

5. From the keyboard, **Ctrl+1** … **Ctrl+9** focus panes in reading order, **Ctrl+Alt+←↑↓→** moves focus to the nearest pane in that direction, and **Ctrl+Alt+Shift+←↑↓→** moves the active tab there instead.

6. Prefer staged control? **Esc** climbs from editing to block selection into pane-select mode — a hint pill at the bottom tells you when it's on (the command palette's **Pane select mode** enters it directly). Arrows step between panes, seams, and window edges; **Enter** on a seam makes a mirror split; typing opens the new pane with the search box pre-filled. Another **Esc** backs out.
What you should see: two note panes that scroll, navigate, and keep tabs independently — source and draft side by side, never fighting over one cursor.

blocks.raw: ## Split the window for true side-by-side

children.raw: 1. Desktop only: right-click a page link or a page in the left sidebar and choose **Open in new window** — the page title's ⋯ menu has it too, and so does the command palette (**Ctrl+Shift+P**) as **Open current page in new window**. The page opens in a separate OS window you can move to another monitor.
2. The window is a full workspace of its own: its own tabs, splits, and back/forward history. Links, **Ctrl+K**, and search results you use there open there. It has no left or right sidebar.
3. Edits made in the window save exactly like edits in the main window, show up in the main window as you type, and **Ctrl+Z** undoes them from either place. Up to 8 windows can be open at once.

4. Close it with its own title-bar button whenever you like — text you just typed is kept. Quitting Tine closes every window; the ones that were open come back, with their tabs, the next time you start Tine. Switching to another graph closes them.
What you should see: the same page in two windows on two screens, edited in either, with every change in the one file on disk.

blocks.raw: ## Open a page in its own window

children.raw: 1. With the layout where you want it — splits, every pane's tabs and histories, both sidebars — click the workspace name at the top of the left sidebar and choose **+ New workspace**, or run **New workspace…** from the command palette (**Mod+Shift+P**); name it once.

2. Come back to it from the same switcher: hover the name for a quick-switch list, or click it for the full menu with **Rename** and **Delete**. Each graph keeps its own set, and the active one comes back after a restart.

What you should see: the saved pane layout, tabs and histories, sidebars, and Recent return together. Workspaces are device-local session state — saving, switching, or deleting one never writes to your graph.

blocks.raw: ## Save the arrangement as a workspace

children.raw: **t f** (focus mode) hides the sidebars and toolbar so the screen is just text — on desktop it also takes the window full screen. Hover the top edge to reach the toolbar again; layered **Esc** steps back out.
**t b** fades every block except the one you're editing. Settings → **Appearance** → **Dim in focus mode** turns that dimming on for you whenever focus mode is on.
**t w** drops the reading-width cap for a wide page; Settings → **Appearance** → **Advanced** lets you set your own **Standard page width** and **Wide page width**.

In a narrow window (below 640 px), the sidebars open as overlays; dismiss them with the shaded edge, Esc, or Android Back. Use **Open tabs** in the left sidebar to switch tabs when the tab strip is hidden. At 640 px or wider, the tab strip is available on every platform. A PDF and its Notes page use the same one-pane history on a narrow screen, so Back returns to the previous surface.

blocks.raw: ## Clear everything else away

children.raw: [[Features/Tips & shortcuts]] has the compact shortcut map, [[Start/Where things are]] is the plain map of the places used here, and [[Workflows/Find and revisit]] covers getting back to anything you parked.

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: The short path: drop a PDF onto a page, read it in a companion pane, and highlight as you go. Each highlight becomes an ordinary bullet you can write under, quote anywhere, and follow back to the exact spot — so a paper turns into linked, searchable notes without leaving Tine. The precise highlight rules live in [[Features/PDF annotation]].

blocks.raw: # Research a document

children.raw: To keep a PDF outside your graph, use a `file://` link. On desktop it opens in your operating system's default PDF viewer, without copying the file into assets or creating annotation files in your graph. Upload it as an asset when you want to annotate it in Tine.

1. Drag a PDF from your file manager onto any page and drop it on a block — or paste one you copied, or run the `/Upload an asset` slash command. Tine stores the file in your graph's `assets/` folder and inserts a link where you dropped it.

2. Click the inserted link. On desktop the document opens as a normal tab in a companion pane beside your notes; drag its tab into another pane or split to move it. On a phone it opens in the current one-pane history, and **Back** returns to the source page.

What you should see: the PDF in an ordinary pane, with a toolbar holding a page-number box, a find button (**Ctrl+F** searches inside the document), zoom controls, an **Area highlight** toggle, a **Notes** button, **Outline**, a ⋯ menu, and the close control at the far edge. In a narrow pane the Area highlight, Notes and Outline buttons move into the ⋯ menu.

blocks.raw: ## Bring the document in

children.raw: 1. Select a passage with the mouse and pick a color in the menu that appears — that's a highlight. Click an existing highlight to reopen its menu: recolor it, or remove it with ✕.

2. To clip a figure or table instead, toggle **Area highlight** in the toolbar (or hold **Shift** on Linux/Windows, **Command** on macOS) and drag a rectangle over the region, then choose its color. Dismiss the color menu and nothing is written.

3. Long document? **Outline** navigates its table of contents, the page-number box jumps straight to a page, and the ⋯ menu offers **Fit width**, **Fit height** and a **Light**, **Warm**, or **Dark** reader theme — remembered on this device, not written into your graph.
What you should see: colored marks on the document — and, behind each mark, a bullet on a notes page named after the PDF.

blocks.raw: ## Read and highlight

children.raw: 1. Press **Notes** in the reader toolbar. On desktop Tine opens the document's highlights page in a companion pane next to the PDF; move its tab if another pane is more useful. On a phone it opens in the same history, so **Back** returns to the PDF. The page name starts with `hls__`, like Logseq, and every highlight is a bullet marked with a colored dot.
2. Write under a highlight bullet: a summary, a question, your own structure. These are ordinary bullets on an ordinary graph page — edit, nest, tag, and search them like any others.
3. Click the colored dot on a highlight bullet (or the highlight itself back in the PDF) to jump between the two: each note goes straight back to its spot in the document.
What you should see: your notes and their source passages stay connected in both directions, and recoloring a highlight updates its dot on the notes page to match.

blocks.raw: ## Turn highlights into notes

children.raw: 1. Click the highlight and choose **Copy ref**, then paste into any bullet in your own notes. The pasted `((…))` renders as link-styled text quoting the highlighted passage, and clicking the quote opens the document at that page.

2. Keep source and words visible while you write: the PDF is a normal tab, so it can sit in any resizable pane or quadrant next to your notes page; **Shift-click** on any bullet's dot parks that note in the right sidebar. On a phone the reader instead fills the width of the screen and the sidebars open as overlays — the two-up layout is a wider-window pattern.
3. Choose **Linked references** on the highlight's menu to list every note that quotes it — the trail from one passage to everywhere you used it.
What you should see: your note cites the source live, not as a copied excerpt — touch nothing, and the quote still opens the PDF at the right page tomorrow.

blocks.raw: ## Quote a passage in your ordinary notes

children.raw: 1. From the notes page title's right-click menu: **Copy / export as…** offers Markdown and rendered copies, and **Export to PDF…** (desktop only) opens print options and then your OS print dialog — choose **Save as PDF**. The page always prints on a light background, whatever your theme.

2. Publishing on the web? Pages marked `public:: true` go into the static export: Settings → **Graph** → **Export HTML and read-only app…** asks for a folder outside your graph. To share just one reading list or project, press **Export…** on a query: you review the pages its results live on, and Tine writes a standalone site in `published-queries/<folder>/` inside the graph. A colliding folder offers Replace (with the previous export kept in recovery) or a separate export, and copied local assets travel with the folder. A query about blocks exports **whole pages**, not just the matched blocks, and the dialog asks you to confirm that. Nothing is uploaded.

Your annotations are stored Logseq-compatibly — the `hls__` page with your notes, an `.edn` sidecar and any clipped area images under `assets/` — so launch snapshots cover your notes, config, and PDF highlight sidecars (not the PDF or other media files), and another Logseq-compatible tool reads the same annotations.

blocks.raw: ## Share the result

children.raw: The exact highlight, merge, and storage rules are mapped in [[Features/PDF annotation]]. For quoting anything else with `((…))` and the reference panels, see [[Workflows/Find and revisit]]; for snapshots and backups, [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

blocks.raw: ## Where next

children.raw: Start with the bullets you already write. Add a few fields when they become useful, then choose a table or board to see the same blocks from a different angle.

blocks.raw: # Structure repeated information

children.raw:
Refresh the Guide examples

blocks.raw:
## A small project tracker
tine.view:: table
tine.fields:: status=enum:planned,active,done;owner=text;estimate=number

children.raw: 1. Make a parent bullet like the tracker above, then add ordinary child bullets for each item.
2. Right-click the parent and choose **Show children as → Table** (or type `/Table`). Use **+ Add column** to add fields such as Status, Owner, and Estimate; edit their values in the cells.
3. When progress matters more than rows, type `/Board` on that parent. Choose **Group by** and select Status to make one column per status.

4. What you should see: the same child bullets appear as editable table rows or status columns. Move a board card to change that block's grouping field; return to the outline and the change is there too.

blocks.raw: ## Turn child bullets into a view

children.raw: 1. Press **Ctrl+K**, then search for `Refresh Guide examples`. The friendly search surface finds that tracker block without needing a query expression.

2. Choose **Open search tab**. There, choose **Filters / Advanced**, then **Edit as visual query**. The query reads as one sentence — *Blocks where …* — over a sheet of conditions; use **+ Add condition** → **Property** to choose Owner and the value Avery.

3. Choose **Table** or **Board** in the view switcher (**Search**, **List**, **Table**, **Board**) above the results. The selection answers *which blocks* to show; the view answers *how* to show them, so you can change the presentation without remaking the selection.

4. Open **Display** beside the conditions to set the rest of the presentation in one place: the view, what the results are grouped by, the sort order, which columns show, what the footer summarizes, and a sample size that limits the rows. Sorts, columns, and summaries are ordered lists you can add to, reorder with the arrows, and remove from.
5. What you should see: a reusable selection of matching tracker blocks, first as search results and then as the table or board you chose.

blocks.raw: ## Find and reuse the same kind of block

children.raw: This board finds the matching tracker bullets above; it does not copy them. Inspect it here, in a copied Guide, or in the public demo, then change its view with the visual controls.

blocks.raw: ### Query-backed board of the same tracker

children.raw: The view-owning parent carries `tine.view:: table` or `tine.view:: board`; the optional `tine.fields::` line declares the columns and their types. The child bullets remain the source blocks with their ordinary properties.

The query-backed example stores `{{query (property owner Avery)}}` to choose its blocks, while its `tine.view:: board` and `tine.group-field:: prop:status` lines choose the presentation. A query groups by a field name — `prop:status` for the property named Status, or `state`, `priority`, `tags`, `page` — so the same word cannot mean two things on two different views. An older graph that says `tine.group-by:: status` keeps working and is rewritten the first time you change the grouping from Display. The visual builder and friendly search lead here without requiring you to type the query syntax.

blocks.raw: ## What is stored, only when you need to inspect it

children.raw: If Estimate needs a computed companion, add a formula from the table header. For the visual formula editor, its read-only results, and the raw-expression escape hatch, use [[Features/Formulas]]. For table, board, and query-view details, return to [[Features/Sheets]].

A labelled page link such as [read the welcome]([[Welcome to Tine]]) shows your words while opening the page. External `[label](https://…)` links are ordinary Markdown, bare URLs and emails autolink, and **Mod+L** inserts a link around the selection. `http`, `https` and `mailto` links open in your browser or mail app. A `file:` link — `[Test](file:///home/you/report.odt)`, or `[Test](file://D:\test.txt)` on Windows — opens that file or folder in whatever application your system uses for it, on desktop; a file that is no longer there is reported instead of doing nothing. A file path is read from the graph folder, from any page or journal: `[report](files/report.pdf)` opens `files/report.pdf` inside the graph, while `[report](../files/report.pdf)` opens a file in the sibling `files` folder outside the graph. Parent steps such as `../../` are preserved. Absolute paths such as `/home/you/report.pdf` and `D:\notes\report.pdf` also open through the same desktop file opener as `file:` links. These links look ordinary and show the resolved path on hover. Use `[spaced](<../files/my file.txt>)` for spaces. Links into the graph's assets folder keep Logseq's established graph asset route. Opening local files is available on desktop only, including for `file:` URLs; Android and iOS report the refusal. Tine does not rewrite links when you move files or graphs. A link to another app, such as `zotero://…`, `obsidian://…` or `shortcuts://…` on iOS, first asks whether to open it, showing the whole link, and then opens it in that app. `javascript:` and `data:` links never open.
