A **query block** is a live list of every block (or page) in your graph that matches a filter. Write it once with `{{query …}}`; Tine keeps the results current as you edit, and the file stays an ordinary Logseq query block. Where an answer can differ from Logseq's, [[Reference/Tine query model]] says how and why.

3. The sheet says what the query finds — **Find blocks ▾ where …** — and shows one row per condition: a handle to drag it (or move it with the arrow keys), a box to select it, the field, operator and value, a switch that turns it off without removing it, a ⋮ for the rest, and an × to remove it. **+ Add condition** adds one.
A `{{tine-query …}}` block holds this language directly and runs like any other query block.

To list the blocks that mention a day after today, use `{{tine-query any(direct_refs, day > today)}}`. It finds a block that links or tags a journal day, such as `[[Oct 22nd, 2026]]`, `#[[Oct 22nd, 2026]]` or `[[2026-10-22]]`, whether or not that day has a journal file yet. Only the block's own links count, not those of its parent, and a `SCHEDULED:` or `DEADLINE:` date is not a mention (use `scheduled` or `deadline` for those). Combine it like any condition, for example `task = 'TODO' and any(direct_refs, day between today and '+7d')`. Inside `any(direct_refs, …)` a link has `name`, `journal` (true for a journal day) and `day`. *Today* is your computer's local day when the query runs. Logseq ignores scheduled/deadline date windows in `{{query}}`, so Tine shows a cue and refuses to run those blocks as written. Click **Convert** to keep the same date-window meaning in `{{tine-query …}}`; the change can be undone.
Tine's query text can follow links between pages. These are page conditions (`@page`), and Logseq's `{{query}}` has no spelling for them, so a query that uses one is saved as `{{tine-query …}}`.

`any(links, …)` — pages that link to a page matching the condition; `any(linked_by, …)` — pages linked to by one. A link is exactly what the **Linked References** panel shows: `{{tine-query @page and any(links, name = 'Reading list')}}` lists the same pages as Reading list's panel. `every(…)` and `none(…)` work too: `{{tine-query @page and none(linked_by, true)}}` lists pages nothing links to.

`near(…, k)` — the pages matching the first condition plus every page within `k` link steps of them, both directions: `{{tine-query @page and near(name = 'Project', 1)}}` is Project, the pages it links to and the pages that link to it. Add `'out'` to follow links forward only, or `'in'` to follow them backwards only: `near(name = 'Paper', 3, 'out')`. `k` is a whole number; `0` means the matching pages alone.

The default, `'both'`, is the pages within `k` steps forward together with the pages within `k` steps backward. Each path keeps one direction, so it is **not** every page within `k` steps when you may switch direction along the way (what other graph tools call "both"): a page that merely links to the same page as Project is not near Project. Write two `near(…)` conditions joined with `or` to combine other shapes.

A page that is only linked to, with no file of its own, counts as a page here: `near(name = 'idea', 1, 'in')` lists the pages that link to it. Renaming a page also updates the names inside `near(…)` and `any(links, …)` of a share or export definition.
The simple query language is Logseq's. Combine filters with `(and …)`, `(or …)` and `(not …)`:

**⋯ → Copy results** opens the same **Copy / export as…** dialog as an outline selection, with Text, OPML and HTML options. Each result tree sits under its page title; journals use their date titles, and descendants keep their hierarchy. A descendant already inside a selected parent is copied once.

Beside a property condition, **declare type…** writes `tine.type:: number`, `date`, `checkbox`, `ref` or `text` on the page named for that property key. Select **list of** for multiple values, or remove the declaration. The badge distinguishes an observed type from a declared one and shows mismatches against a declaration.

`{{query {:query [:find (pull ?b [*]) :where …]}}}` and `#+BEGIN_QUERY` blocks run a supported subset of Logseq's datalog: task markers, priority, page references, properties, page, namespace, page tags, scheduled/deadline and journal date ranges.

**Share…** in a query's **⋯** menu (or its share icon) opens the share dialog with this query, reviews the pages it selects and exports them; the export is saved as a definition so it can be repeated. See [[Features/Share pages]].

Use **⋯ → Export…** on a query. Review the complete pages selected by the result, then choose an external folder. Tine creates a new named site there, with a read-only browser view and static HTML fallback. A block result publishes its whole owner page, so review those pages before continuing. The built-in Scheduled & Deadline section has no Export button.

**Share** opens from the share icon in the top bar (in a narrow window it is **Share this page** in the **···** menu), the share icon beside a page title, **Share…** in a page's **⋯** menu and right-click menu, and **Share…** (or the share icon) on a query block. It shares the page you are looking at; from a query block it starts from that query.
**Folder** exports a static site and read-only app into `published-queries/<folder>/` in your graph, the same export as a query's **Export…**. You name the folder on the next step.

After a successful export Tine saves the selection as a definition so you can repeat it. From **This page** or a query you built in the dialog, it adds a query block with `tine.export:: <folder>` to the **Exports** page, which Tine creates on first use (marked `tine.exports:: true` and `public:: false`, with a block listing every definition; if you already have a page called Exports it uses Exports 2). From a query block you did not change, it adds `tine.export:: <folder>` to that block. Open **Share…** on a definition again and it shows the same selection. Nothing is exported again until you choose Export.

**Settings → Sharing** lists the links made on this device with **Copy link**, **Check**, **Delete** and **Forget**. **Check** asks GitHub whether an upload whose result was uncertain went through. **Find shares on GitHub** lists Tine shares in your account that this device has no record of; you can delete them, but cannot recover their keys. **Pending in this graph** lists query blocks marked `tine.share:: pending/…` (an upload that was not confirmed); **Check** finishes the ones this device recorded, and **Remove marker** clears one that no device is still uploading.

2. Leave **This page** selected and choose **Folder**, then **Export to folder…** and name the folder. What you should see: a `published-queries/<folder>/` export and an **Exports** page with one definition.

Folder exports of a single query, including **Export…**, are described in [[Features/Queries]]. Exports of the whole graph, PDF and **Copy / export as…** are in [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].
The **+ Add row** label stays at the visible edge when a wide table scrolls sideways. **Copy / export…** can produce HTML from the same table content.

**Replying.** Hover or focus a thread and click its **Reply…** box at the bottom. **Enter** or **Reply** submits, **Shift+Enter** adds a line, and **Escape** or **Cancel** discards the draft. An abandoned empty reply creates no block and does not save the page. Selecting words inside a thread and choosing **Comment** or pressing **Ctrl/Cmd+R** adds a reply with a short quote inside that same thread.

**Paste as link** turns what you copied into a link without typing the syntax. Copy a URL or a block reference, select some words in a block you are editing, and run it: `see context` becomes `[context](https://…)` or `[context](((id)))`. With nothing selected the link is inserted bare. It ships without a key, so assign one under **Settings → Shortcuts** (the command palette lists it too, but opening the palette leaves the editor, so use the key). Ordinary paste over a selection is unchanged.

Use the **…** beside an ordinary page title for its complete actions menu: open the source file, copy/export, inspect properties, rename, carry tasks, or delete. It is the same menu as right-click and works from the keyboard and touch.

**Settings → Help & diagnostics** creates a privacy-safe diagnostic report of this run and the previous one to attach to a bug report: operation names, outcomes, timings, counts, platform and build, never page content, titles, file paths or queries. If Tine did not close cleanly last time, it says so when it starts. Review the report and choose **Copy report**, or on desktop **Save report…**; nothing is uploaded, and the recorder keeps at most 1 MiB in Tine's own app data, never in your graph. The same tab also offers **Rescan graph** and **Verify synchronized graph**.
**Export to PDF…** saves pending page edits before preparing the printout. If a page cannot be saved, Tine stops the export and shows an error so the PDF does not silently omit your changes.

**Page icons**: add a property like `tine.icon:: 📚` at the very top of a page (the ⌨️ on this page comes from Logseq's `icon::`, which Tine reads too). `tine.icon` stays visible in the page-properties block; Logseq's `icon`, `title` and `filters` stay hidden there. Use **Page properties…** to change them.

**Hidden metadata** follows Logseq: built-in lines such as `heading::`, `background-color::`, PDF highlight metadata and flashcard scheduling stay out of the text editor. Keys listed in `:block-hidden-properties` in `logseq/config.edn` also stay hidden in editors and rendered property lists. Editing or clearing the visible text keeps the original hidden property lines in the file, in Markdown and Org. Use **Properties…** to change or remove hidden values; heading and block colour also have their own block-menu controls. Ordinary `title`, `icon`, `filters`, `logseq.color` and `logseq.table.*` lines remain visible while editing.

**Page and block properties** are editable from a form, not only as raw `key:: value` lines: use **Page properties…** in the page menu (or `/page properties` while editing), or right-click a block for **Properties…**. The form lists every property the page or block really has; a page's form always offers Aliases, Tags, Display title, Icon and Public. Any other property can be changed or removed, and **Add a property** takes any key you like — it does not have to be plain ASCII. `id::`, `collapsed::` and `tine.` keys keep their own surfaces. Markdown writes `key:: value`, an Org page a `#+key: value` directive, and an Org block its `:PROPERTIES:` drawer. A read-only page offers no property editing at all.

When you open that graph in the app, `serve` finishes admitted work, stops and hands over ownership. The app shows **Finishing the command line's work on this graph…** while it waits. If the handover has not finished after 60 seconds, opening fails and names `tine serve GRAPH --stop`; the app does not take ownership on a timeout. Read commands retry through a busy handover for up to 30 seconds.

**If Tine crashes or quits while a page cannot be saved,** that page's unsaved text is kept in Tine's app data (never in your graph). On the next start Tine puts it back on the page and saves it, and a message names those pages: “Recovered unsaved edits … — Tine is saving them”. If the file changed on disk in the meantime, the page shows the changed-on-disk banner instead (see [[Reference/Troubleshooting and recovery]]), so nothing is written over unseen. Text that saved normally is not kept there. Crash-recovery copies from an older Tine are left untouched as a backup; a message names their file once.

Each snapshot is one ordinary `.zip` file (snapshots from an older Tine are folders; see below). You can open it with your system's archive tool, without Tine: inside, every file sits at its path in your graph (`pages/…`, `journals/…`, `logseq/config.edn`, asset sidecars under `assets/`), next to `tine-backup.json`, the list Tine checks the zip against. Snapshot names start with the date and time they were taken, in UTC. To get back a single page by hand, copy it out of the zip into your graph; Tine picks it up like any external change.

Settings → **Graph** → **Export HTML and read-only app…** exports your `public:: true` pages as a standalone site. Give the export a name and choose a destination folder outside the graph; tick **Include every page not marked public:: false** to export pages that carry no `public::` property as well. A page marked `public:: false` is never exported, not even with that box ticked or with `:publishing/all-pages-public? true` in `config.edn`, and its blocks never appear in another page's embeds, queries or references. A graph with no `public:: true` page exports 0 pages, and the result line says that only `public:: true` pages are exported. Nothing is uploaded, and your graph is not touched.

**Export…** in a query's header exports the pages its results live on as a standalone site. Pages marked `public:: false` and the exports page stay out even when the query matches them; the review lists what was left out and says when the export includes the page the query is written on. Readers see the pages, not the query itself, unless you tick **Include the query text**. Review the page list first; Tine writes the export to `published-queries/<folder>/` inside your graph. If that folder exists, choose **Replace** (the previous export is kept in recovery and its path is reported) or **Create a separate export**. A query about blocks exports **whole pages**, not just the matched blocks, and the dialog asks you to confirm that.

A query export carries referenced local assets in its own `assets/` folder, so you can move or share the whole export folder. Missing assets are reported as warnings. Settings → **Graph** → **Query export size limit** sets the copied-asset budget for this device (default **1 GiB**). An export that exceeds it stops before replacing any previous export, with **Adjust limit in Settings…** to raise it.

Sheets on an exported page (tables, boards and grids) come out as the same tables, boards and grids you see in the app, including formula columns, filters and aggregate footers: Tine computes them with the app's own sheet code before it writes the export, in **Export HTML and read-only app…**, a query's **Export…** and **Export to PDF…** alike. The command-line export (`tine export static` or `tine export live`) has no app to compute them, so it writes a sheet as the plain outline of its rows. A sheet that cannot be computed, or that changed while the export was being prepared, is written the same way with a visible note, and the export still succeeds. A table or board that shows a query's results is written the same way — the query's own columns and its rows on the page they came from — when the block holds just that one query; a result on a page the export does not publish is left out of the table (and of its counts and totals), and if the results changed while the export was being prepared the block is written as the query's usual result list instead. A query table's exported totals summarize only the rows it exports, so they can differ from the live footer's totals over the query's complete sample.

Right-click a page title → **Export to PDF…** prints one page on a light background. It is offered on desktop only: printing is unavailable inside a mobile WebView, so Android and iOS do not show it. **Export HTML and read-only app…** works on every platform.

To find HTML export quickly, open the command palette and run **Export graph as HTML and read-only app…**; it opens the same Graph settings export control. The folder picker starts at your last successful export destination on this device. The result shows the exported site's path; on desktop, **Show in folder** reveals it in the file manager. Mobile keeps its existing folder picker behaviour and does not offer the desktop reveal action.

**Copy / export as…** on a block or page offers **Plain text** (without formatting markers) or **Markdown** / **Org** (with formatting preserved), then Text / OPML / HTML destinations with cleanup and depth controls. Markdown, Org, HTML and OPML resolve block references and expand page and block embeds, without adding source captions. Embedded outlines keep their children; expansion stops after five nested embeds. Internal properties such as `id::` are hidden. Text exports keep user properties as `key:: value` unless **Remove properties** is selected; page properties are omitted.

Settings → **Journals** → **New-journal template** inserts a template into each new day (`:default-templates {:journals …}` in `config.edn`); “(none)” means blank days, the default. Make a template from a block's right-click menu (**Make a template…**). A page can be a template too: put `template:: Name` among the page's own property lines at its top (the lines before the first bullet), and `/Name` inserts those property lines (without `template::`) as one block, as in Logseq.

**Today's sections page.** To choose what shows under today's journal without editing `config.edn`, hover today's journal and click **Customize today's sections…**. Tine creates a page named *Journal sections* (marked `tine.journal-sections:: true`) holding your current sections: each `:default-queries` entry as a `#+BEGIN_QUERY` block, then the Scheduled & Deadline agenda as a query block. The generated page does not include Upcoming. Today's journal shows query blocks and the Upcoming macro in outline order, including nested blocks; reorder, edit, delete or add them like on any page, and the change shows on today's journal at once. Supported sections are `{{query …}}`, `{{tine-query …}}`, `#+BEGIN_QUERY` blocks, the agenda query seeded by Customize, and `{{upcoming}}`. Other text on the page is just notes. The page can be renamed; the marker is what counts. Delete the page, or set the marker to `false`, to go back to `config.edn`, with Upcoming hidden. Logseq ignores the page and keeps using `:default-queries`, and Tine never writes to `config.edn` for this. While the page exists, the Agenda window setting no longer applies: edit the agenda query on the page instead. The small header on this page opens this Guide in the right sidebar. On ordinary pages, `{{upcoming}}` remains an unknown macro.

To set an icon without knowing the property syntax, open **Page actions** (the ⋯ beside the title), then **Set page icon…** below **Page properties…**. Enter an emoji or short text such as `AB`, then press Enter or **Save icon**. On Windows, Win + . opens the native emoji picker; on macOS, use Control + Command + Space. **Remove page icon** clears it. Icons in the sidebar lists follow edits immediately, including external file changes. Markdown stores `tine.icon::`; Org stores `#+tine.icon:` through the same page-property editor. A page that only has `icon::` is edited in place, and **Remove page icon** clears both properties.

A labelled page link such as [read the welcome]([[Welcome to Tine]]) shows your words while opening the page. External `[label](https://…)` links are ordinary Markdown, bare URLs and emails autolink, and **Mod+L** inserts a link around the selection. `http`, `https` and `mailto` links open in your browser or mail app. A `file:` link — `[Test](file:///home/you/report.odt)`, or `[Test](file://D:\test.txt)` on Windows — opens that file or folder in whatever application your system uses for it, on desktop; a file that is no longer there is reported instead of doing nothing. A file path is read from the graph folder, from any page or journal: `[report](files/report.pdf)` opens `files/report.pdf` inside the graph, while `[report](../files/report.pdf)` opens a file in the sibling `files` folder outside the graph. Parent steps such as `../../` are preserved. Absolute paths such as `/home/you/report.pdf` and `D:\notes\report.pdf` also open through the same desktop file opener as `file:` links. These links look ordinary and show the resolved path on hover. Use `[spaced](<../files/my file.txt>)` for spaces. Links into the graph's assets folder keep Logseq's established graph asset route. Opening local files is available on desktop only, including for `file:` URLs; Android and iOS report the refusal. Tine does not rewrite links when you move files or graphs. A link to another app, such as `zotero://…`, `obsidian://…` or `shortcuts://…` on iOS, first asks whether to open it, showing the whole link, and then opens it in that app. `javascript:` and `data:` links never open.

Properties are the `key:: value` lines at the top of a page and under a block's first line, and every one of them is editable from a form — not only by typing raw lines. Click **Page actions** beside a page's title (or right-click the title) and choose **Page properties…**, or type `/page properties` while editing; right-click a block for **Properties…**. The form lists the properties that page or block really has. Page properties always stay at the top of their page: moving or dragging a block above them, or pressing Tab on the block right under them, does nothing and shows a short notice saying so.

Hover a page link or block reference for a preview of its blocks. The preview opens after a one-second pause and closes a moment after the pointer leaves, as in Logseq. It stops at 600 pixels or half the window, whichever is taller (never more than the window), and scrolls inside, and shows code blocks, callouts, quotes and folds the way the page does: a block the page keeps folded shows its closed bullet. Its arrow folds or unfolds the source block, saving the same `collapsed::` property as the page; the preview and an open page stay in step, and Undo restores both. If the source cannot be written or has no source block, the fold stays local to the preview. An alias shows its source page's title and page properties. Click the title to open that page in a new tab, a block bullet to open that block in a new tab, or **Open source** to open the preview's source. These actions switch to the new tab. The preview stays open while its **… → Page actions** menu is open. The blocks in a preview are the page's own blocks, as in Logseq: click a block's text to edit it right there, and the change is saved to its page. While you edit, the preview stays open even when the pointer leaves it or the page scrolls; the first **Esc** ends the edit and the next one closes the preview. Inside a preview a query shows as its text and an embed is read-only; open the source to use them. A block reference's preview also offers **Edit link** and **Remove** for that one reference, as described below.

**Ctrl+K**, the quick switcher, searches page titles plus the visible text of blocks. Sections are Pages, Create, Commands, Blocks and — inside a page — Current page; with an empty query it lists recent pages. **Enter** opens the highlighted result; **Shift+Enter** opens it in the right sidebar; **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** opens it in a background tab and keeps the switcher open; **Alt+Enter** opens it in another pane; middle-click opens a background tab. **Load more results…** appears when more are available.

Search scans your loaded graph text directly, so results are always current with your own edits; while it works the switcher says **Searching…**, an empty answer says **No matched results**, and **More matches exist — narrow your query to see them.** means the list was cut short.

**Open search tab** in the switcher footer turns the current search into a graph-scoped search tab titled "Search: …" with its own search box. The tab survives restarts and writes nothing to your graph until you name it. Clicking a result opens a new tab and keeps Search unchanged; if you would rather a plain click or **Enter** open the result in the Search tab itself, with **Back** returning to the results, choose **This tab** in **Settings → Editor → Advanced → Search results open in** (**New tab** is the default, saved on this device). Middle-click or Ctrl/Cmd-click opens a background tab; Shift-click opens the right sidebar and Alt-click opens another pane. Page results offer the same right-click menu as the switcher.
A query that asks about pages rather than blocks — `(page-property …)`, `(page-tags …)`, `(namespace …)` — lists the pages themselves.

**Long-press a page reference or tag to preview its page** without navigating away. Choose the **…** button in the preview header for **Page actions**, the same menu offered by a desktop right-click. Tap outside the preview to dismiss it; a quick tap still follows the link. Other links keep their long-press context menu, and holding ordinary text keeps the system's text selection and selection toolbar.

Shared items follow Logseq's mobile rules for each platform. On Android a link becomes a titled link, YouTube and similar video links become `{{video …}}`, posts on X or Twitter become `{{twitter …}}`, and text highlighted in a browser goes before its link. On iOS the shared text is kept as it is and the link follows it unchanged, as Logseq's iOS share does. Images follow as asset links, one per line.

The same destinations open from `tine://today`, `tine://capture`, `tine://search?q=…` and `tine://page/<name>` (a page of the open graph). Each one only opens something in Tine and never writes to your graph.

Tine reads Logseq's query syntax — `{{query …}}` blocks and the common advanced (datalog) queries — but runs them on its own engine, not on a datalog database. This page lists every place where the answer can differ from Logseq's, and why. How to write and display queries is on [[Features/Queries]].
**`(sort-by …)` knows built-in fields**: priority, page, scheduled and deadline as well as any property. Logseq sorts only by a property of that name.

**Tine-only features** (scheduled and deadline ranges, grouping, totals, typed comparisons, inline-tag and parent, child or descendant conditions, a bare has-a-scheduled-date or has-a-deadline check, `search`, `content-regex`) have no equivalent `{{query}}` spelling. Saving one turns the block into `{{tine-query …}}`, says so, and offers **Undo that change**. For example, `{{tine-query @block scheduled between today and '+7d'}}` checks a scheduled date; OG Logseq drops the condition in `(between scheduled …)` or `(between deadline …)`.

Tine 0.6 differs from this page where it has known bugs, fixed in Beta: it sorts ascending by default; `(sample N)` sorts first; a query of only directives returns everything; `(namespace x)` matches every depth; `(all-page-tags)` returns the tagged pages; `not` with several operands, `(priority [A])`, `(between created-at …)` and page-header properties misbehave; journal groups run oldest first; an advanced query with an unknown clause runs the clauses it understands; query text ignores case and accents; every property value is split on commas; Logseq's table settings are ignored.

2. Review the report, then choose **Copy report** (or **Save report…** on desktop). Nothing is uploaded automatically. The recorder excludes graph content, paths, page titles, queries, URLs, credentials, and the opt-in detailed debug log.
2. What you should see: the button reads **Rescanning…** while it works, then **Last rescan finished at** followed by the time. Create a diagnostic report afterwards to see how long that rescan took.
2. On one device choose **Copy graph report** (or **Save graph report…** on desktop) and paste it into the box **Report from the other device** on the other, then choose **Compare reports**.

2. Later, use the graph-name menu at the top of the left sidebar → **Open graph…**, or Settings (**t s**) → **Graph** → **Open another graph…**. Graphs you have opened appear in the same sidebar menu for one-click switching.

Use **Up/Down** to choose a graph, **Home/End** to reach the first or last, and **Enter** to open it in this window. On desktop, **Shift+Enter** opens it in a new window. **Tab** reaches each graph's actions, including **Remove from this list**, which leaves its files untouched, plus **Open graph…** and **New graph…**.
Choose **Create a new graph** on Welcome, or **New graph…** in the sidebar graph menu. Choose its parent folder on desktop or iOS; Android uses its default graph location.

On Windows, use `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\…` for a graph in WSL: Windows access through a distro package's `LocalState\rootfs` can corrupt Linux files, so Tine refuses new graphs there and warns when opening an existing one.

At the very top sits the workspace switcher — saved window layouts, covered in [[Workflows/Keep context visible]]. Just under it, the graph-name menu switches between the graphs Tine knows, with **Open graph…** and **New graph…** beside them — on desktop, Shift-click a graph row to open it in a second window instead of switching this one. Right-click a row for the same thing as a menu item — **Open in a new window** — along with **Open here**, **Show in folder**, **Copy path**, and **Remove from this list**. The row for the graph you already have open shows the two open actions greyed out, so the menu keeps its shape wherever you click.

1. With the caret anywhere in a bullet, press **Ctrl+Enter** (Cmd on Mac). The bullet becomes `TODO …`; press again for `DOING`, again for `DONE`, once more to drop the marker. (Under the NOW / LATER workflow — the default — the cycle is LATER → NOW → DONE.)
2. Look for a `var(--tine-…)` or `var(--ls-…)` in the rule that draws what you want to change. Setting that variable in `custom.css` is the stable way to change it.

4. Developing or sideloading instead? **Install a local package** (under **Browse**, button **Choose package…**) takes a `manifest.json` and its `.wasm` file together — with the same installed-disabled rule.

What you should see: exactly the contribution the plugin declared — a command-palette entry, a slash command, or a decoration — and nothing else. If the package does not support your device, its button reads **Unavailable on …** instead of Install.

A plugin that declares settings gets a **Settings** section on its details page (**Settings…** beside it in the **Installed** list), but Tine draws the controls — toggles, dropdowns, numbers, text — from the plugin's declared schema. Values are validated scalars, **stored on this device only** and never written into your graph. A changed key offers **Reset**; **Reset all settings** restores the schema defaults.
**Uninstall…** removes only that package version from this device. Tine asks first and states the boundary: it removes the plugin from this device and does not change your graph or notes.

Themes live separately under Settings → **Appearance**. **Style** controls typography, journal headings, and other Tine-owned presentation styles; **Color scheme** selects Default, Nord, Solarized, Gruvbox, Soft, or the colors from an installed package. Style and colors are independent, so you can keep one package's style while using another palette. Declarative packages install from the **Theme packages** list or a local `theme.json` file (**Choose theme.json…**) and contain no scripts, selectors, imports, font files, or remote assets. The choices stay on this device, and no theme ever reads or writes your graph.

2. Too many hits? Narrow with the **Search syntax** forms listed in the switcher footer: `-draft` excludes a word, `OR` offers alternatives, quotes pin an exact phrase, `/…/` is a case-sensitive regular expression.

The `((` picker says **Searching blocks…** while reading, offers **Retry** if the read fails, and says **No matched blocks** only after a successful empty search. Retry keeps your text; **Escape** closes the picker.

2. Open **⋯ → Edit** for the inline builder: **Find blocks ▾ where …** and one row per condition. **+ Add condition** adds one. The real results remain below the editor as your live preview. An empty new query asks you to add a condition.

3. Both **+ Add condition** and a row's `field ▾` open the same list, and that list is your graph: the built-in fields first, then every property key you actually use, each with the type Tine has observed. Type to narrow it. A key the list does not already show is offered by name at the bottom — **Use "…" as a block property** and, on a block query, **Use "…" as a page property** — so a key the graph does not have yet, and a key it has only on pages, both stay writable.

8. That list of your graph's own keys is one read Tine makes when the sheet opens. While it is still reading, the list says **Reading this graph's properties…** and the built-in fields below it stay usable. If that read fails instead, the list says what failed and offers **Try again**.

3. The vocabulary, in full. On a block row: `content`, `task`, `priority`, `scheduled`, `deadline`. On a page row: `name`, `journal`, `namespace`. `[[Page name]]` and `#tag` are page references; `prop('key')` is a property; `page.name` reaches the block's own page. The comparisons are `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `like` (with `%` wildcards), `match` (full-text), `between … and …`, `in (…)`, and `is null` / `is not null`.

4. Three forms are Tine's own. `any(children, …)` and `every(prop('tags'), …)` ask about the things a row contains — a block's children, a page's blocks, a key's values. `off(…)`, or a line beginning `-- `, keeps a condition in the query without running it. And `tag('x')` and `page_tag('x')` spell out what `#x` means on each kind of row.

1. A property key means more when Tine knows what its values ARE. Open a property in **Edit as visual query** and Tine names the type it has observed across your graph — `text`, `number`, `date`, `checkbox`, or `ref` (a page link) — and says `list of …` when the key normally holds several values at once.

2. Observation can be wrong, and an empty key has nothing to observe. Choose **declare type…** on the property and pick the type yourself; tick **list of** when the key is meant to hold several values. The declared type is then the one Tine uses.

4. The type decides which comparisons you are offered: `is` and `is not` for a checkbox or a page link, `before`, `after` and `between` for a date, `<`, `≤`, `>`, `≥` for a number, `contains` and `starts with` for text. On a `list of …` key the equality operator reads `contains this value`, because the test is against the list.

A hand-written advanced query stays editable as text. A `{{query {:query …}}}` or `#+BEGIN_QUERY` block runs only when Tine can read every clause of it; otherwise it is refused whole ("Advanced (datalog) query not run") and the notice names the clauses Tine could not run, rather than show a wider answer than you asked for.

5. From the keyboard, **Ctrl+1** … **Ctrl+9** focus panes in reading order, **Ctrl+Alt+←↑↓→** moves focus to the nearest pane in that direction, and **Ctrl+Alt+Shift+←↑↓→** moves the active tab there instead.

1. With the layout where you want it — splits, every pane's tabs and histories, both sidebars — click the workspace name at the top of the left sidebar and choose **+ New workspace**, or run **New workspace…** from the command palette (**Mod+Shift+P**); name it once.

1. Click the highlight and choose **Copy ref**, then paste into any bullet in your own notes. The pasted `((…))` renders as link-styled text quoting the highlighted passage, and clicking the quote opens the document at that page.

1. From the notes page title's right-click menu: **Copy / export as…** offers Markdown and rendered copies, and **Export to PDF…** (desktop only) opens print options and then your OS print dialog — choose **Save as PDF**. The page always prints on a light background, whatever your theme.

2. Publishing on the web? Pages marked `public:: true` go into the static export: Settings → **Graph** → **Export HTML and read-only app…** asks for a folder outside your graph. To share just one reading list or project, press **Export…** on a query: you review the pages its results live on, and Tine writes a standalone site in `published-queries/<folder>/` inside the graph. A colliding folder offers Replace (with the previous export kept in recovery) or a separate export, and copied local assets travel with the folder. A query about blocks exports **whole pages**, not just the matched blocks, and the dialog asks you to confirm that. Nothing is uploaded.

The exact highlight, merge, and storage rules are mapped in [[Features/PDF annotation]]. For quoting anything else with `((…))` and the reference panels, see [[Workflows/Find and revisit]]; for snapshots and backups, [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

2. Choose **Open search tab**. There, choose **Filters / Advanced**, then **Edit as visual query**. The query reads as one sentence — *Blocks where …* — over a sheet of conditions; use **+ Add condition** → **Property** to choose Owner and the value Avery.

blocks.raw: 2. **Right-click a table column header** — or right-click the table body / open its **⋮** menu — and choose **Add formula…**. Give it a short lowercase name like `plan`.
4. To change it later, right-click the formula column and choose **Edit formula…**.

A **query block** is a live list of every block (or page) in your graph that matches a filter. Write it once with `{{query …}}`; Tine keeps the results current as you edit, and the file stays an ordinary Logseq query block. Where an answer can differ from Logseq's, [[Reference/Tine query model]] says how and why.

3. The sheet says what the query finds — **Find blocks ▾ where …** — and shows one row per condition: a handle to drag it (or move it with the arrow keys), a box to select it, the field, operator and value, a switch that turns it off without removing it, a ⋮ for the rest, and an × to remove it. **+ Add condition** adds one.
A `{{tine-query …}}` block holds this language directly and runs like any other query block.

To list the blocks that mention a day after today, use `{{tine-query any(direct_refs, day > today)}}`. It finds a block that links or tags a journal day, such as `[[Oct 22nd, 2026]]`, `#[[Oct 22nd, 2026]]` or `[[2026-10-22]]`, whether or not that day has a journal file yet. Only the block's own links count, not those of its parent, and a `SCHEDULED:` or `DEADLINE:` date is not a mention (use `scheduled` or `deadline` for those). Combine it like any condition, for example `task = 'TODO' and any(direct_refs, day between today and '+7d')`. Inside `any(direct_refs, …)` a link has `name`, `journal` (true for a journal day) and `day`. *Today* is your computer's local day when the query runs. Logseq ignores scheduled/deadline date windows in `{{query}}`, so Tine shows a cue and refuses to run those blocks as written. Click **Convert** to keep the same date-window meaning in `{{tine-query …}}`; the change can be undone.
Tine's query text can follow links between pages. These are page conditions (`@page`), and Logseq's `{{query}}` has no spelling for them, so a query that uses one is saved as `{{tine-query …}}`.

`any(links, …)` — pages that link to a page matching the condition; `any(linked_by, …)` — pages linked to by one. A link is exactly what the **Linked References** panel shows: `{{tine-query @page and any(links, name = 'Reading list')}}` lists the same pages as Reading list's panel. `every(…)` and `none(…)` work too: `{{tine-query @page and none(linked_by, true)}}` lists pages nothing links to.

`near(…, k)` — the pages matching the first condition plus every page within `k` link steps of them, both directions: `{{tine-query @page and near(name = 'Project', 1)}}` is Project, the pages it links to and the pages that link to it. Add `'out'` to follow links forward only, or `'in'` to follow them backwards only: `near(name = 'Paper', 3, 'out')`. `k` is a whole number; `0` means the matching pages alone.

The default, `'both'`, is the pages within `k` steps forward together with the pages within `k` steps backward. Each path keeps one direction, so it is **not** every page within `k` steps when you may switch direction along the way (what other graph tools call "both"): a page that merely links to the same page as Project is not near Project. Write two `near(…)` conditions joined with `or` to combine other shapes.

A page that is only linked to, with no file of its own, counts as a page here: `near(name = 'idea', 1, 'in')` lists the pages that link to it. Renaming a page also updates the names inside `near(…)` and `any(links, …)` of a share or export definition.
The simple query language is Logseq's. Combine filters with `(and …)`, `(or …)` and `(not …)`:

**⋯ → Copy results** opens the same **Copy / export as…** dialog as an outline selection, with Text, OPML and HTML options. Each result tree sits under its page title; journals use their date titles, and descendants keep their hierarchy. A descendant already inside a selected parent is copied once.

Beside a property condition, **declare type…** writes `tine.type:: number`, `date`, `checkbox`, `ref` or `text` on the page named for that property key. Select **list of** for multiple values, or remove the declaration. The badge distinguishes an observed type from a declared one and shows mismatches against a declaration.

`{{query {:query [:find (pull ?b [*]) :where …]}}}` and `#+BEGIN_QUERY` blocks run a supported subset of Logseq's datalog: task markers, priority, page references, properties, page, namespace, page tags, scheduled/deadline and journal date ranges.

**Share…** in a query's **⋯** menu (or its share icon) opens the share dialog with this query, reviews the pages it selects and exports them; the export is saved as a definition so it can be repeated. See [[Features/Share pages]].

Use **⋯ → Export…** on a query. Review the complete pages selected by the result, then choose an external folder. Tine creates a new named site there, with a read-only browser view and static HTML fallback. A block result publishes its whole owner page, so review those pages before continuing. The built-in Scheduled & Deadline section has no Export button.

**Share** opens from the share icon in the top bar (in a narrow window it is **Share this page** in the **···** menu), the share icon beside a page title, **Share…** in a page's **⋯** menu and right-click menu, and **Share…** (or the share icon) on a query block. It shares the page you are looking at; from a query block it starts from that query.
**Folder** exports a static site and read-only app into `published-queries/<folder>/` in your graph, the same export as a query's **Export…**. You name the folder on the next step.

After a successful export Tine saves the selection as a definition so you can repeat it. From **This page** or a query you built in the dialog, it adds a query block with `tine.export:: <folder>` to the **Exports** page, which Tine creates on first use (marked `tine.exports:: true` and `public:: false`, with a block listing every definition; if you already have a page called Exports it uses Exports 2). From a query block you did not change, it adds `tine.export:: <folder>` to that block. Open **Share…** on a definition again and it shows the same selection. Nothing is exported again until you choose Export.

**Settings → Sharing** lists the links made on this device with **Copy link**, **Check**, **Delete** and **Forget**. **Check** asks GitHub whether an upload whose result was uncertain went through. **Find shares on GitHub** lists Tine shares in your account that this device has no record of; you can delete them, but cannot recover their keys. **Pending in this graph** lists query blocks marked `tine.share:: pending/…` (an upload that was not confirmed); **Check** finishes the ones this device recorded, and **Remove marker** clears one that no device is still uploading.

2. Leave **This page** selected and choose **Folder**, then **Export to folder…** and name the folder. What you should see: a `published-queries/<folder>/` export and an **Exports** page with one definition.

Folder exports of a single query, including **Export…**, are described in [[Features/Queries]]. Exports of the whole graph, PDF and **Copy / export as…** are in [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].
The **+ Add row** label stays at the visible edge when a wide table scrolls sideways. **Copy / export…** can produce HTML from the same table content.

**Replying.** Hover or focus a thread and click its **Reply…** box at the bottom. **Enter** or **Reply** submits, **Shift+Enter** adds a line, and **Escape** or **Cancel** discards the draft. An abandoned empty reply creates no block and does not save the page. Selecting words inside a thread and choosing **Comment** or pressing **Ctrl/Cmd+R** adds a reply with a short quote inside that same thread.

**Paste as link** turns what you copied into a link without typing the syntax. Copy a URL or a block reference, select some words in a block you are editing, and run it: `see context` becomes `[context](https://…)` or `[context](((id)))`. With nothing selected the link is inserted bare. It ships without a key, so assign one under **Settings → Shortcuts** (the command palette lists it too, but opening the palette leaves the editor, so use the key). Ordinary paste over a selection is unchanged.

Use the **…** beside an ordinary page title for its complete actions menu: open the source file, copy/export, inspect properties, rename, carry tasks, or delete. It is the same menu as right-click and works from the keyboard and touch.

**Settings → Help & diagnostics** creates a privacy-safe diagnostic report of this run and the previous one to attach to a bug report: operation names, outcomes, timings, counts, platform and build, never page content, titles, file paths or queries. If Tine did not close cleanly last time, it says so when it starts. Review the report and choose **Copy report**, or on desktop **Save report…**; nothing is uploaded, and the recorder keeps at most 1 MiB in Tine's own app data, never in your graph. The same tab also offers **Rescan graph** and **Verify synchronized graph**.
**Export to PDF…** saves pending page edits before preparing the printout. If a page cannot be saved, Tine stops the export and shows an error so the PDF does not silently omit your changes.

**Page icons**: add a property like `tine.icon:: 📚` at the very top of a page (the ⌨️ on this page comes from Logseq's `icon::`, which Tine reads too). `tine.icon` stays visible in the page-properties block; Logseq's `icon`, `title` and `filters` stay hidden there. Use **Page properties…** to change them.

**Hidden metadata** follows Logseq: built-in lines such as `heading::`, `background-color::`, PDF highlight metadata and flashcard scheduling stay out of the text editor. Keys listed in `:block-hidden-properties` in `logseq/config.edn` also stay hidden in editors and rendered property lists. Editing or clearing the visible text keeps the original hidden property lines in the file, in Markdown and Org. Use **Properties…** to change or remove hidden values; heading and block colour also have their own block-menu controls. Ordinary `title`, `icon`, `filters`, `logseq.color` and `logseq.table.*` lines remain visible while editing.

**Page and block properties** are editable from a form, not only as raw `key:: value` lines: use **Page properties…** in the page menu (or `/page properties` while editing), or right-click a block for **Properties…**. The form lists every property the page or block really has; a page's form always offers Aliases, Tags, Display title, Icon and Public. Any other property can be changed or removed, and **Add a property** takes any key you like — it does not have to be plain ASCII. `id::`, `collapsed::` and `tine.` keys keep their own surfaces. Markdown writes `key:: value`, an Org page a `#+key: value` directive, and an Org block its `:PROPERTIES:` drawer. A read-only page offers no property editing at all.

When you open that graph in the app, `serve` finishes admitted work, stops and hands over ownership. The app shows **Finishing the command line's work on this graph…** while it waits. If the handover has not finished after 60 seconds, opening fails and names `tine serve GRAPH --stop`; the app does not take ownership on a timeout. Read commands retry through a busy handover for up to 30 seconds.

**If Tine crashes or quits while a page cannot be saved,** that page's unsaved text is kept in Tine's app data (never in your graph). On the next start Tine puts it back on the page and saves it, and a message names those pages: “Recovered unsaved edits … — Tine is saving them”. If the file changed on disk in the meantime, the page shows the changed-on-disk banner instead (see [[Reference/Troubleshooting and recovery]]), so nothing is written over unseen. Text that saved normally is not kept there. Crash-recovery copies from an older Tine are left untouched as a backup; a message names their file once.

Each snapshot is one ordinary `.zip` file (snapshots from an older Tine are folders; see below). You can open it with your system's archive tool, without Tine: inside, every file sits at its path in your graph (`pages/…`, `journals/…`, `logseq/config.edn`, asset sidecars under `assets/`), next to `tine-backup.json`, the list Tine checks the zip against. Snapshot names start with the date and time they were taken, in UTC. To get back a single page by hand, copy it out of the zip into your graph; Tine picks it up like any external change.

Settings → **Graph** → **Export HTML and read-only app…** exports your `public:: true` pages as a standalone site. Give the export a name and choose a destination folder outside the graph; tick **Include every page not marked public:: false** to export pages that carry no `public::` property as well. A page marked `public:: false` is never exported, not even with that box ticked or with `:publishing/all-pages-public? true` in `config.edn`, and its blocks never appear in another page's embeds, queries or references. A graph with no `public:: true` page exports 0 pages, and the result line says that only `public:: true` pages are exported. Nothing is uploaded, and your graph is not touched.

**Export…** in a query's header exports the pages its results live on as a standalone site. Pages marked `public:: false` and the exports page stay out even when the query matches them; the review lists what was left out and says when the export includes the page the query is written on. Readers see the pages, not the query itself, unless you tick **Include the query text**. Review the page list first; Tine writes the export to `published-queries/<folder>/` inside your graph. If that folder exists, choose **Replace** (the previous export is kept in recovery and its path is reported) or **Create a separate export**. A query about blocks exports **whole pages**, not just the matched blocks, and the dialog asks you to confirm that.

A query export carries referenced local assets in its own `assets/` folder, so you can move or share the whole export folder. Missing assets are reported as warnings. Settings → **Graph** → **Query export size limit** sets the copied-asset budget for this device (default **1 GiB**). An export that exceeds it stops before replacing any previous export, with **Adjust limit in Settings…** to raise it.

Sheets on an exported page (tables, boards and grids) come out as the same tables, boards and grids you see in the app, including formula columns, filters and aggregate footers: Tine computes them with the app's own sheet code before it writes the export, in **Export HTML and read-only app…**, a query's **Export…** and **Export to PDF…** alike. The command-line export (`tine export static` or `tine export live`) has no app to compute them, so it writes a sheet as the plain outline of its rows. A sheet that cannot be computed, or that changed while the export was being prepared, is written the same way with a visible note, and the export still succeeds. A table or board that shows a query's results is written the same way — the query's own columns and its rows on the page they came from — when the block holds just that one query; a result on a page the export does not publish is left out of the table (and of its counts and totals), and if the results changed while the export was being prepared the block is written as the query's usual result list instead. A query table's exported totals summarize only the rows it exports, so they can differ from the live footer's totals over the query's complete sample.

Right-click a page title → **Export to PDF…** prints one page on a light background. It is offered on desktop only: printing is unavailable inside a mobile WebView, so Android and iOS do not show it. **Export HTML and read-only app…** works on every platform.

To find HTML export quickly, open the command palette and run **Export graph as HTML and read-only app…**; it opens the same Graph settings export control. The folder picker starts at your last successful export destination on this device. The result shows the exported site's path; on desktop, **Show in folder** reveals it in the file manager. Mobile keeps its existing folder picker behaviour and does not offer the desktop reveal action.

**Copy / export as…** on a block or page offers **Plain text** (without formatting markers) or **Markdown** / **Org** (with formatting preserved), then Text / OPML / HTML destinations with cleanup and depth controls. Markdown, Org, HTML and OPML resolve block references and expand page and block embeds, without adding source captions. Embedded outlines keep their children; expansion stops after five nested embeds. Internal properties such as `id::` are hidden. Text exports keep user properties as `key:: value` unless **Remove properties** is selected; page properties are omitted.

Settings → **Journals** → **New-journal template** inserts a template into each new day (`:default-templates {:journals …}` in `config.edn`); “(none)” means blank days, the default. Make a template from a block's right-click menu (**Make a template…**). A page can be a template too: put `template:: Name` among the page's own property lines at its top (the lines before the first bullet), and `/Name` inserts those property lines (without `template::`) as one block, as in Logseq.

**Today's sections page.** To choose what shows under today's journal without editing `config.edn`, hover today's journal and click **Customize today's sections…**. Tine creates a page named *Journal sections* (marked `tine.journal-sections:: true`) holding your current sections: each `:default-queries` entry as a `#+BEGIN_QUERY` block, then the Scheduled & Deadline agenda as a query block. The generated page does not include Upcoming. Today's journal shows query blocks and the Upcoming macro in outline order, including nested blocks; reorder, edit, delete or add them like on any page, and the change shows on today's journal at once. Supported sections are `{{query …}}`, `{{tine-query …}}`, `#+BEGIN_QUERY` blocks, the agenda query seeded by Customize, and `{{upcoming}}`. Other text on the page is just notes. The page can be renamed; the marker is what counts. Delete the page, or set the marker to `false`, to go back to `config.edn`, with Upcoming hidden. Logseq ignores the page and keeps using `:default-queries`, and Tine never writes to `config.edn` for this. While the page exists, the Agenda window setting no longer applies: edit the agenda query on the page instead. The small header on this page opens this Guide in the right sidebar. On ordinary pages, `{{upcoming}}` remains an unknown macro.

To set an icon without knowing the property syntax, open **Page actions** (the ⋯ beside the title), then **Set page icon…** below **Page properties…**. Enter an emoji or short text such as `AB`, then press Enter or **Save icon**. On Windows, Win + . opens the native emoji picker; on macOS, use Control + Command + Space. **Remove page icon** clears it. Icons in the sidebar lists follow edits immediately, including external file changes. Markdown stores `tine.icon::`; Org stores `#+tine.icon:` through the same page-property editor. A page that only has `icon::` is edited in place, and **Remove page icon** clears both properties.

A labelled page link such as [read the welcome]([[Welcome to Tine]]) shows your words while opening the page. External `[label](https://…)` links are ordinary Markdown, bare URLs and emails autolink, and **Mod+L** inserts a link around the selection. `http`, `https` and `mailto` links open in your browser or mail app. A `file:` link — `[Test](file:///home/you/report.odt)`, or `[Test](file://D:\test.txt)` on Windows — opens that file or folder in whatever application your system uses for it, on desktop; a file that is no longer there is reported instead of doing nothing. A file path is read from the graph folder, from any page or journal: `[report](files/report.pdf)` opens `files/report.pdf` inside the graph, while `[report](../files/report.pdf)` opens a file in the sibling `files` folder outside the graph. Parent steps such as `../../` are preserved. Absolute paths such as `/home/you/report.pdf` and `D:\notes\report.pdf` also open through the same desktop file opener as `file:` links. These links look ordinary and show the resolved path on hover. Use `[spaced](<../files/my file.txt>)` for spaces. Links into the graph's assets folder keep Logseq's established graph asset route. Opening local files is available on desktop only, including for `file:` URLs; Android and iOS report the refusal. Tine does not rewrite links when you move files or graphs. A link to another app, such as `zotero://…`, `obsidian://…` or `shortcuts://…` on iOS, first asks whether to open it, showing the whole link, and then opens it in that app. `javascript:` and `data:` links never open.

Properties are the `key:: value` lines at the top of a page and under a block's first line, and every one of them is editable from a form — not only by typing raw lines. Click **Page actions** beside a page's title (or right-click the title) and choose **Page properties…**, or type `/page properties` while editing; right-click a block for **Properties…**. The form lists the properties that page or block really has. Page properties always stay at the top of their page: moving or dragging a block above them, or pressing Tab on the block right under them, does nothing and shows a short notice saying so.

Hover a page link or block reference for a preview of its blocks. The preview opens after a one-second pause and closes a moment after the pointer leaves, as in Logseq. It stops at 600 pixels or half the window, whichever is taller (never more than the window), and scrolls inside, and shows code blocks, callouts, quotes and folds the way the page does: a block the page keeps folded shows its closed bullet. Its arrow folds or unfolds the source block, saving the same `collapsed::` property as the page; the preview and an open page stay in step, and Undo restores both. If the source cannot be written or has no source block, the fold stays local to the preview. An alias shows its source page's title and page properties. Click the title to open that page in a new tab, a block bullet to open that block in a new tab, or **Open source** to open the preview's source. These actions switch to the new tab. The preview stays open while its **… → Page actions** menu is open. The blocks in a preview are the page's own blocks, as in Logseq: click a block's text to edit it right there, and the change is saved to its page. While you edit, the preview stays open even when the pointer leaves it or the page scrolls; the first **Esc** ends the edit and the next one closes the preview. Inside a preview a query shows as its text and an embed is read-only; open the source to use them. A block reference's preview also offers **Edit link** and **Remove** for that one reference, as described below.

**Ctrl+K**, the quick switcher, searches page titles plus the visible text of blocks. Sections are Pages, Create, Commands, Blocks and — inside a page — Current page; with an empty query it lists recent pages. **Enter** opens the highlighted result; **Shift+Enter** opens it in the right sidebar; **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter** opens it in a background tab and keeps the switcher open; **Alt+Enter** opens it in another pane; middle-click opens a background tab. **Load more results…** appears when more are available.

Search scans your loaded graph text directly, so results are always current with your own edits; while it works the switcher says **Searching…**, an empty answer says **No matched results**, and **More matches exist — narrow your query to see them.** means the list was cut short.

**Open search tab** in the switcher footer turns the current search into a graph-scoped search tab titled "Search: …" with its own search box. The tab survives restarts and writes nothing to your graph until you name it. Clicking a result opens a new tab and keeps Search unchanged; if you would rather a plain click or **Enter** open the result in the Search tab itself, with **Back** returning to the results, choose **This tab** in **Settings → Editor → Advanced → Search results open in** (**New tab** is the default, saved on this device). Middle-click or Ctrl/Cmd-click opens a background tab; Shift-click opens the right sidebar and Alt-click opens another pane. Page results offer the same right-click menu as the switcher.
A query that asks about pages rather than blocks — `(page-property …)`, `(page-tags …)`, `(namespace …)` — lists the pages themselves.

**Long-press a page reference or tag to preview its page** without navigating away. Choose the **…** button in the preview header for **Page actions**, the same menu offered by a desktop right-click. Tap outside the preview to dismiss it; a quick tap still follows the link. Other links keep their long-press context menu, and holding ordinary text keeps the system's text selection and selection toolbar.

Shared items follow Logseq's mobile rules for each platform. On Android a link becomes a titled link, YouTube and similar video links become `{{video …}}`, posts on X or Twitter become `{{twitter …}}`, and text highlighted in a browser goes before its link. On iOS the shared text is kept as it is and the link follows it unchanged, as Logseq's iOS share does. Images follow as asset links, one per line.

The same destinations open from `tine://today`, `tine://capture`, `tine://search?q=…` and `tine://page/<name>` (a page of the open graph). Each one only opens something in Tine and never writes to your graph.

Tine reads Logseq's query syntax — `{{query …}}` blocks and the common advanced (datalog) queries — but runs them on its own engine, not on a datalog database. This page lists every place where the answer can differ from Logseq's, and why. How to write and display queries is on [[Features/Queries]].
**`(sort-by …)` knows built-in fields**: priority, page, scheduled and deadline as well as any property. Logseq sorts only by a property of that name.

**Tine-only features** (scheduled and deadline ranges, grouping, totals, typed comparisons, inline-tag and parent, child or descendant conditions, a bare has-a-scheduled-date or has-a-deadline check, `search`, `content-regex`) have no equivalent `{{query}}` spelling. Saving one turns the block into `{{tine-query …}}`, says so, and offers **Undo that change**. For example, `{{tine-query @block scheduled between today and '+7d'}}` checks a scheduled date; OG Logseq drops the condition in `(between scheduled …)` or `(between deadline …)`.

Tine 0.6 differs from this page where it has known bugs, fixed in Beta: it sorts ascending by default; `(sample N)` sorts first; a query of only directives returns everything; `(namespace x)` matches every depth; `(all-page-tags)` returns the tagged pages; `not` with several operands, `(priority [A])`, `(between created-at …)` and page-header properties misbehave; journal groups run oldest first; an advanced query with an unknown clause runs the clauses it understands; query text ignores case and accents; every property value is split on commas; Logseq's table settings are ignored.

2. Review the report, then choose **Copy report** (or **Save report…** on desktop). Nothing is uploaded automatically. The recorder excludes graph content, paths, page titles, queries, URLs, credentials, and the opt-in detailed debug log.
2. What you should see: the button reads **Rescanning…** while it works, then **Last rescan finished at** followed by the time. Create a diagnostic report afterwards to see how long that rescan took.
2. On one device choose **Copy graph report** (or **Save graph report…** on desktop) and paste it into the box **Report from the other device** on the other, then choose **Compare reports**.

2. Later, use the graph-name menu at the top of the left sidebar → **Open graph…**, or Settings (**t s**) → **Graph** → **Open another graph…**. Graphs you have opened appear in the same sidebar menu for one-click switching.

Use **Up/Down** to choose a graph, **Home/End** to reach the first or last, and **Enter** to open it in this window. On desktop, **Shift+Enter** opens it in a new window. **Tab** reaches each graph's actions, including **Remove from this list**, which leaves its files untouched, plus **Open graph…** and **New graph…**.
Choose **Create a new graph** on Welcome, or **New graph…** in the sidebar graph menu. Choose its parent folder on desktop or iOS; Android uses its default graph location.

On Windows, use `\\wsl.localhost\<distro>\…` for a graph in WSL: Windows access through a distro package's `LocalState\rootfs` can corrupt Linux files, so Tine refuses new graphs there and warns when opening an existing one.

At the very top sits the workspace switcher — saved window layouts, covered in [[Workflows/Keep context visible]]. Just under it, the graph-name menu switches between the graphs Tine knows, with **Open graph…** and **New graph…** beside them — on desktop, Shift-click a graph row to open it in a second window instead of switching this one. Right-click a row for the same thing as a menu item — **Open in a new window** — along with **Open here**, **Show in folder**, **Copy path**, and **Remove from this list**. The row for the graph you already have open shows the two open actions greyed out, so the menu keeps its shape wherever you click.

1. With the caret anywhere in a bullet, press **Ctrl+Enter** (Cmd on Mac). The bullet becomes `TODO …`; press again for `DOING`, again for `DONE`, once more to drop the marker. (Under the NOW / LATER workflow — the default — the cycle is LATER → NOW → DONE.)
2. Look for a `var(--tine-…)` or `var(--ls-…)` in the rule that draws what you want to change. Setting that variable in `custom.css` is the stable way to change it.

4. Developing or sideloading instead? **Install a local package** (under **Browse**, button **Choose package…**) takes a `manifest.json` and its `.wasm` file together — with the same installed-disabled rule.

What you should see: exactly the contribution the plugin declared — a command-palette entry, a slash command, or a decoration — and nothing else. If the package does not support your device, its button reads **Unavailable on …** instead of Install.

A plugin that declares settings gets a **Settings** section on its details page (**Settings…** beside it in the **Installed** list), but Tine draws the controls — toggles, dropdowns, numbers, text — from the plugin's declared schema. Values are validated scalars, **stored on this device only** and never written into your graph. A changed key offers **Reset**; **Reset all settings** restores the schema defaults.
**Uninstall…** removes only that package version from this device. Tine asks first and states the boundary: it removes the plugin from this device and does not change your graph or notes.

Themes live separately under Settings → **Appearance**. **Style** controls typography, journal headings, and other Tine-owned presentation styles; **Color scheme** selects Default, Nord, Solarized, Gruvbox, Soft, or the colors from an installed package. Style and colors are independent, so you can keep one package's style while using another palette. Declarative packages install from the **Theme packages** list or a local `theme.json` file (**Choose theme.json…**) and contain no scripts, selectors, imports, font files, or remote assets. The choices stay on this device, and no theme ever reads or writes your graph.

2. Too many hits? Narrow with the **Search syntax** forms listed in the switcher footer: `-draft` excludes a word, `OR` offers alternatives, quotes pin an exact phrase, `/…/` is a case-sensitive regular expression.

The `((` picker says **Searching blocks…** while reading, offers **Retry** if the read fails, and says **No matched blocks** only after a successful empty search. Retry keeps your text; **Escape** closes the picker.

2. Open **⋯ → Edit** for the inline builder: **Find blocks ▾ where …** and one row per condition. **+ Add condition** adds one. The real results remain below the editor as your live preview. An empty new query asks you to add a condition.

3. Both **+ Add condition** and a row's `field ▾` open the same list, and that list is your graph: the built-in fields first, then every property key you actually use, each with the type Tine has observed. Type to narrow it. A key the list does not already show is offered by name at the bottom — **Use "…" as a block property** and, on a block query, **Use "…" as a page property** — so a key the graph does not have yet, and a key it has only on pages, both stay writable.

8. That list of your graph's own keys is one read Tine makes when the sheet opens. While it is still reading, the list says **Reading this graph's properties…** and the built-in fields below it stay usable. If that read fails instead, the list says what failed and offers **Try again**.

3. The vocabulary, in full. On a block row: `content`, `task`, `priority`, `scheduled`, `deadline`. On a page row: `name`, `journal`, `namespace`. `[[Page name]]` and `#tag` are page references; `prop('key')` is a property; `page.name` reaches the block's own page. The comparisons are `=`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `like` (with `%` wildcards), `match` (full-text), `between … and …`, `in (…)`, and `is null` / `is not null`.

4. Three forms are Tine's own. `any(children, …)` and `every(prop('tags'), …)` ask about the things a row contains — a block's children, a page's blocks, a key's values. `off(…)`, or a line beginning `-- `, keeps a condition in the query without running it. And `tag('x')` and `page_tag('x')` spell out what `#x` means on each kind of row.

1. A property key means more when Tine knows what its values ARE. Open a property in **Edit as visual query** and Tine names the type it has observed across your graph — `text`, `number`, `date`, `checkbox`, or `ref` (a page link) — and says `list of …` when the key normally holds several values at once.

2. Observation can be wrong, and an empty key has nothing to observe. Choose **declare type…** on the property and pick the type yourself; tick **list of** when the key is meant to hold several values. The declared type is then the one Tine uses.

4. The type decides which comparisons you are offered: `is` and `is not` for a checkbox or a page link, `before`, `after` and `between` for a date, `<`, `≤`, `>`, `≥` for a number, `contains` and `starts with` for text. On a `list of …` key the equality operator reads `contains this value`, because the test is against the list.

A hand-written advanced query stays editable as text. A `{{query {:query …}}}` or `#+BEGIN_QUERY` block runs only when Tine can read every clause of it; otherwise it is refused whole ("Advanced (datalog) query not run") and the notice names the clauses Tine could not run, rather than show a wider answer than you asked for.

5. From the keyboard, **Ctrl+1** … **Ctrl+9** focus panes in reading order, **Ctrl+Alt+←↑↓→** moves focus to the nearest pane in that direction, and **Ctrl+Alt+Shift+←↑↓→** moves the active tab there instead.

1. With the layout where you want it — splits, every pane's tabs and histories, both sidebars — click the workspace name at the top of the left sidebar and choose **+ New workspace**, or run **New workspace…** from the command palette (**Mod+Shift+P**); name it once.

1. Click the highlight and choose **Copy ref**, then paste into any bullet in your own notes. The pasted `((…))` renders as link-styled text quoting the highlighted passage, and clicking the quote opens the document at that page.

1. From the notes page title's right-click menu: **Copy / export as…** offers Markdown and rendered copies, and **Export to PDF…** (desktop only) opens print options and then your OS print dialog — choose **Save as PDF**. The page always prints on a light background, whatever your theme.

2. Publishing on the web? Pages marked `public:: true` go into the static export: Settings → **Graph** → **Export HTML and read-only app…** asks for a folder outside your graph. To share just one reading list or project, press **Export…** on a query: you review the pages its results live on, and Tine writes a standalone site in `published-queries/<folder>/` inside the graph. A colliding folder offers Replace (with the previous export kept in recovery) or a separate export, and copied local assets travel with the folder. A query about blocks exports **whole pages**, not just the matched blocks, and the dialog asks you to confirm that. Nothing is uploaded.

The exact highlight, merge, and storage rules are mapped in [[Features/PDF annotation]]. For quoting anything else with `((…))` and the reference panels, see [[Workflows/Find and revisit]]; for snapshots and backups, [[Reference/Files, external edits, and backups]].

2. Choose **Open search tab**. There, choose **Filters / Advanced**, then **Edit as visual query**. The query reads as one sentence — *Blocks where …* — over a sheet of conditions; use **+ Add condition** → **Property** to choose Owner and the value Avery.
